New findings suggest that "food challenges" can help prevent children from being saddled with unnecessary allergy diagnoses.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A peanut allergy diagnosis in infancy can mean years of avoiding the food or undergoing treatments to build tolerance. But a recent study suggests that more than one-third of babies thought to have the allergy may stop reacting badly to peanuts within months of that diagnosis.

In an analysis published in The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice, researchers conducted supervised "food challenges" with infants diagnosed with a peanut allergy. These challenges involved giving the babies increasing amounts of peanut protein, with the intention of confirming whether they indeed had an allergy.

The team found that more than 1 in 3 infants who underwent the food challenge tolerated the peanut protein, meaning they didn't experience symptoms of an allergic reaction.

"This rate is much higher than we thought," study co-author Dr. Timothy Brettig, a pediatric allergist at the National Allergy Centre of Excellence in Australia, told Live Science.

Between April 2024 and October 2025, Brettig and colleagues retroactively reviewed the medical records of 1,275 infants who had been referred to Australian public hospitals after having a reaction to peanuts before their first birthday. These babies had first been assessed by allergy specialists at a median of 10 months of age.

For their initial diagnosis, the babies had to have a history of an allergic reaction to peanuts and show evidence of peanut sensitization on an allergy test. These tests included a skin-prick test, in which peanut extract is placed on the skin before it's lightly pricked, to check for a local reaction; and blood tests that detect antibodies against peanut proteins.

"Children under 1 year of age are an interesting group, as their immune system is still in rapid development and existing allergy tests may not reflect their allergic status well," said Dr. Alexandra Santos, a professor of pediatric allergy at King's College London who was not involved in the study. While these tests can hint that a child is sensitized to certain foods, they don't necessarily confirm that a baby will have an allergic reaction upon eating said food; the tests can also give false positives.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Of the 1,275 infants, 778 later underwent a food challenge roughly six months after their first recorded allergic reaction; at that point, their median age was 13 months old. They were given up to seven gradually increasing doses of peanut protein, ranging from 15 to 1,300 milligrams. These doses were given at 15-minute intervals while medical staff monitored the children for signs of an allergic reaction.

Nearly 35% of the participants — 271 kids — completed the challenge without reacting.

"This is an excellent article," said Dr. Drew Bird, a pediatric allergist at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center who was not involved in the study. "The take-home message is to strongly consider a supervised oral food challenge when an infant's peanut allergy diagnosis is uncertain."

Bird emphasized that these challenges should ideally be done before a child starts oral immunotherapy, a treatment in which patients regularly consume carefully measured amounts of the food they are allergic to. The dose is gradually increased under medical supervision, with the goal of helping the patient tolerate greater amounts of the allergen and reducing the risk of reactions from accidental exposure.

An incorrect diagnosis can prompt families to unnecessarily avoid exposing their children to peanuts.

The starting dose is often determined through a similar oral food challenge to the one used in this study, though. So in theory, that challenge would help reveal whether the child needs treatment in the first place.

Bird cautioned that food challenges should be performed by a board-certified allergist-immunologist and an experienced allergy team in a setting equipped to treat anaphylaxis — a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction.

In this study, 507 infants reacted during the food challenge, and of those, 61 developed anaphylaxis and were treated with epinephrine (the hormone in EpiPens).

"In an ideal world, with infinite resources," Santos said, "all patients except for those with a history of severe reactions would have a food challenge for diagnosis."

Because that is not the case, the families of infants whose allergy diagnosis is uncertain may be advised to avoid peanut products while they await a formal food challenge, she noted. But in the interim, they may miss an opportunity to help the child develop tolerance and, in turn, increase the risk that their allergy will persist.

Food challenges should be prioritized for infants whose allergy diagnoses are uncertain, she said. This would include babies who have low levels of peanut-specific antibodies in their blood or who show only small welts on skin-prick tests.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6396. A New Iron Age? Scientists Uncover a Potential Game Changer for Clean Energy

Scientists are exploring how iron powder could transform renewable energy storage and transportation while giving aging coal power plants a new purpose.

Iron powder could help transform old coal power plants into a source of climate-neutral electricity, according to a new study from the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT). Researchers found that this recyclable fuel could help keep Europe’s power supply stable during extended periods of weak wind and sunlight, particularly in regions where other forms of energy storage are limited.

The process relies on a cycle in which iron powder is burned to generate heat, producing iron oxide, commonly known as rust. Hydrogen produced using renewable energy can then remove the oxygen from the iron oxide, restoring the metal so it can be used again. “This works in a cycle that emits no carbon dioxide or environmentally harmful substances,” said Julia Schuler from KIT’s Institute for Industrial Production (IIP).

One potential advantage is that iron powder could be used in existing coal power plants without replacing all their equipment. “When burned, iron powder behaves very much like coal. We wanted to find out whether it was possible to repurpose existing coal power plants to iron-firing,” said Schuler.

According to Schuler, most modifications would involve the equipment responsible for generating heat. Other major components, including steam turbines, generators, and connections to the electricity grid, could remain in service. Germany may be particularly well suited to this approach because of its large fleet of coal power plants and the possibility of retaining existing heating networks and other infrastructure.

Iron powder could also provide a practical way to move renewable energy across long distances. Electricity generated by coastal wind farms or solar facilities in desert regions could be used to produce hydrogen, which would convert iron oxide into iron. The resulting powder could then be transported to another location and burned to recover the stored energy.

Unlike hydrogen, which requires specialized pipelines, import terminals, and underground storage facilities, iron powder is relatively straightforward to transport and store for extended periods. This could reduce the infrastructure investment needed to move renewable energy between regions. Surplus renewable electricity generated within Europe could also be used to regenerate iron locally through an intermediate hydrogen production step.

To investigate the technology’s potential, KIT scientists built on findings from the Clean Circles research project. In a study funded by Stiftung Energieforschung Baden-Württemberg (Baden-Württemberg energy-research foundation), they expanded the established PERSEUS energy model to include iron-fueled power plants, facilities for regenerating iron, and the infrastructure needed for storage and transportation.

The researchers then simulated the development of a climate-neutral European energy system through 2050, comparing iron with competing technologies such as batteries, hydrogen storage, and hydrogen power plants. Iron-fired power plants appeared in the lowest-cost energy system across every scenario examined, although the results did not suggest that iron would replace hydrogen.

The greatest benefits emerged in countries with limited hydropower resources or few suitable locations for underground hydrogen storage. In these regions, iron could help maintain electricity supplies during prolonged shortages of wind and solar generation. It could also reduce demand on hydrogen pipelines and import facilities when their capacity becomes constrained.

“Iron might play a very special, but economically meaningful role for reaching climate-neutrality and in reliably making renewables available,” said Schuler.

Whether a new “iron age” emerges in electricity generation will depend largely on two unresolved technical and economic questions: how extensively existing coal power plants must be modified and how efficiently iron oxide can be converted back into reusable iron. The simulations indicate that iron could complement hydrogen in a climate-neutral energy system, but its practical competitiveness will depend on how these processes perform outside the model.

Reference: “A new iron age? The potential role of iron fuel in Europe’s clean energy transition” by Julia Schuler, Armin Ardone, Viktor Slednev and Wolf Fichtner, 8 June 2026, Chem Circularity. DOI: 10.1016/j.checir.2026.100047

Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.Follow us on Google and Google News.

The weakest links in this proposal for eliminating CO2 are mining, beneficiating the ore, pelletizing, smelting, and then converting the iron to powder. Next is transporting the burned iron to the hydrogen facility, crushing to make a powder, and then back to the burner. Make no mistake, these are energy intensive operations. Where is that energy going to come from?

#6395. A new telescope in Chile found two more stable Neptune trojans in just its first three weeks

Rubin Observatory's test survey spotted 2025 MH348 and 2025 NN80, doubling the known stable Neptune trojans in the trailing cloud from two to four.

On June 21, 2025, the camera of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory picked up two faint moving objects. A new test survey on Cerro Pachón in Chile had begun just one day earlier.

One of them got the designation 2025 MH348. It orbits the Sun at about 30 times Earth’s distance. It also belongs to the trailing group of Neptune trojans, small icy bodies that ride behind the planet.

Meg Schwamb of Queen’s University Belfast and 14 co-authors now report two confirmed members of that group and one candidate.

Before this, only two long-lived trailing trojans were on the books. Still, the team says its sample is too small to estimate how many exist.

Neptune trojans move on Neptune’s orbit in two swarms. One sits about 60 degrees ahead of the planet, at a Lagrange point called L4, and the other sits 60 degrees behind it, at L5.

By the time the authors wrote the paper, surveys had found over 30 Neptune trojans. However, most of what astronomers know about them comes from L4.

Seen from Earth, L5 sat on or close to the Galactic center for more than 15 years. Fields less than 10 degrees from the Galactic plane teem with stars. The paper says that high stellar density “significantly hindered” the discovery of trailing trojans.

By 2025 a large swath of the L5 cloud had come out of the Galactic plane. Then Rubin’s test fields covered part of it by chance, even though their designers had not aimed them at Neptune trojans.

According to the paper, trojans on orbits stable for billions of years are primordial, not recent arrivals. So their sizes, colors, spin rates and orbits carry information about the disk of planetesimals Neptune migrated through.

For every known Neptune trojan, the Minor Planet Center lists about 450 trojans of Jupiter, even though earlier surveys estimate the Neptune population is 4 to 10 times larger.

Rubin’s Science Validation survey started on June 20, 2025. It took 30-second exposures in six filters and imaged its fields every night, instead of every three or four nights as in the main survey, and covered about 3,000 square degrees near the ecliptic over the commissioning window.

The Simonyi Survey Telescope has an 8.4-meter (27.6-foot) mirror and a 3.2-gigapixel camera with a 9.6-square-degree field of view. The authors wrote that this makes Rubin “an ideal discovery machine” for the region.

2025 MH348 and the candidate 2025 MD138 turned up on UT June 21, 2025, and 2025 NN80 on UT July 7.

The searches used Rubin’s Solar System Processing pipeline with two codes, an expanded version of HelioLinC and a newer program called pointdexter, developed by Matt Holman and Kevin Napier to look for distant moving objects.

The detections were reported to the Minor Planet Center in February 2026. Users of the Minor Planet Mailing List, an online group of amateur and professional asteroid observers, then flagged the three as possible L5 trojans, and the paper credits those discussions with helping inspire the work.

Afterward, astronomers linked older detections by the Pan-STARRS1 telescope in Hawaii to 2025 MH348 and 2025 NN80. That allowed orbit fits over several oppositions. The data arc for 2025 MH348 grew to 2,595 days and for 2025 NN80 to 1,547 days.

The team took orbits from NASA JPL’s Small-Body Database, dated June 5, 2026. It ran them in the Small Body Dynamics Tool, with the Sun and the four giant planets pulling on each object.

For each body it also drew 100 clones from the JPL covariance matrix, which gives orbits nudged within the measurement errors, and ran high-resolution 10-million-year integrations before extending them to 1 billion years.

All 100 clones of 2025 MH348 and all 100 of 2025 NN80 were still in step with Neptune at 1 billion years. JPL lists their orbital periods at about 164 years, the same as Neptune’s.

The two older stable L5 trojans are 2008 LC18 and 2011 HM102. Scott Sheppard and Chad Trujillo reported 2008 LC18 in 2010. With the Rubin pair added, the list of trailing trojans on gigayear-stable orbits has four names.

Each of the four has an inclination above 25 degrees (28.7 and 29.7 degrees for the new pair), which fits earlier models in which trojan stability peaks near 30 degrees and again below 10 degrees.

Rubin measured the objects in the g, r, i and z filters. 2025 NN80 had 32 measurements, 2025 MH348 had 11 and 2025 MD138 had 15.

The new three are bluer than the two L5 trojans measured in a 2023 study. Put together with the earlier pair, the L5 colors fall in the same locus as the L4 swarm. The authors take that as further support for a single parent population.

A spectrum-reconstruction model matched all three to a water-ice spectral type that is common among Neptune trojans. The paper calls this a probabilistic assignment and says it does not replace near-infrared spectra.

Co-authors work in São Paulo, Tucson, Seattle, Ann Arbor and Belfast. The authors thank Breakthrough Listen and Queen’s University Belfast for supporting the LSST solar system First Data Sprint.

2025 MD138 remains a candidate because its 38 days of Rubin observations leave large error bars on its distance and orbit shape.

Its best-fit orbit stays stable for a billion years. Of its 100 clones, 36 behaved like trojans over 10 million years and 23 lasted to 1 billion.

Its inclination is about 6 degrees, and all 23 surviving clones kept that low tilt. If follow-up confirms it, it would be the first known long-lived L5 trojan on a low-tilt orbit.

There is no population estimate in the paper either. Rubin has not yet published how efficient its early moving-object search was. So the authors did not compare their haul with predicted numbers.

Rubin started its 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time at the end of June 2026. Rain and snow on Cerro Pachón halted it in mid-July. Science work was due to resume in early southern spring, after a planned engineering shutdown.

The observatory released its first images of the sky in June 2025, and by April 2026 its early data had produced more than 11,000 newly discovered asteroids. The decade-long survey of the southern sky covers nearly all the area where L5 trojans should be.

Co-author Joseph Murtagh, of the University of Washington, led a 2026 study. It predicts that the survey will quadruple the known Neptune trojans. It expects tens to hundreds in the trailing swarm, most of them in the first two years.

Other bodies have been found moving in step with Neptune farther out, and a second trojan sharing Earth’s orbit was confirmed in 2022.

The authors describe the three objects as “the tip of the iceberg” for the Neptune trojan science Rubin will enable. Sixteen years after astronomers reported the first L5 trojan, the count of long-lived ones stands at four. Two of them came from Rubin’s first weeks of testing.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#6394. The 8 Best Air Purifiers for Your Home

Whether you’re dealing with smoke or pet dander, these are the most effective (and affordable) models we stand behind based on testing and research.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Clean indoor air has become more important than ever. While allergens like dust, dander, mold, and bacteria are all teaming up to infiltrate the air you breathe, the widespread wildfire smoke affecting much of the U.S. right now is also proving just how quickly outdoor pollution can make its way inside. According to the EPA, Americans spend about 90 percent of their time indoors, where pollutant concentrations can sometimes be even higher than they are outside. An air purifier protects your airways from airborne irritants while providing clean, fresh air indoors (which is why we think everyone should invest in an air purifier).

We got our hands on air purifiers from brands like Coway, Levoit, and GermGuardian and put them to the test. Filtration was our main concern, so we could determine the air purifiers’ efficiency. Then we moved along to other factors such as noise while running, how well they work in a given room, and convenience features. After our in-home testing, these are the air purifiers that came out on top.

We tried out several air purifiers with a range of filtration systems, noise levels, and features. We tested these models in multiple different apartments, placing them in various rooms of the home to measure their efficiency. We considered the different uses of an air purifier, like if you’re an allergy sufferer or have a home filled with furry friends, and tested special features like light-up displays and automatic shutoff to determine their ease of use and effectiveness. We considered the amount of time it took to set up the different purifiers and install their filter systems.

For units that we haven’t tested, we combed through dozens of potential products and their specifications, reviews, and user complaints to identify what we thought were the best air purifiers. We settled on the following list, which includes options that are budget-friendly, sleekly designed, and high-performing.

The Airmega Mighty2 is the latest version of our previous Best Overall pick, the Coway AP-1512HH. The newest model combines power, quality filters, and robust controls to help you breathe easier.

The Mighty2 uses a three-stage filtration system to capture 99.7 percent of airborne particles, and cleans spaces up to 1,800 square feet in 60 minutes. It has three standard fan speeds, but there’s a turbo mode that will kick on if there’s a big uptick of matter in the air.

The original version just used an indicator light system that let you know basic air quality levels, but this updated model has a built-in air quality index sensor that measures and displays particulate matter counts in real time.

Our tester tried the air purifier in his New York apartment, putting it up against pet odors, litterbox dust, and other household allergens. “Results after about a day were already noticeable. The air in the room seemed clearer and there was less dust on the ground in the area immediately around the litterbox. Not enough that I’m going to have to sweep up any less, mind you, but there was a material difference that I wasn’t getting from using a smaller purifier.”

Full Coway Airmega Mighty2 Air Purifier Review

This air purifier from Clorox uses a three-stage filtration system to trap allergens, pollutants, and VOCs, and it successfully cleared strong scents and odors from the apartment we tested in.

It was quiet enough that you hardly hear it activate, especially if it kicks on automatically while you’re cooking to clear the kitchen of smoke. But on higher settings, you do tend to notice its noise a bit more. The 360-degree, cylindrical shape of the filter offers purification from all directions, and the unit covers 1,000 square feet so you don't have to be as strategic about placement.

We also liked that it has a color-coded indicator light on the front that tells you how hazardous the air is in the room where it's located (though it will add insult to injury when it turns purple while you’re trying your best to sear a steak.)

If you’re a pet owner, specifically with cats, then you know that the litter box smell lingers long after your little fur ball has left the lavatory. The Vital 200S-P from Levoit is a great way to combat the odors that candles and air fresheners just can’t cover up. I set the air purifier up in my living room and noticed a clear improvement in scent after running for the day.

This unit has a traditional air inlet, along with a unique U-shaped inlet that is ideal for trapping pet hair without clogging up the filters. If you pair your air purifier with the app and select Pet Mode, it automatically alternates between fan speeds, too. The pre-filter is easy to remove and wash, so you don't have to purchase replacements as often.

Since we tested the Vital 200S-P in a smaller apartment, it was a bit obtrusive. But the air purifier covers up to 1,875 square feet, so if you live in a townhouse or single-family home, this unit will accommodate.

Full Levoit Vital 200S-P Air Purifier Review

The Airmega 100 is the first cylindrical unit in the Coway line, which is a nice switch-up from the rectangular model that we tested in the past. It tucked nicely into the corner of the living room, and you can change the light between blue, orange, and off, which is ideal if you’re using the purifier in a bedroom.

I tried the fan on various settings, and the lowest mode could barely be heard over the TV playing at an average volume, which aligns with its claimed 20-decibel noise level. You can manually adjust everything on the control panel, or let the purifier do its thing and adapt accordingly as it monitors the air quality of the room.

Setup of the unit was simple; you essentially just need to click the filter into place. This model uses a 3-in-1 filtration system, with a HEPA filter sandwiched between a vacuumable pre-filter and deodorizing filter. The deodorizer layer is especially useful if you have pets, love to cook, or live in an apartment or complex with odors.

Full Coway Airmega 100 Air Purifier Review

For smaller rooms or office spaces, the smart Blueair 511i Max offers much of the same performance and features as larger, more capable models. It only purifies areas of up to 465 square feet, but does so within just 30 minutes on the highest setting. The three-layer filtration system captures up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles, too.

We appreciate that the air quality level is clearly displayed on the front in a five-color scale, and that the display has auto-brightness controls if you're running it overnight while you're sleeping. Advanced features are available through the app, including scheduling and air quality reports.

This unit has a four-stage filtration system, along with Blueair's proprietary HEPASilent filter that uses a combination of electrostatic charge and mechanical filtration to capture 99.97 percent of airborne pollutants and contaminants. This type of filtration technology is less dense than other filter options, so it's designed to run quieter and use less energy.

The value offered by such a small air purifier is unmatched, considering it targets both allergens and odors—all with relatively quiet operation.

If you have a large space or even an entire apartment that needs air purification, the Coway Airmega 400 is the smart model you need. It's designed to cover up to 1,560 square feet in 30 minutes, and has a variety of smart features and sleep settings, all packed into a compact yet capable unit. While this is the most expensive option we recommend, it's relatively affordable considering its capacity, and you shouldn’t have to supplement with an additional air purifier.

It’s surprisingly quiet given its size, reaching only 22 decibels on its lowest setting. We like that it uses multi-stage purification methods, combining a pre-filter, an activated carbon filter, and a True HEPA filter to capture the tiniest of particles. The pre-filter is washable, but the air filter indicator light will let you know when it actually needs to be replaced.

The Airmega 400 has a three-setting smart mode that adapts to its environment, with a fan speed that automatically adjusts based on air quality or lighting conditions. We also appreciate the option to use eco mode, which turns the fan on and off when the room has remained purified for 30 minutes, and there’s also a timer and pollution sensor.

The GermGuardian isn’t a flashy design with robust features, but it aids in keeping the air in my apartment free of pet odors, dust, and smoke.

I have a self-cleaning litter box, which significantly cuts down on smells and dust associated with cat waste, but it doesn’t solve every problem. I let the purifier run during one of the Litter Robot’s cleaning cycles, and thanks to the GermGuardian’s built-in air quality index (AQI) sensor and display screen, I was able to see the particulate matter count in the air reach triple digits in seconds. The automatic fan speed varied as needed, and it wasn’t long before air quality was back to a healthy level.

I put the GermGuardian up against incense smoke, too, and it went to work quickly. The fan had to run at high speed for longer, but by the end, my living room was clear of any lingering haze and odor.

In addition to a HEPA filter and activated carbon, this model also has a UVC light, which is claimed to disinfect bacteria, viruses, and mold. While I did give this feature a try, I didn’t keep it on for long because it’s hard to prove whether these lights are actually useful in an air purifier.

Read Full GermGuardian AC4880B Air Purifier Review

The Sans HEPA 13 air purifier offers quiet operation, whole-home purification, and smart features. This unit runs at only 25 decibels on the lowest fan setting, and I could hardly tell that it was on, even when standing next to the unit.

The air purifier is best used for whole-home use, as it purifies spaces up to 1,854 square feet. The internal sensors monitor and show you the air quality index in real time, and the reading is visible on the touch display. I’m able to view PM2.5, which is particles that are 2.5 microns or smaller, such as dust, smoke, pollen, and pet dander, as well as PM10, which are slightly larger particles up to 10 microns, like coarser dust and mold spores.

This unit pairs a medical-grade HEPA 13 filter with a pre-filter, activated carbon filter, and UV-C light to capture 99.9 percent of particles. This might be overkill for general household use, but I’ve appreciated the multi-stage approach. The only downside I’ve come across is that overall cost will likely be higher, considering the Sans recommends replacing the filter every three months.

There is no shortage of air purifiers on the market, and many of them use a lot of the same tech to achieve better air quality. We’re often testing many different models to find the top recommendations. Ahead are some that haven’t made it to this roundup, but are still worth considering.

Rabbit Air A3 Air Purifier: This air purifier uses a six-stage filtration system to rid your home of smoke, dander, odors, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and germs. The lowest fan setting clocks in around 20 decibels, which is extremely quiet, so you can run this model daily without being disturbed. The build is relatively bulky so it’s not the easiest to tuck into a corner and out of the way, and the $760 price tag is pretty steep.

GermGuardian AirSafe+ XL: This model is shaped like our best portable pick above, and comes with a lot of the same features as the other GermGuardian we recommend, and it has a companion app for tracking air quality metrics. That said, the app doesn’t specify what type or size particulate matter the sensor is measuring, so it’s hard to tell what common allergens are actually floating around your home.

Air purifiers vary in filtration range, so it's important to first consider your room size before buying. To find a model that accommodates your space, the EPA recommends that you first multiply the length and width of the area where you intend to operate the air purifier to calculate the square footage.

Most air purifiers have a maximum coverage area listed, so just compare to your calculations to find an air purifier that is the best fit for your home.

If you have an open floor plan or high ceilings, opt for an air purifier with more coverage. You should also place the air purifier in the room you use most regularly, and make sure it’s in an area where the airflow isn’t obstructed.

The filter system of your air purifier might differ depending on the model and issue you're trying to target such as allergy relief, odor elimination, or germ protection. You’ll often see three-stage filtration (or four-, five-, or six-stage), which includes all three of the filter types detailed below.

Pre-filters are typically the first line of defense in an air purifier and trap larger particles like dust, hair, and fur, which helps extend the lifespan of the main filter and improves the overall efficiency of the unit.

All of our selections on this list involve a multi-step filtration system to target a majority of common pollutants and allergens in your household.

Purvi Parikh, MD, an allergist and immunologist with NYU Langone Health, recommends selecting an air purifier that comes with a HEPA filter. “Make sure it's a HEPA air purifier since these filter down to 0.3 microns and have a robust amount of studies done showing their efficacy.” HEPA filters remove at least 99.97 percent of airborne particles like dust, bacteria, and pollen, and are the gold standard for air purification.

Activated carbon filters are more porous and help get rid of gases and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are commonly found in household items like surface cleaners and candles. These filters absorb molecules onto carbon and are best used in environments with strong odors or smoke.

With laundry machines, dishwashers, and fans all emitting their own noise, adding another loud appliance into the mix could be overkill, especially since air purifiers are meant to run the entire day.

Look for models that range from 10 to 30 decibels. A whisper is around 30 decibels, so expect air purifiers in this noise range to be almost virtually silent.

“Air purifiers need to be kept clean, and filters should be changed every six months,” Parikh says. Since air purifier filters are designed to collect and trap different-sized particles, contaminants, and hair, they get gunky pretty easily. This buildup could even reduce the efficiency and the air quality of the purifier if not cleaned often enough. Most air purifiers come with reusable filters, so just rinse them off in between replacements.

App compatibility, savvy control panels, remotes, check filter indicators, and variable settings are beneficial features that make it easier to use your air purifier. If you want to monitor the air quality levels in your home or keep tabs on filter life, look for an air purifier that pairs with an app. If you’re easily overstimulated by loud noises, consider an air purifier that has different modes for adjusting the speed of the internal fan.

Air purifiers use a fan to draw air into the unit, then pass it through a series of filters to remove particles and contaminants. Said filters vary in effectiveness and normally target a specific concern like odors, smoke, and viruses. Once the air has passed through the fan and all of the appropriate filters, it is recirculated back into the room for a cleaner and healthier environment.

“Air purifiers filter out pollutants, improve air quality, remove infectious agents and pollen,” says Parikh. “They limit your level of exposure and reduce lung damage and flare-ups of underlying chronic conditions such as asthma attacks, COPD exacerbations, and heart issues.”

“It can affect everyone’s health by causing inflammation and lung damage over time that may be either reversible or irreversible,” Parikh says. “It is especially dangerous for those with underlying heart disease, lung disease, pregnant women, children, and immunocompromised individuals.”

#6393. Bandicoot snouts reveal an evolutionary puzzle hiding in plain sight

Bandicoot skulls vary with climate and location, with climate explaining more shape differences than body size alone does.

Most bandicoots and bilbies find their food the same way: by scratching and digging through soil.

Their snouts, however, look very different from one species to the next. Some are short and sturdy, while others are long and narrow.

A new study of museum skulls found that climate and location help explain those differences, and that body size alone does not.

The researchers concluded that skull shape, more than size, is where these small to medium-sized marsupials changed most as they spread across Australia and New Guinea.

The work was led by Dr. Meg Martin and colleagues in Professor Natalie Warburton’s research group at Murdoch University’s Harry Butler Institute.

The team collaborated with Dr. Kenny Travouillon of the Western Australian Museum.

The researchers worked only with skulls, so no living animals were observed digging.

“When people think of bandicoots, they often picture a fairly similar group of small, digging marsupials,” Warburton said.

“But when we compared their skulls in three dimensions, we found remarkable differences, particularly in the length and shape of their snouts.”

The researchers scanned 127 adult skulls from 25 species, most of them from the museum’s mammal collection. Three of the species are extinct.

Teeth are shiny, so to cut down on reflections, each skull was first coated with a thin white layer of magnesium oxide. The coating was made by burning strips of magnesium in a fume hood.

Each skull was then scanned in two positions on a rotating platform, and the scans were combined into a single 3D model.

The researchers marked the same 54 points on every model, such as the seams where skull bones meet and spots on certain teeth.

They left out the cheekbones and a few other areas, because those parts were often damaged or worn on old museum specimens and fossils.

Comparing the 54 points across skulls allowed the team to measure shape separately from size.

That step matters, because a bigger animal can have a differently shaped head partly because it’s bigger. Warburton said a single skull can tell researchers a lot about an animal.

“Its shape is influenced by ancestry, feeding, sensory systems, and the mechanical demands placed on the head, so comparing skulls across species gives us another way of understanding how animals have adapted over evolutionary time,” she said.

The biggest difference was between short, broad skulls with wide braincases and long, slender skulls with narrow faces.

Short-nosed bandicoots, including the quenda of south-western Australia, had the short, sturdy type, and the smallest of these bandicoots had the most extreme versions.

A group of bandicoots called Perameles had longer snouts and narrower skulls, while the New Guinea species were in between.

Of the two bilby species measured, one had a skull close to the average for the whole group, and the other was more like Perameles.

Closely related bandicoots also tended to have similar skulls.

Knowing a skull’s genus, a group of closely related species, explained about 55% of the differences in shape, while knowing its exact species explained about 75%.

So why would close relatives end up with such different faces? Warburton pointed to the way each animal finds its food.

“For animals that spend a lot of their time searching and digging for food, the snout is an important part of how they interact with their environment,” she said.

“A long, narrow snout may help an animal probe through soil and fallen leaves for food, while a shorter, stronger snout may be better suited to digging.”

That idea fits what is known about other mammals. Long, thin snouts often belong to animals that pick small, scattered bits of food out of soil or leaf litter, and anteaters and echidnas are well-known examples.

Diet may matter too. Short-nosed bandicoots eat tubers and other underground plant parts, which can be tougher to chew than many insects.

New Guinea’s bandicoots, by contrast, appear to eat a lot of fungi and soft-bodied invertebrates from the forest floor.

The researchers suggest that tougher food, or deeper and more forceful digging, may help explain why short-nosed bandicoots have sturdier skulls.

Still, most bandicoots eat a wide mix of foods, and many species have little detailed diet information, so the team didn’t treat skull shape as a direct guide to diet.

To test the role of climate, the team looked up climate data for the place where each skull was collected, using a global database called WorldClim.

They kept six measures of temperature and rainfall that didn’t overlap much.

Together, climate, location and body size accounted for about 35% of the differences in skull shape. Climate on its own explained about 13%, nearly twice as much as size on its own.

That makes climate the bigger factor of the two, although most of the differences in skull shape remain unexplained.

The single strongest link was with latitude, meaning how far north or south a skull was collected.

Among the climate measures, rainfall in the driest month of the year had the strongest link.

Other studies of rodents and of carnivores in the dog and cat families have also linked skull shape to climate.

Size still played a part, but after the team removed its effect, the groups still differed clearly in shape. Males had bigger skulls than females, yet their skull shapes didn’t differ reliably.

These results point to links rather than causes, so they can’t tell how climate affected the skulls.

Bandicoot fossils go back about 26 million years, and although the record is patchy, it includes skull shapes no living species has.

The extinct pig-footed bandicoots, which ate mostly plants, had an unusually broad back to the roof of the mouth.

Partial skulls from the Riversleigh fossil sites in Queensland couldn’t be measured, but their features were compared.

Some early bandicoots were tiny, weighing about 3.5 to 5.3 ounces (100 to 150 grams), with snouts shorter than any living bandicoot’s.

Their skulls look like those of antechinuses, small marsupials from a different family, which suggests these early bandicoots ate insects.

Long snouts appear later, in a fossil species called Madju variae. Its place on the family tree suggests long snouts evolved before the modern bandicoot families split apart.

The tiny insect-eaters and some larger meat-eating bandicoots died out as Australia was becoming drier and its climate less stable.

Most survivors were omnivores, and the researchers suggest that eating many kinds of food mattered more than specializing.

Short-nosed bandicoots later evolved shorter snouts again. In this group, the earliest branch has the longest snout and a later branch the shortest, a sign of a fairly recent change.

For 13 of the 25 species, the team had only three skulls or fewer.

Many fossil species couldn’t be measured at all, so bandicoot skulls were probably even more varied than this study could capture.

The rest of the skeleton is also a gap. The researchers wrote that it’s still poorly understood how the body below the head contributes to digging.

Future studies of the whole skeleton, along with Riversleigh fossils that haven’t been described yet, could help show how extinction and climate change shaped the bandicoots living today.

The full study was published in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society.

#6390. Tropical forests are changing in profound ways that are overlooked when simply studying average temperatures

Decades of weather records reveal more extreme heat in two tropical forests, while rainfall patterns are shifting in different directions.

Tropical rainforests experience relatively little temperature variation through the year.

At two well-studied forests in the Caribbean basin, the average temperature has risen only slowly over the past few decades.

The hottest days, though, have become far more common, and the rain has turned more extreme in a different way at each site.

The plants and animals in these forests are adapted to steady temperatures, the researchers wrote.

So a jump in extreme heat can matter even when the averages hardly move, and at these two forests, the extremes are where the change showed up most clearly.

Alonso Ramírez, a professor in the Department of Applied Ecology at North Carolina State University, led the work. He has a long history with both forests.

Ramírez worked as a field technician at one of the forests before graduate school, and he directed the other for 15 years.

The team pulled decades of daily weather records from two stations. The La Selva Research Station is in a lowland rainforest in Costa Rica.

The El Verde Field Station is a mountain forest site in Puerto Rico and the main base of the Luquillo Long-Term Ecological Research program.

Temperature records ran from 1992 at La Selva and from 2000 at El Verde, and the rain records went back even further.

The average day is about 77°F (25.1°C) at La Selva and about 74°F (23.6°C) at El Verde.

At both sites, the gap between the coolest month and the warmest is less than about 7°F (4°C). In other words, temperatures vary little between seasons.

To find extreme heat, the researchers ranked every day on record at each site and flagged the hottest 5% as hot days.

“In La Selva prior to 2024, you had an average of eight hot days – days where the temperature exceeded the 95th percentile of temperatures at that site – per year,” Ramírez said.

“Now that number is up to 30. These spikes in temperature are becoming more severe and more common.”

El Verde had the same rise. The team got the same result with stricter cutoffs, the hottest 3% and the hottest 1% of days. The hot days themselves also got hotter over time.

Much of the jump came from 2023 and 2024, when temperatures ran high at both forests.

The team estimated that average temperatures at both sites rose by about 0.52°F (0.29°C) per decade.

That’s close to the warming earlier studies have reported across the wider Caribbean.

That estimate depends heavily on the regional figure the researchers gave their model as a starting point, as the authors made clear.

A rise in hot days, they wrote, may not be visible in average temperature records at all.

Total annual rainfall showed no significant trend at either site.

Both forests are very wet, with La Selva averaging about 164 inches (4,166 millimeters) a year and El Verde about 143 inches (3,636 millimeters).

At La Selva, days with more than about 3.7 inches (93 millimeters) of rain rose from around one a year in 1983 through 1985 to six in 2024. Days with no rain at all dropped from 128 in 1983 to 70 in 2024.

More frequent heavy downpours can disturb a forest even when the yearly total stays the same, the authors wrote.

El Verde moved the other way. Its count of heavy rainfall days didn’t change. But days with almost no rain, less than about a twentieth of an inch (1.4 millimeters), rose from 152 to 170 a year.

Marcelo Ardón, a co-author of the study, is a professor in the Department of Forestry and Environmental Resources and the Center for Geospatial Analytics at NC State.

“That was surprising, that one is getting wetter and one is getting drier,” Ardón said.

“Given how close they are to each other, we expected to find similar trends across the two sites. This shows how climate change is happening right now, and we can demonstrate that with data that doesn’t stretch that far back.”

The researchers wrote that the El Verde result supports projections of a drier Caribbean, including Puerto Rico.

Rainforests are adapted to steady rain, they added, and are especially vulnerable to drought.

The team also checked small forest streams. Water in a La Selva stream warmed by about 0.4°F (0.2°C) between 2007 and 2024.

A stream at El Verde warmed by about 1.6°F (0.9°C) between 2006 and 2024.

The La Selva stream is fed partly by groundwater estimated at about 2,500 years old, which the authors suggested may help explain its smaller rise.

The El Verde stream depends less on groundwater and runs through a forest that hurricanes often damage.

Earlier field and lab studies suggest that even small changes in water temperature can change which insects live in a stream and how fast their young develop.

At La Selva, rising temperatures have already been linked to lower forest productivity and to a drop in the number of insect species.

“A lot of people tend to think of the tropics as being stable and unchanging, especially in protected areas like the ones we’re studying,” said Ramírez.

“Conventional wisdom would say that these places should not show much of a change from anthropogenic impacts,” he added.

“Instead, these two sites that are hotspots for research are showing clear changes in climate and in the environment, which then affects the functioning of the ecosystem.”

Two forests are a small sample of a big region. The authors see La Selva and El Verde as typical of Caribbean settings, so similar shifts may be happening across the region, but that hasn’t been tested.

Streams at both sites also spent more time at high water, with the yearly hours at those levels roughly doubling.

The statistics behind that trend were weak, so it’s possible the pattern came up by chance.

The researchers haven’t yet checked whether the warmer temperatures and changing rainfall patterns are changing life in these streams.

The next step is to find out whether the insects and other animals in the streams at both forests are already responding.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Climate.

#6389. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

J.M. Young et al. Recent intensification (2004 – 2020) of permafrost mass‐wasting in the central Mackenzie Valley foothills is a legacy of past forest fire disturbances. Geophysical Research Letters. 2022. doi: 10.1029/2022GL100559

Scientists in the U.S. and Canada are decoding grizzly bears' behavior to learn how they navigate a human-dominated world. What they find could build a safer future for both species.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Across 53 challenging days between fall 2020 and spring 2021, a 360-pound (160 kilograms) young male grizzly bear nicknamed "Lingenpolter" tried to cross Interstate 90 in western Montana 46 times. High-resolution GPS tracking showed him moving parallel to four lanes of roaring traffic, bouncing off the highway like a furry pinball as he searched for a gap.

Eventually, Lingenpolter beat the odds, probably by slipping under a river bridge. But his hero's journey shows what a formidable barrier a busy highway can be for wildlife, Cecily Costello, a research wildlife biologist at Montana's Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks, told Live Science. "It is easy to imagine the difficulty this grizzly bear experienced trying to reach the other side," Costello said.

A map of all the places Lingenpolter attempted to cross the road before making it across.

This past May, another grizzly wasn't so lucky. Braving a crossing near one of Lingenpolter's attempts, the 27-year-old male bear was struck and killed by a truck, triggering a multicar rollover.

It's crucial for grizzly bears (Ursus arctos), also known as brown bears, to have room to roam. When they can't move between populations to mate, small groups get genetically isolated. And what's true for bears can also be true for other wildlife. "It's really challenging to be a small, fragmented population," said Michael Proctor, a wildlife biologist at Birchdale Ecological Ltd., a Canada-based environmental consulting firm. Such fragmentation is "one of the mechanisms by which we lose entire communities, and sometimes whole species," he told Live Science.

Nowhere is this challenge more urgent than in the 2,100 mile long (3,400 kilometers) region stretching along the spine of the Rocky Mountains between Yellowstone in Wyoming and the Yukon in northern Canada. The area, which spans five U.S. states, two Canadian provinces, and more than 75 Indigenous territories "represents the most intact, connected, wild, large mountain region in the world," Jordan Reeves, program director of landscape connectivity at the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative (Y2Y), which aims to secure connectivity throughout the region told Live Science.

The terrain between Yellowstone and the Yukon is the most intact wild large mountain region, and is crucial for bear migration.

But as highways, rail lines, and human development fragment its valleys, maintaining connected pathways for grizzly bears across this landscape has become a challenge.

Grizzlies range across vast, diverse terrain, spanning high-elevation alpine habitats, mid-mountain slopes, and low valley bottoms, which means safeguarding their movement can also protect passageways for coexisting species, including wolverines, mountain goats, elk and bighorn sheep, Proctor said. That's why researchers are trying to understand why, where and when grizzlies move. And what stops them in their tracks.

"We're looking at how a bear sees the world," Andrew Derocher, a bear biologist at the University of Alberta who has used GPS collars on grizzly bears to trace their movements, told Live Science.

When Sarah Sells started her graduate studies in animal behavior, her supervisor told her to "try to crawl into their fur brains and understand how they think," Sells told Live Science. Although we can't recreate exactly what's going on between a grizzly's ears, GPS collars that track animal movement hourly can tell scientists a lot about how animals behave, said Sells, who is currently the assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey's Montana Cooperative Wildlife Research Unit.

That tracking data is starting to produce an incredibly detailed picture not just of where bears go but also how and why they're making those choices.

"Bears are food finding machines," Chris Servheen, a bear biologist with the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Bear Specialist Group, told Live Science. "So remembering where they found food is critical to their success in life."

Using a combination of telemetry data (information collected by tracking devices) and movement modeling, Derocher and colleagues have investigated how well grizzlies remember where food is and when it is best to visit a foraging patch. Derocher's research showed that about two-thirds of the bears have a great memory for where and in what season they previously found food. His tracking data also revealed that wild bears generally avoid humans. But bears have only a few months to fatten up for winter. If food is scarce, many bears go into human environments and sometimes get killed, Proctor said.

The data is also offering insight into different bear "personalities." Bears are ultimately individuals, with their own traits and quirks, Servheen said.

A young male bear named Lingenpolter tried to cross the Interstate 90 in western Montana 46 times before successfully making it across.

Tracking data suggests that a lot of bear behavior is transmitted culturally via a mother's influence. Sometimes, the wrong behavior can get passed down to the next generation, Servheen said. For example, an infamous female grizzly known as 399 jaywalked potentially hundreds of times in the Jackson Hole valley in Wyoming while managing to keep her distance from humans. Her 20-odd cubs learned to follow her example, but they lacked her strategic caution. Several were killed by vehicles or management euthanizations.

"It's a risky thing to teach your kids to do stuff like that," Servheen said. "And her offspring weren't as smart as she was."

Further north along the region between Yellowstone and the Yukon, Proctor's first DNA survey across 1,500 square miles (4,000 square kilometers) of southern British Columbia in the late 1990s shattered his illusion that the bears, along with bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis) and other species in this province, were free to roam. Instead, he found a "cracked windshield" landscape, where roads and human sprawl had fractured the wilderness into isolated genetic islands. In the 2000s, the genetic diversity of the South Selkirk grizzly bears — a detatched subpopulation inhabiting southeastern British Columbia, northern Idaho, and northeastern Washington — was so low, for example, that biologists feared the bears wouldn't survive.

But Proctor and his colleagues went on to use bear movement data to model pathways through human-settled valleys. Proctor was so convinced about the viability of one potential corridor that he paid 10,000 Canadian dollars ($7,000) of his own money to buy a key piece of land right in the middle of it. "That was the first canoe over the waterfall of purchasing connectivity land," Proctor said

Proctor’s land secured a segment of a crucial connectivity corridor and, in the following years, he and other scientists partnered with trusts to purchase other land parcels, build fences, and establish safe corridors for grizzlies in the Creston Valley in southeastern British Columbia. These actions helped bears move north and south (sometimes across the border) and between the South Selkirk Mountains and Purcell Mountains. The researchers then watched bears like "Captain Hook," who'd been shot in the leg, hobble into the South Selkirks and breed with eight females. By 2021, nine immigrant bears had produced 27 new offspring within the population.

"This is gene flow; this is connectivity," Proctor said. "We took a completely isolated population and pretty much recovered it."

The peaks of the Purcell and Rocky Mountain ranges frame the Rocky Mountain Trench insoutheastern British Columbia—a core component of the Yellowstone to Yukon region. Steeptopography forces both wildlife and human activity into the same low-elevation valley bottoms.

Despite efforts to safeguard corridors through human occupied landscape, roads continue to stop bears in their tracks. When Servheen tracked bears near Highway 2 in northwest Montana, he found that many of the grizzlies avoided the highway altogether and those that crossed did so at night. But he also found that the bears' crossings clustered in specific sections of the road. Finding the crossing zones has helped researchers identify good locations for constructing overpasses and underpasses on many busy highways, but a crossing structure on its own is not enough, Servheen cautioned.

A bear's memory for where to find food is exemplary, but there's no special reward in a bear's brain for crossing a road safely — only a fatal penalty when they don't, Servheen said. So conservationists can't rely on bears to remember where crossings are. Instead, they must build fencing along the highway to funnel wildlife into the underpasses or overpasses. Then, the immediate land on each side needs to allow animals safe passage. "Otherwise, you have a bridge to nowhere," Servheen said.

Now researchers such as Sells are trying to use data about bears' likeliest routes to determine potential corridors in locations where they have little tracking data or where few bears live yet.

To do this, Sells is developing a virtual "Sims for Bears" that recreates the Continental Divide Ecosystem in Montana. In the life-simulation video game "The Sims," players give virtual humans personality traits, preferences and needs, and then drop them into a virtual environment to see how they behave.

Sells built the model using the GPS collaring data from 65 grizzly bears navigating individual paths through greenery, riparian areas and around forests and roads. Then, she "parachutes" an individual digital bear into a detailed computer simulation of real-world terrain and has them take thousands of virtual steps. By running these multiple simulated bears through thousands of iterations across the digital terrain, the researchers can watch where the virtual bears repeatedly choose to walk, effectively creating a map of predicted movement corridors.

Sells has used the model to predict how grizzly bears might recolonize the Bitterroot ecosystem of Idaho and Montana, which Lingenpolter was heading toward when attempting to cross Interstate 90.

To get to the Bitterroot Mountains, bears must pass through a valley filled with people, roads, garbage and fruit trees. "So knowing where they are more likely to end up is helpful to address things that could be difficult for humans or bears," Sells told Live Science.

The data is also confirming that the greatest barrier bears face comes from human contact or transportation infrastructure across the entire Yellowstone-to-Yukon region. Studies from across west-central North America report that humans directly or indirectly caused between 77% and 90% of grizzly bear deaths from 1989 to 2015. Hunting, managed kills in urban areas and road and rail collisions all take a toll.

Bears running across the road in Glacier National Park.

Bears in the wild usually avoid people, but some bears seek out human-dominated areas because they know these places are a source of food. People move to the Elk Valley in southeastern British Columbia because they love nature, but then they plant apple trees in their backyard, which attract bears, said Clayton Lamb, a wildlife scientist at the nonprofit Biodiversity Pathways.

Quickly, a bear eating backyard apples gets labeled a "problem bear," "when really it is a 'people problem,'" Lamb told Live Science.

Even human recreation takes a toll on bears' health and ability to move freely. Lamb's research has shown that grizzly bears try to avoid areas next to busy cycling and hiking trails.

To minimize human-bear conflict, Michelle McLellan, a wildlife ecologist at Biodiversity Pathways, has tracked trail use by both people and grizzlies in the West Kootenay region of British Columbia. McLellan documented people's habits using trail cameras and apps such as Strava Metro. Her research shows that the bears use the trails to move quickly between foraging spots but have learned not to use the trails that are most popular with humans. Consequently, the Nelson Cycling Club decided to close certain trails in the spring and cautioned riders about when and how to use the open trails. "Ride aware, make noise, slow down when needed," the club cautioned in its May newsletter.

Working with information from McLellan, the club has cut back overgrown vegetation along sight lines to prevent mountain bikers from startling bears at close range. They've also constructed wooden platforms on sections of trails that clatter and rumble as bikes pass over them, giving bears early notice of approaching riders. "The key is to not surprise them by making a lot of noise." McLellan told Live Science, noting that grizzlies are more likely to attack if they are surprised.

One advantage of having human mountain biking and hiking trails concentrated close to towns is that it focuses recreation into specific areas, Lamb said. Keeping trails condensed supplies multiple accessible paths and reduces humans encroaching on true wilderness — prime bear habitat. "The goal would be to ensure that there's sufficient recreation opportunities for people to stay healthy and connected to their local landscape while ensuring that wildlife can still move around and access their habitats," Lamb said

As humans increasingly live, work and play in bear territory, it's important to recognize the impact on the animals, Servheen said. "The bears never get a day off," he said. "Every day, they're trying to stay away from people and make a living in a place with multiple people on the landscape."

Bears expend a lot of much-needed energy trying to avoid people, and they won't be able to do that forever, Servheen said. As humans increase the development of private lands and recreation in bear territory, the squeeze is on. "There's going to be more conflicts with bears, and more dead bears," Servheen said.

The bears have done their part, Lamb said. His research has shown that bears living near humans are adapting by becoming mostly nocturnal, which reduces their odds of clashing with humans. "So, we need to meet them where they are at and see what we can do to share the space," Lamb said.

On the human side, people need to make it less tempting for bears to be in human dominated areas, McLellan said. That means keeping garbage stowed and making sure there is no ripe fruit available. "If you live rurally, you want them to be able to pass through your property but not linger near your home or in your front yard," McLellan said.

Bears have proved to be adaptable and persistent; Lingenpolter tried to cross the highway dozens of times before finding a way under. However, Servheen warned that we are putting them in a tough spot. To keep bear populations stable, scientists need data on bear behavior to help inform land management policies that create safe pathways for grizzlies to move through human dominated areas and regulate recreation with bears in mind, Servheen said.

"If we want to have bears in the future, we need to think about the needs bears have for some level of space on the landscape," Servheen said.

Securing that space across the vast Yellowstone to Yukon landscape requires more than just land acquisitions and highway overpasses — it requires increasing public awareness and counteracting the perception that bears are inherently aggressive and irrational, Proctor said. If people understand bear behavior, they can learn to act in ways that neither attract bears nor threaten them. And understanding the totality of bears’ strong drive to survive, and protect each other, can elicit empathy and motivation to protect this iconic species.

Early in his career, Proctor captured, immobilized and radio-collared a mother grizzly with her two yearlings, or newly adolescent bears. While the research team worked, the young bears circled quietly at a distance. When the scientists finally stepped back and the mother began to stir, the yearlings approached cautiously. As the mother's groggy head rested on a log, the yearlings' long-clawed front paws delicately explored the radio collar. Then, each one rested its head directly on hers, to form a quiet pile of three bear heads.

"They just wanted to touch mom after this ordeal," Proctor said. "Yes, grizzlies can be rough and dangerous but they can also be gentle at times," Proctor said.

#6386. Researchers warn that warmer weather is helping mosquitoes spread dangerous diseases like malaria and dengue

A century of data shows bed nets, drugs and growing cities explain much of why malaria and dengue went separate ways as the planet warmed.

Scientists have long predicted that a warmer world would bring more disease from mosquitoes, and dengue has kept rising along with the heat. Malaria went the other way.

Over a century of increasing temperatures, the area where malaria was a constant presence shrank to about half of what it had been, while dengue infections climbed to record highs.

According to a new review of the evidence, much of that split comes from outside the weather. People pushed malaria back with decades of bed nets, spraying, and drugs, while the growth of cities favored the mosquitoes that carry dengue.

Toby Cumming, a research fellow at the Health and Climate Initiative in Monash University’s School of Public Health, led the work with three colleagues. It is a review of studies that other teams have already published, not a new experiment.

In an interview with Earth.com, Cumming said the climate in many parts of the world is becoming more suitable for diseases spread by mosquitoes. “We cannot draw a straight line from climate suitability to rates of malaria and dengue transmission,” Cumming added.

Both diseases reach people through a bite. Malaria comes from a parasite carried by Anopheles mosquitoes, which bite mostly at night. Dengue comes from a virus carried by Aedes mosquitoes, which bite during the day.

Mosquitoes are cold-blooded, so their body temperature follows the air around them. At 59°F (15°C), a young Aedes aegypti takes 40 days to become an adult. At 95°F (35°C), it takes seven.

Warmth also makes mosquitoes bite more often. It also shortens the time the parasite or virus needs to develop inside the insect before it can infect a person.

There’s a ceiling, though. Past a certain point, heat starts to hurt the mosquito. Models suggest malaria spreads best at about 77°F to 82°F (25°C to 28°C). For dengue, it’s about 79°F to 84°F (26°C to 29°C).

Rain works in both directions. Heavy downpours can wash eggs and larvae away, while drought can leave stagnant pools in riverbeds and push families to store water in open containers near their homes.

Asked how people can protect themselves from dengue, Cumming said the best thing is to avoid bites, with long, loose clothing and insect repellent. Emptying containers that hold water around the home helps too.

The authors put numbers on how much warming has already shifted the odds. Between the 1950s and the decade ending in 2024, the climate’s estimated potential to spread dengue rose 12 percent for Aedes aegypti and 49 percent for its cousin, Aedes albopictus.

Over the same stretch, the area where the climate suits malaria grew by only about 2 percent. In Africa, the malaria map is moving.

One analysis cited in the review found that the elevation limit of malaria mosquitoes rose about 21 feet (6.5 meters) a year from 1898 to 2016.

Even so, the authors call the evidence for climate-driven shifts in malaria more contested than for dengue.

Dengue’s spread is easier to see. The disease has spread locally in places where it hadn’t before, including the southern United States, and it’s showing up more often in mainland France. Earth.com has also reported on rising dengue risk in California.

More than 14 million dengue cases were reported to the World Health Organization in 2024. That was more than double the previous annual record.

The longest view comes from a 2010 analysis in the journal Nature. Around 1900, malaria was a constant presence across an estimated 58 percent of the world’s land. By 2007, that figure had fallen to 30 percent.

Within the smaller area, far fewer people carried the parasite. In Africa, the share of people infected with the deadliest malaria parasite fell from 40 percent in 1900 to 1929, to 24 percent in 2010 to 2015.

Europe shows the same pattern. Malaria began to fade there in the 1800s while temperatures were rising, and the review credits better living conditions, better health care, and improved irrigation and drainage.

Cold didn’t stop the disease, either. Malaria was common in the marshy parishes of England from the 16th to the 18th centuries, during an especially cold period. In Finland, mosquitoes survived freezing winters by sheltering inside houses and stables.

The two diseases differ first in the tools people built to fight them. Efforts to wipe out malaria go back to the 1950s, with house spraying and mass drug campaigns, and later with bed nets treated with insecticide.

Global spending on malaria rose from $1.5 billion to $4.3 billion between 2000 and 2016. Over that time, the yearly rate of new cases fell 36 percent and the death rate fell 60 percent.

“What started as a climate story – the impact of temperature, rainfall and humidity on malaria and dengue – became a human story,” Cumming told Earth.com.

Dengue had no matching toolkit. There are still no drugs that treat the virus, vaccines are only now arriving, and bed nets do little against mosquitoes that bite in daylight.

And mosquitoes are building resistance to insecticides, a problem the authors flag for both diseases.

Cities are the second difference. Aedes mosquitoes lay eggs in gutters and water containers, and cities offer plenty of those, along with lots of people to bite.

Anopheles prefer more natural pools, which cities tend to lack, so urban growth tends to cut malaria.

The authors flag one important exception. Anopheles stephensi, a malaria mosquito from Asia that breeds in artificial containers, has now settled into cities in the Horn of Africa.

The good news on malaria has slowed. New cases per 1,000 people at risk fell from 79 in 2000 to 59 in 2015. By 2024, the figure was back up to 64.

In 18 countries, the rate rose by at least 70 percent between 2015 and 2024. Resistance to key malaria drugs is a growing concern too.

Extreme weather can undo progress quickly. After record flooding hit Pakistan in 2022, malaria cases there rose fivefold.

Asked what should be done first to curb the spread, Cumming said the answer is a renewed commitment from the global community to fight malaria and dengue.

That includes scaling up public health measures that work and speeding up research on new ways to prevent and treat both diseases.

The forecasts don’t agree on malaria. Some models predict it will spread into new areas as the planet warms. Others predict that hotter, drier conditions will shrink it in parts of Africa where it’s common today.

Adding wealth to a model changes the picture. Using climate alone, one model estimated that 5.2 billion people would be at risk of malaria by 2050. When it also counted each country’s economic output per person, the estimate dropped to 2.0 billion.

Much of the temperature evidence also comes from lab studies that were never checked in the field. And mosquitoes may adapt to local heat, which fixed temperature rules can’t capture.

For dengue, newer tools are arriving. One vaccine has been licensed in many countries since 2022. The World Mosquito Program, a not-for-profit group owned by Monash University, releases mosquitoes carrying a bacterium called Wolbachia, which makes them less able to spread the virus.

It’s still unclear whether those tools can do for dengue what bed nets and drugs did for malaria. In order to find out, researchers will need years of dengue case records from the places that use them.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.
