#6385. What happens when engineers grind up eggshells and squeeze them into a lightweight metal?

Eggshell powder pressed into magnesium bonded to the metal and made tiny samples tougher to crush.

Most eggshells end up in the trash or the compost bin. Yet a shell is almost pure calcium carbonate, the same calcium compound that metal makers normally get from mined rock.

Engineers have now packed ground-up kitchen eggshells into a block of magnesium metal and pressed it through a spinning die. The shell powder spread evenly through the metal.

Part of it also reacted with the magnesium around it, which bonded shell to metal chemically. That makes a kitchen scrap a workable ingredient for a lightweight metal, at least in a small lab test.

The work came from the lab of Bharat Gwalani, an assistant professor of materials science and engineering at North Carolina State University.

It was a first test on small rods, and the finished metal wasn’t measurably harder than plain magnesium. Its gain in strength showed up only in microscopic crush tests.

Magnesium is a light metal. A recent antenna design for Mars helicopters used a magnesium frame.

“Calcium is added to magnesium to improve its mechanical properties,” Gwalani said. “We wanted to see if we could use biogenic waste – eggshells – to produce the necessary calcium materials during the manufacturing process.”

Biogenic waste just means leftovers from living things. Eggshells already appear on lists of food leftovers that could be recovered and reused, and other labs have turned food waste into plastic.

Industry makes one of those compounds, calcium oxide, by heating limestone in industrial kilns until it gives off carbon dioxide.

Earlier teams had already blended eggshell powder into magnesium, either by melting the metal or by stirring the powder into its surface.

However, little was known about what happens to the shell inside the metal during a friction-based press like this one.

Gwalani’s co-authors included researchers at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, where first author Aniruddha Malakar now works, and at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi.

The eggshells came from ordinary households. The team washed them, dried them in an oven at about 300°F (150°C) for four hours, and ground them with a mortar and pestle.

Then they cut small grooves, each about an eighth of an inch (3 mm) wide, into a short magnesium cylinder about an inch (25.4 mm) across. The eggshell powder filled the grooves in the metal and made up roughly 8.4 percent of the block by volume.

That’s a pinch of shell in a lot of metal.

A die spinning 300 times a minute pressed into the block at about 3 inches (75 mm) a minute and squeezed it out as a rod. Friction and squeezing heated the metal to roughly 930°F (500°C), hot enough to soften it without melting it.

Most of the shell particles measured 2 to 4 micrometers across, far thinner than a human hair. They were spread evenly through the rod.

Metal is made of tiny crystals called grains. In a plain magnesium rod made the same way, the grains averaged 16 micrometers across. With eggshell mixed in, they averaged 8.

Smaller grains usually make a metal stronger. Even so, the eggshell rod wasn’t measurably harder than the plain one when the team pressed a diamond tip into its surface.

The eggshell’s effect appeared only after the metal started to give way. The researchers carved microscopic pillars out of grains pointing in the same direction in both metals. Then they crushed them.

Both kinds of pillar began to give way at about the same stress. Once they did, the eggshell pillars kept resisting harder as they squashed.

Their peak strength reached about 32,600 pounds per square inch (225 megapascals), compared with about 29,000 pounds per square inch (200 megapascals) for plain magnesium.

The team thinks the shell bits help tiny flaws in the metal’s crystals pile up as it deforms. The more of those flaws that build up, the harder the metal is to squash further.

The second finding was chemical. Calcium carbonate usually breaks apart into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide at about 1,650 to 1,740°F (900 to 950°C) under normal air pressure.

Inside the press, the metal reached only about 930°F (500°C). Several of the smallest shell fragments broke down, at least partly. The team established this by measuring calcium, oxygen and carbon across individual particles.

The researchers think the spots where shell met metal got much hotter than the overall reading. They suspect sudden swings in pressure helped too.

Near the edges of some particles, the measurements pointed to magnesium oxide. The likeliest source, the team concluded, was carbon dioxide from the broken-down shell reacting with the surrounding magnesium.

The reaction was patchy, though. Larger particles, a few micrometers or more across, stayed mostly unchanged. The finished rod held a mix of untouched shell, partly broken-down shell and areas rich in calcium oxide.

One compound didn’t form. That compound, Mg2Ca, is a compound of magnesium and calcium that can strengthen magnesium alloys, and the team didn’t detect it. The calcium stayed mostly locked up as calcium oxide.

The authors wrote that their goal was to understand what happens inside the metal, not to make the strongest possible material.

They tested only one spin speed and one feed rate. The team also didn’t measure whether the process uses less energy than making calcium compounds from rock, although Gwalani said it should.

“There are fewer steps,” Gwalani said. “You have a reliable, sustainable supply chain. Eggshells are inexpensive.”

Gwalani’s group in NC State’s Department of Materials Science and Engineering has also used the same kind of press to work magnetic powder into scrap aluminum.

The next step is to push the chemistry further. The authors suggested heating the shell powder before it goes in, running the press longer or hotter, or working in a sealed chamber with less oxygen.

Any of those might free the calcium from its oxide and get it into the magnesium itself, the step that this first test didn’t reach.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Magnesium and Alloys.

#6384. Can weight-loss drugs protect the brain? The evidence is complicated

A new review examines whether GLP-1 weight-loss drugs could preserve memory and why their potential benefits for brain health remain uncertain.

Semaglutide can help people lose weight and lower cardiovascular risk. But can it also help preserve memory and thinking skills?

That question sits at the center of a new review covering nearly 200 preclinical studies and some of the largest clinical trials ever run on these medications.

The short version: maybe. The honest version: we still don’t know how, or even if.

The review was led by Stina Börchers and Christoffer Clemmensen at the University of Copenhagen. What they’ve assembled is part map, part warning label.

Look at population-level studies and the picture is seductive.

Trawl through insurance databases and clinical registries and you’ll find that people with type 2 diabetes taking GLP-1 receptor agonists consistently develop dementia at lower rates than those on other glucose-lowering therapies.

The REWIND trial flagged a 14% lower hazard of substantial cognitive decline with dulaglutide. Headlines practically write themselves.

Cognition was an exploratory outcome in REWIND. The 14% reduction emerged after a post hoc adjustment for participants’ baseline cognitive scores.

A meta-analysis pooling five randomized clinical trials, 7,732 adults with type 2 diabetes in total, found no clear improvement in global cognitive performance.

The observational findings remain promising, but randomized trials have not established a clear cognitive benefit.

The sharpest disappointments came from Alzheimer’s research. ELAD tested liraglutide in 204 people with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s for a year.

It missed its primary endpoint, which measured brain glucose metabolism.

Some MRI measures and a secondary cognitive outcome favored liraglutide, but measures of daily functioning and overall clinical severity did not show significant benefits.

EVOKE and EVOKE+ went much bigger. These phase 3 trials enrolled 3,808 participants with mild cognitive impairment or early Alzheimer’s.

Participants were assigned to oral semaglutide, with a target dose of 14 mg daily, or placebo for two years.

The drug didn’t slow decline on the Clinical Dementia Rating scale and it didn’t help with daily functioning.

It did nudge some biomarkers, though – roughly 10% reductions in cerebrospinal fluid levels of phosphorylated tau and neurogranin.

But biomarker movement, by itself, is not evidence that a disease is being modified.

GLP-1 receptors are sprinkled across brain regions you’d want a cognition drug to reach – hippocampus, amygdala, prefrontal cortex, substantia nigra.

Preclinical work shows effects on synaptic plasticity and neurotrophic signaling through CREB and BDNF pathways. On paper, the biology is there.

In practice, these drugs are large peptide molecules. They don’t cross the blood-brain barrier easily.

Most evidence suggests they reach circumventricular organs – spots where capillaries are naturally leaky – and parts of the brainstem.

Whether these drugs ever touch the hippocampus in pharmacologically relevant concentrations depends on the compound, the species, the dose, and the detection method. Nobody has a clean answer.

This raises a question about GLP-1 drugs and the brain: Could any cognitive benefits come indirectly from better metabolic health?

They could be side effects of side effects – downstream consequences of tighter blood sugar, less inflammation, healthier blood vessels, better sleep.

Semaglutide cut cardiovascular events by 20% in the SELECT trial. It reduced major kidney outcomes by 24% in FLOW.

Tirzepatide dramatically improved obstructive sleep apnea in the SURMOUNT-OSA trials. Every one of those improvements could benefit the brain indirectly.

“We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit,” Börchers said.

Obesity and diabetes can affect attention, planning, and processing speed.

Alzheimer’s disease often affects the ability to remember events and experiences early in its course. These patterns can overlap, but their underlying causes and responses to treatment may differ.

These are not the same problem dressed in different clothes. They arise from different biology.

A drug that might improve executive function in someone with metabolic syndrome is not necessarily going to rescue memory in someone with amyloid plaques.

Worse, the relationship between blood sugar and cognition runs in both directions.

Hypoglycemia damages thinking. But cognitive impairment also makes dangerous blood sugar crashes more likely. Picking apart cause and effect inside that loop is a nightmare.

Rapid weight loss can reduce muscle mass, potentially worsening frailty in vulnerable older adults.

It can cause dehydration, malnutrition, and reduced protein intake. Fatigue shows up more often with incretin-based therapies than with placebo.

In people already teetering toward frailty, these side effects could erase whatever cognitive benefit the metabolic improvements might deliver.

The review calls for trials that track body composition, nutritional status, and treatment tolerability alongside cognition.

Newer treatments combine GLP-1 activity with effects on GIP, glucagon, or amylin pathways. Different combinations may have different effects on brain function.

GIPR agonism and antagonism, for instance, appear to activate entirely different brain mechanisms rather than simply opposing each other.

Brain-penetrant peptides and small-molecule agonists could eventually bypass the blood-brain barrier problem altogether.

The OxSENSE study is already testing semaglutide’s acute effects on reward sensitivity, memory, and emotional processing in healthy adults.

“Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function,” Clemmensen said.

“By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function.”

The review is published in the journal Science.

#6383. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

#6382. Permafrost Is Thawing From the Inside Out—and It’s Unleashing an Entirely New Kind of Landslide

Wildfires from decades ago may be secretly melting the frozen ground from below, setting off a disastrous chain of events in the present.

The largest northward-flowing river in North America, Canada’s Mackenzie River carries roughly 78 cubic miles of freshwater out of Great Slave Lake, winds through the frozen expanse and pristine forests of the Northwest Territories, and eventually empties into the Beaufort Sea, a marginal sea of the larger Arctic Ocean. The river represents the second-largest drainage basin on the continent, covering roughly 20 percent of Canada’s total landmass. The river valley served as the ancestral home of the Dene people, who in Slavey (a group of Athabaskan languages) called the river dehcho, or simply “big river.”

For thousands of years before the arrival of industrial revolution, permafrost—soil, rock, and sediment that stays frozen at least two consecutive years—encased this part of the world in frozen beauty. But with rising anthropogenic carbon emissions, that immemorial stability is crumbling away. And in some places in the central Mackenzie Valley, melting permafrost is changing the landscape in surprising ways.

In 2017 and 2018, two gargantuan landslides impacted the area, moving 4.5 and 18 million cubic meters of frozen ground respectively. Landslides, on their own, aren’t necessarily surprising. As the climate warms and permafrost thaws, boreal and tundra ecosystems, whether in Canada, Alaska, or other northern regions of the world, have seen an increasing risk of landslides. However, the leftover evidence of these huge terrestrial deluges raised a few questions, chiefly because they appeared to carry large chunks of frozen ground with them.

In 2019, permafrost geologist Joseph Young, then with the University of Alberta as a Ph.D. student, traveled by helicopter to a remote field site when he spotted slopes “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” he told Science News. Young admits he was puzzled by these particular landslides because permafrost typically melts from the top down, making a muddy slurry that forms a slow-moving landslide.

However, the Mackenzie Valley landslides contained chunks of still-frozen earth that had moved hundreds of meters, and initial ground observations showed that sliding occurred roughly 20 meters under the top layer of permafrost. To better understand the mechanics of this strange landslide formation, Young and a team of researchers from the University of Alberta set up instruments to track ground temperature from 2020 until 2022. They hypothesized that wildfires—including some that occurred decades in the past—and rising summer temperatures formed tension cracks, allowing water to seep in and cause the permafrost to thaw from below. They called this new kind of landslide “permafrost detachment slides” and reported their observations in the journal Geophysical Research Letters.

“Climate warming and wildfire work together to drive heat to depth over decades, weakening the permafrost base,” the authors wrote. “Exposed ice-rich scarps continue thawing, triggering secondary landslides and irreversibly reshaping the landscape.”

Melting permafrost isn’t just rearranging these long-standing slopes, it's also unleashing previously trapped metals into riverbeds, turning them in some cases a bright, eye-popping orange. Shifting permafrost is also swallowing up villages in Alaska’s remote tundra, and studies estimate that continued thawing could cause upwards of $50 billion in damage to buildings and roads in Alaska by 2050.

The impact of climate change can’t be ignored, from rising sea levels inundating coastal communities to roiling wildfires that blanket world-renowned cities in smoke. And in the coldest regions of the world, climate change is quite literally changing the ground beneath our feet.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6381. Scientists designed a new way to hunt for signs of life in space using electricity and artificial intelligence

An electrical sensor told mirror-image amino acids apart, one molecule at a time, taking a step toward small instruments that can look for signs of life.

Your left and right hands are made of the same parts, yet a left hand won’t fit properly into a right glove. Many of the molecules in living things come in the same two mirror-image versions, and life on Earth builds its proteins overwhelmingly from just one of them.

A team led by researchers in Japan has now told those two versions apart, one molecule at a time, using only an electrical current.

The sensor could one day help a small spacecraft instrument look for that lopsided mix on another world. The team also tested it on extracts from a meteorite and from desert soil, where it caught the broad pattern but missed on several details.

Takahito Ohshiro and Masateru Taniguchi of the University of Osaka led the work with colleagues at Georgia Tech, NASA Goddard, MIT and the University of Chicago. Everything so far has happened in a lab, and no flight instrument exists yet.

Amino acids, the small molecules that link up into proteins, mostly come in mirror images, a left-handed form and a right-handed form. Scientists label them L and D. Chemistry without life tends to make the two in equal amounts, while living things lean heavily toward one, the L form.

A strong tilt toward one hand is therefore a possible sign of biology. Some researchers have proposed an excess of more than 20 percent in several amino acids as a threshold that would point to life.

Meteorites once seemed to carry such a tilt, but those results are now generally blamed on contamination from Earth. Samples brought back from the asteroids Ryugu and Bennu showed roughly equal mixes.

In an interview with Earth.com, Taniguchi was careful about what the measurement can show. “Importantly, chirality should not be viewed as proof of life by itself,” Taniguchi said.

“It would become much more powerful when combined with molecular identity, abundance, chemical context, and other biosignatures.”

The sensor starts as a thin gold wire that is pulled until it snaps. The two broken tips sit a little more than half a billionth of a meter apart. That’s more than 100,000 times narrower than a human hair.

A small voltage pushes a trickle of current across that gap. When an amino acid drifts in, the current jumps for a few thousandths of a second, then drops back.

Each jump has a shape, and the L and D forms of the same amino acid leave slightly different shapes. A machine-learning program trained on thousands of these spikes learned to sort them.

“We are not measuring only an average signal from a large population of molecules,” Taniguchi said.

Standard lab methods for telling the two mirror-image molecules apart rely on light or chemical reagents. The electrical approach needs neither. Taniguchi said spacecraft instruments have to be small, sturdy, sensitive and energy-efficient, and dropping the optics could help with that.

The team tested 19 amino acids that come in both forms. Working from a single spike, the program picked the right form about 88 percent of the time on average. The hardest pair, glutamine, came in at 78 percent, and the easiest, isoleucine, at 97 percent.

One spike is a weak basis for a verdict, and a five-minute run collects hundreds. By the team’s calculation, a program that is right 90 percent of the time on each spike would be right 99.9 percent of the time after 16 spikes.

A harder test asked the program to name both the amino acid and its hand from all 39 possible forms at once. It was right about half the time, far better than the 1-in-39 rate that a guess would give.

Mixtures were harder still. In test solutions holding four or five amino acids, some counted shares landed close to the true values. One was off by 56 percent.

Next came real samples. The team ran extracts from a fragment of the Murchison meteorite, supplied by the Smithsonian. It also tested soil from two sites in Chile’s Atacama Desert, a Mars-like environment. A standard lab instrument analyzed the same extracts for comparison.

The program only counted spikes it was confident about, and it rejected about 93 percent of the spikes from a blank sample that contained no extract.

Both methods found glycine to be the most common amino acid in the meteorite, at 48 percent by the sensor and 63 percent by the standard instrument.

Other results drifted. The sensor put serine at nearly 12 percent of the meteorite’s amino acids, compared with well under 1 percent by the standard method. It also found no glutamic acid at all in either desert soil.

For handedness, the sensor matched the standard method on aspartic acid in the meteorite, but not on alanine or valine.

“In that sense, the real samples were not only a demonstration of the technology, but also an important test of its current limits,” Taniguchi told Earth.com.

The authors wrote that the method should be treated as a targeted tool for a shortlist of known molecules, not a full chemical inventory. It can’t yet recognize a molecule it wasn’t trained on, and a messy natural sample adds background signals that blur the counts.

Taniguchi listed what a flight version would need. It would have to measure amounts more accurately, flag unfamiliar molecules, prepare its own samples and keep out contamination from Earth.

It would also need shrunken electronics that survive vibration, radiation and temperature swings.

“Ultimately, we envision a compact instrument in which sample preparation, single-molecule electrical detection, and AI-based molecular identification operate as one system,” Taniguchi said.

Only a working prototype can show whether the sensor works away from a clean lab bench, on a sample from Mars, an icy moon or an asteroid.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6380. Plant-based dairy swaps may leave a key nutrient behind

A UK modeling study suggests replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives could deepen iodine shortfalls, especially among teenage girls and women.

Plant-based milk, yogurt and cheese make it easy to cut back on dairy without rethinking every meal.

In the UK, though, dairy is one of the main places people get iodine, a mineral the body uses to make thyroid hormones. Most plant-based versions contain very little of it.

A new modeling study estimates that swapping about a third of dairy for store-bought plant-based products would leave more teenage girls and young women short of iodine.

The same model also tested a fix, and adding iodine to both the plant-based products and bread kept every age group at least as well supplied as before.

Researchers at the University of Surrey and Queen’s University Belfast asked no one to change their diet.

The study, led by Katie Nicol, used real food diaries and calculated how much of four vitamins and minerals people would get if some of their dairy were replaced.

“With the rise in plant-based alternative foods, we need to know whether they are like-for-like replacements for the micronutrients that are found in dairy products,” said Nicol.

Cow’s milk in the UK is rich in iodine partly because farmers add it to cattle feed to keep animals healthy. Iodine-containing disinfectants used in dairy production add to it.

Many countries add iodine to table salt. The UK doesn’t have that policy, and iodized salt is hard to find in British shops, so dairy has become the country’s main iodine source.

In the team’s earlier survey of UK supermarkets, only 12% of plant-based alternatives had added iodine, and even those often contained less than cow’s milk.

Sarah Bath, an associate professor in public health nutrition at the University of Surrey, was also involved in the study.

“People may also be unaware of the importance of iodine, which is needed to make thyroid hormones to regulate our metabolism, support healthy growth and brain development,” said Bath.

The team started with the UK’s National Diet and Nutrition Survey.

Between 2016 and 2019, the survey asked 3,558 people, from 18-month-olds to adults up to 100, to write down everything they ate for four days.

The researchers focused on the 3,095 people who ate some dairy during those days, since there’s nothing to swap in a diet without it.

On an average day, these people had about 237 grams of milk, cheese and yogurt.

The team then replaced that dairy, gram for gram, with plant-based versions from UK supermarket websites. Each one was picked at random, so the results reflected how widely those products vary.

The researchers tested four levels of change, replacing 20%, 35%, 50% or all of a person’s dairy. The first two match the UK climate plan’s call to cut meat and dairy by 20% by 2030 and 35% by 2050.

The 50% level reflects international advice to cut animal foods worldwide by more than half. Dairy contributes substantially to greenhouse gas emissions.

Teenage girls were the worst off from the start, and those aged 14 to 18 ate less dairy than any other group.

The team estimated that 54% of them fell short of the daily iodine benchmark nutritionists use to judge whether a group is getting enough.

In a population with enough iodine, only about 2% to 3% of people would fall below that line.

The model estimates that replacing just over a third of their dairy would push the share of teenage girls falling short to 65%.

For women of childbearing age, 19 to 49, it would climb from 32% to 42%.

The authors wrote that iodine is especially important during pregnancy, infancy and adolescence.

If all dairy were replaced, the model estimates that 80% of teenage girls and 72% of teenage boys would fall short.

Young children, teenagers and adult women had the biggest drops overall.

Calcium, riboflavin (a B vitamin) and vitamin B12 intakes also fell, but shortfalls became more common only when half or all of the dairy was replaced. Iodine was the most sensitive of the four.

Next, the team tested three fixes. The first required every plant-based product to contain all four nutrients, at the minimum level needed to be labeled a source of each one.

The requirement kept average intakes steady, but it didn’t fix the shortfall teenage girls already had. Between 56% and 59% of them still fell below the iodine benchmark.

The second option was bread, which six in 10 people in the survey ate. Australia and New Zealand already require bakers to use iodized salt in bread.

In the model, doing the same with all commercially made bread cut the share of teenage girls short on iodine from 54% to 37%.

For women aged 19 to 49, iodized bread helped less as dairy disappeared.

Their shortfall dropped from 32% to 24% when a fifth of their dairy was replaced, but rose to 44% once all of it was gone.

The best results came from doing both. With iodine added to plant-based products and to bread, every age group kept or improved its iodine supply, even with no dairy at all.

None of the policies raised the share of any group getting too much iodine.

“Nutrition policy must evolve in tandem with environmental targets; however, it is important that shifts towards more sustainable diets do not compromise on public health,” Nicol said.

The study is a set of calculations, not a trial in which people changed what they ate. It assumes everyone shifts in the same way, even though interest in plant-based products varies with age, sex and culture.

Without sales figures, the model gave every product the same chance of being picked, though real shoppers don’t buy them equally.

The product data also come from a 2020 survey, and recipes in this market may change.

Nor did the team look at how well the body absorbs nutrients from fortified foods. People who ate no dairy at all, 13% of the survey, were left out, so it’s unknown how fortification would affect them.

Whether real diets will shift the way the model assumes remains an open question.

The authors called for continued tracking of what people eat, and how much of each nutrient they get, as the food supply keeps changing.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet Planetary Health.

#6379. Hubble spots a ghostly trail that may lead back to two shattered worlds

Hubble’s first visible-light view of the Cat’s Tail near Beta Pictoris offers clues to a possible collision between two large icy worlds.

Near the young star Beta Pictoris, a long streak of dust reflects so little starlight that it had escaped detection in visible light, the kind our eyes can see.

Now the Hubble Space Telescope has caught it for the first time. Its faintness fits dark, carbon-rich dust left over from a crash between two worlds at least about the size of Pluto’s moon Charon.

Beta Pictoris is about 65 light-years from Earth and roughly 18.5 million years old.

It’s still surrounded by rubble left over from building its planets, and astronomers nicknamed the streak the Cat’s Tail when they first spotted it in 2024.

The James Webb Space Telescope first revealed the tail in infrared light emitted by its warm dust.

Arin Avsar, a doctoral student at the Lunar and Planetary Laboratory of the University of Arizona, led the new study.

“The Cat’s Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies – think something like Pluto,” Avsar said.

“Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while.”

Avsar’s team stacked Hubble images taken in six rounds between 2012 and 2025. The result is the deepest Hubble picture of the system so far, but the signal is still weak.

Near its tip, the tail is barely brighter than the surrounding dust.

In visible light, the Cat’s Tail is roughly 200 to 1,000 times fainter than it looks to Webb in infrared.

“We think the Cat’s Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it’s made of,” Avsar said.

“It consists almost entirely of what we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they’re quite black.”

The team tested that idea with computer models of dust grains made from different mixtures. Rocky grains are made of the same kinds of minerals found in Earth’s crust.

A tail made mostly of them would have been about 100 to 10,000 times brighter in visible light than what Hubble recorded.

Dust that was 85% to 99% carbon-rich material by weight, with a little rock mixed in, matched best. Webb’s earlier infrared measurements had found the same thing.

Avsar’s team also checked that no single round of observations had created the tail by mistake. They left out one round at a time and rebuilt the image.

The tail showed up every time, though it got noisier near the tip.

The dust isn’t only dark. The models also showed that each grain is extremely porous, with somewhere between 55% and 93% of its volume taken up by empty space.

Dark, fluffy dust grains this tiny are an odd combination.

“How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that’s part of why we study this feature,” Avsar said.

What turned a young planetary body into fluffy dust is still a matter of speculation, Avsar added.

Kevin Wagner, a co-author and a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at the university’s Steward Observatory, offered one possibility.

“It’s possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that’s how they became so porous,” Wagner said.

The Webb team that found the tail in 2024 estimated that the crash behind it happened roughly 100 to 200 years ago. That team also calculated how much carbon-rich dust the tail holds.

Avsar’s team then asked how big the colliding bodies had to be to supply that much carbon.

Using measurements of a comet, the dwarf planet Haumea, and the dust that drifts between stars, they settled on a range of 14% to 38% carbon-rich material by weight.

Depending on the assumed carbon content, the team calculated a minimum diameter of roughly 750 to 1,000 miles (1,200 to 1,600 kilometers) for each body.

That’s about the size of Charon or Makemake, two icy worlds in the Kuiper Belt, the region beyond Neptune where Pluto orbits.

These are minimum sizes, rather than estimates of the bodies’ most likely sizes.

The team assumed the debris was equally dense at every size, but the tail’s fluffy grains are much less dense than solid chunks, so the real bodies were likely bigger.

The carbon most likely came from deep inside them.

Pluto’s reddish surface is coated with similar material, but that coating holds far too little of it to build a tail like this one.

Webb’s pictures are flat, like any photo, so they can’t show how far the tail stretches toward or away from us.

Astronomers measure distances like this in astronomical units, the average distance between Earth and the sun, about 93 million miles (150 million kilometers).

Visible light helps here. Dust scatters visible light differently depending on the angle between the star, the dust, and the telescope.

The heat it gives off looks the same from every angle. Comparing the two telescopes’ views let Avsar’s team estimate that angle.

“We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat’s Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it,” Avsar said.

“It’s essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it.”

The team’s models can’t settle it completely. They lean slightly toward a tail that extends somewhat behind the star. But they can’t rule out a tail in the same plane as the star, as seen from Earth.

A faint cloud of fine dust, called a halo, surrounds the disk above and below its flat middle.

With the new images, Hubble traced the disk out to about 500 astronomical units from the star, roughly 46 billion miles (75 billion kilometers), for the first time.

Telescopes on the ground had mapped that halo in 1995, but Hubble’s view is about 20 times sharper.

The sharper images show the halo is lopsided and warped. On one side it bulges outward above the disk, and on the other side it bulges below.

The disk’s main layer has a similar warp, and earlier studies traced it to Beta Pictoris b, a giant planet whose orbit is tilted compared with the disk.

Avsar’s team suggested that the same planet, or possibly the recently found planet Beta Pictoris d, may shape the halo too.

“This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force,” Avsar said.

“It’s a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units.”

Confirming that will take computer models that include all three planets and the push of starlight on small grains, the authors wrote.

By one estimate, icy moons and dwarf planets in our solar system are about 45% to 70% rock by weight. Much of their carbon-rich material is mixed into their rocky cores.

A crash that smashed two of them apart should have released plenty of rock along with the carbon, yet the Cat’s Tail has almost none.

Starlight may have separated the debris. It pushes carbon-rich grains harder than rocky ones, so the two kinds could have ended up in different places.

The rock might be in other dusty clumps that Webb has already seen in the disk.

Hubble also picked up a faint smudge near a second, tilted disk around the star, too weak to tell whether it’s real dust or a flaw in the image.

Deeper Hubble observations planned for the system should settle that.

With more detailed models of how these grains scatter light, astronomers could also tell where the tail really points.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

A high-status burial surprised archaeologists when they discovered leprosy in a man's bones from the fifth century.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists investigating the genomes of a dozen people buried in an abandoned Roman-era settlement in northwestern Germany have discovered a surprising organism lurking in one man's remains: a rare strain of Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy.

This strain of leprosy has never been seen in this part of Europe before, which hints that the individual had traveled and interacted with people from across the Roman world. The man was buried in a wooden boat surrounded by unusual objects, indicating he was a high-status person, according to a research study.

"The results were particularly striking in the case of one individual," study co-author Ben Krause-Kyora, an archaeologist at the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Kiel University in Germany, said in a Nov. 3 statement. "He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser [rivers]."

In the study, published online Oct. 15 in the journal iScience, Krause-Kyora and colleagues analyzed the genomes of people buried at the coastal settlement of Fallward. The settlement originated in the first century B.C. but gradually declined and became a cemetery by the fifth century A.D. Among the 200 cremation burials and 60 inhumation burials originally excavated in the 1990s was a distinctive grave made from a wooden boat.

The oak boat was over 13 feet (4 meters) long and sealed with a roof-like structure, the researchers said. It held the skeleton of a man who was about 50 years old when he died some time between A.D. 425 and 450. His grave goods included a small box shaped like a water bird, an ornate chair or throne carved out of alder wood, a bronze basin and a maple stool with a hunting scene and a runic inscription. The maritime artifacts coupled with the man's well-developed upper arm bones suggest he may have worked as a fisherman or boatman just before he died, the researchers wrote.

"The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest," study co-author Hauke Jöns, an archaeologist at the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research, said in the statement. "The man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances."

Archaeologists found a chair made from the trunk of an alder tree near the man's burial. The chair was likely a symbol of authority or power.

To learn more about this unusual burial and to determine where the man was from, researchers analyzed his DNA.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Genetic analyses confirm that a man buried at Fallward originated from the Danube region," study first author Daniel Myburgh, an ancient DNA researcher at IKMB, said in the statement. "He was also infected with a very rare leprosy pathogen."

The researchers found the DNA of the bacterium M. leprae in one of the man's teeth and in a foot bone. Because the leprosy DNA was so well preserved, the researchers were able to narrow down the strain that had infected him. This strain of leprosy may have evolved in Egypt around the fourth to second centuries B.C. and had never before been found in Central or Northern Europe, according to the statement.

But the man showed no signs of leprosy lesions in his skeleton, the researchers said. Leprosy first attacks the nerves and skin, but it can eventually eat away at the bones of the skeleton, particularly affecting the nose, jaw, hands and feet.

"Leprosy is a chronic disease," study co-author Almut Nebel, a biologist at IKMB, said in the statement. "Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease."

While the researchers don't know exactly what happened in this man's life, they suggested he might have been a mercenary who served in the Roman army and later retired to northwest Germany, becoming a high-status member of the community who was honored with an alder-wood "throne" in his burial. But he also may have acquired the Roman belt through trade, inheritance or as a war trophy, the researchers wrote.

Either way, the man's skeleton and his grave goods suggest that northwest Germany had long-distance connections in Europe even after the fall of the Roman Empire, according to the statement.

Myburgh, D. A., da Silva, N. A., Romeyer-Dherbey, J. H., Grefen-Peters, S., Jöns, H., Peek, C., Nebel, A., & Krause-Kyora, B. (2026). Paleogenomics reveals leprosy at the late antique burial site of Fallward in northern Germany. iScience, 29(11), 117877. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.117877

#6376. Scientists make the case for a specific year when human activity began transforming Earth, calling it the ‘Anthropocene epoch’

Scientists argue the Anthropocene began in 1952, separating a sharp global transformation from thousands of years of human influence.

Evidence of lead pollution and soil changes caused by early humans can be found buried in the earth dating back thousands of years ago. But when did human activity begin transforming Earth on a truly global scale?

A group of 37 researchers argues that early human impacts and the planet’s recent transformation are different stories.

Using one name for both, they write, obscures how sharply conditions changed in the mid-20th century.

They propose reserving “Anthropocene” for a geological epoch beginning in 1952, while giving the longer history of human influence a separate name.

The argument appears as a perspective piece, built on published evidence rather than a new dataset. Its lead author is Jan Zalasiewicz of the University of Leicester, who co-chairs the Anthropocene Working Group.

Co-authors include Buhm Soon Park of KAIST in South Korea, Julia Adeney Thomas of the University of Notre Dame, and Jürgen Renn of Germany’s Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology.

“The Anthropocene is a common language for understanding how rapidly and extensively humans are changing the Earth,” Park said.

“By clarifying its meaning and criteria, we can compare changes in the global environment more accurately and discuss together how we should respond.”

The relatively stable climate of the Holocene, which began about 11,700 years ago, helped people develop farming and build cities.

The authors’ case is that this stability ended in the middle of the 20th century.

That period saw the postwar surge of industry, population, and consumption known as the Great Acceleration.

The surge left marks in mud and ice. Across sites around the world, the chemical and physical traces of human activity pile up in layers centered on 1952.

That is also the year fallout from the first hydrogen bomb test settled across the globe. Those layers are the evidence the proposal rests on.

Humanity has used more energy since the 1950s than in the whole of the Holocene before it, most of it from fossil fuels.

A formal proposal to add the Anthropocene to the geological time scale, starting in 1952, went to the International Commission on Stratigraphy in October 2023.

The commission rejected it in March 2024, amid disagreement over whether an epoch only seven decades old was too brief to count.

The rejection did not retire the word, and the authors sort its uses into two families.

The meaning they defend is a geological epoch beginning when the Earth system stopped behaving as it had during the Holocene.

The other, which they call the extended Anthropocene, gathers up every substantial human impact over tens of thousands of years, from the earliest reshaping of ecosystems to the steam engine.

Proposed starting points have ranged widely. Some put it at 1784, when James Watt improved the steam engine.

Others point to European colonization of the Americas in the 1600s, or to farmed soils thousands of years earlier.

The authors call the extended version a valid idea but a different one. It can’t be pinned to a layer of rock, so the “-cene” ending, which marks a geological epoch, doesn’t fit it.

They suggest a separate label, such as “anthroposphere,” to keep the two apart.

The authors’ table of changes since the 1950s reads like an inventory of a different planet. Global freshwater use rose more than 300%, and the water held behind dams rose 1,500%.

Those dams are one reason rivers now deliver half as much sediment to the sea as they did.

The changes also reshaped marine and terrestrial life.

Predatory marine fish have declined about 90% since 1950 as the global catch quadrupled, and coral reefs, kelp forests, and mangroves have each lost about half their extent.

Humans and their livestock now make up about 98% of the mass of mammals on land, a shift other researchers have described as pushing life toward a mass extinction.

The authors lean on the planetary boundaries framework, which sets safe limits for nine Earth processes against pre-1950s Holocene baselines.

Seven of the nine have been crossed. That framework already treats the 1950s as the dividing line, they wrote, and a formal epoch would make that comparison standard.

Whether the commission will vote again is open, and the authors call formal recognition an ongoing aim.

The evidence keeps growing as new sites are analyzed, they wrote, from ocean chemistry to the plastics and persistent pollutants piling up in modern sediments.

They also acknowledged that a formal name on the time scale would not, by itself, make other fields adopt it.

In the scenario the authors describe, atmospheric carbon dioxide would still approach 500 parts per million even if the world reaches net zero carbon dioxide emissions by 2050.

Most polar sea ice and coral reefs would be lost, and sea level rise would keep accelerating.

Their research priorities are tracking heat, acidity, and plastics through the oceans, and pinning down the planetary boundaries and the tipping points behind them.

For now, 1952 remains a proposed boundary, and the Anthropocene remains a term with more than one meaning.

The perspective was published in the journal Nature Reviews Earth & Environment.

#6375. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

#6374. Early galaxies in the newborn universe spread elements like carbon and oxygen way faster than anyone expected

Webb found carbon, oxygen and silicon in moving gas around young galaxies, so heavy elements had already spread just 500 million years after the Big Bang.

In its first moments, the Universe held almost nothing but hydrogen and helium. Carbon, oxygen and other heavy elements came later, made inside stars.

Yet those elements had already spread into the gas around a galaxy seen just 500 million years after the Big Bang, and around two others seen a little later.

So the recycling that carries material from one generation of stars to the next was already working in at least some galaxies. The Universe was less than 4 percent of its present age.

Yongda Zhu, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Arizona and its Steward Observatory, led the work with colleagues there and at UC Riverside and the University of Michigan. Their sample is three bright galaxies, so the team can’t yet say how typical those galaxies were.

Light carries a record of whatever it passes through. Each element absorbs its own set of colors, and those colors show up as thin dark gaps when the light is spread out into a spectrum.

Zhu’s team used the starlight from each galaxy as its own light source. On its way to Earth, that light crossed the gas around the galaxy, and the gas left its gaps behind.

Catching gaps this faint took NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope. The light had been traveling for more than 13 billion years, and Webb collected it for about 29 hours with the setting that captured those colors.

All three came from a deep Webb survey of one patch of sky, and they were the only galaxies in it bright enough for this kind of measurement. The team chose them on brightness alone, before checking for any gaps, and all three turned out to have them.

The gaps matched oxygen, carbon and silicon. Some of the oxygen atoms were intact. Some of the silicon and carbon atoms had lost one electron, and others had lost three, which takes harsher, more energetic conditions.

All of those versions showed up at overlapping speeds. A single calm cloud of gas inside a galaxy would have a hard time producing that mix. It points instead to gas in several states, moving together and tied to each galaxy.

The pattern of gaps looked broadly like the one astronomers see in star-forming galaxies from more than a billion years later. Elements like these went on to build later stars and rocky planets.

In an interview with Earth.com, Zhu tied the moving gas to stellar feedback – the push that massive stars and their explosions give the gas around them.

“You can picture young galaxies as both factories and distributors,” he said. “Stars inside them produce elements such as carbon, oxygen, and silicon, and stellar feedback then pushes some of this enriched gas outward.”

The gaps didn’t land exactly where they would for gas at rest alongside each galaxy. They were shifted slightly toward bluer colors, which happens when gas is moving toward the telescope.

The gas lay between each galaxy and Earth, so moving toward Earth meant moving away from the galaxy. The shifts match speeds of roughly 31 to 155 miles per second (50 to 250 kilometers per second). Even the low end would cross the continental United States in about a minute and a half.

“In our JWST spectra, we see this gas moving relative to the galaxies themselves, showing that these elements were already being spread into their surroundings,” Zhu said.

The speeds can’t show how far out the gas reached. A wind blowing close to a galaxy and gas spread farther around it would produce the same shift, and churning motions inside the galaxy could add to it.

The most heavily stripped atoms may have been moving faster than the rest, but sharper spectra will be needed to confirm that.

Webb had already found heavy elements inside galaxies even older than these three, including oxygen in one of the most distant galaxies known.

Outside galaxies, most earlier measurements came from later times. They relied on light from extremely bright, distant galaxy cores shining through random stretches of gas, which were only loosely connected to any one galaxy.

“The speed of the process was the most striking part,” Zhu told Earth.com.

“Previous JWST observations had already shown that very early galaxies could produce heavy elements, but our results show that galaxies were also beginning to redistribute those elements into their environments remarkably early.”

The very first stars would have formed from pure hydrogen and helium. Astronomers have spent years looking for them, and they’ve proved hard to find.

Zhu said the result may help explain why. Once the first generations of stars began enriching their surroundings, he said, “chemically pristine environments may have disappeared rapidly.”

The heavy elements needn’t have come mostly from those first stars, though. Other researchers’ models show that a later generation of stars, with some reaching 200 to 300 times the mass of the Sun, could make carbon and oxygen this quickly.

Three bright galaxies can’t show how common this was. Some other gas clouds seen in the early universe hold almost no heavy elements, so the spreading was probably patchy, reaching some places well before others.

At this level of detail, Webb’s spectra also blur fine structure, and the team couldn’t map where the gas ends. An actively feeding black hole in one of the galaxies can’t be fully ruled out either, though the spectra show no clear sign of black hole activity.

“The next major question is how common this process was,” Zhu said. He wants deeper observations of more galaxies, to learn whether outward-moving enriched gas was common in the early universe. Sharper spectra could also separate the motions of the gas in its different states.

For now, the finding rests on three of the brightest galaxies of their time. Larger samples will show whether the rest of the young universe was spreading its elements just as early.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

#6373. Wanting a digital detox may reveal something unexpected about you

A new study explores why people want a digital detox and how their attitudes relate to self-control, mindfulness, and screen habits.

Eighty-one percent of people feel positive about the idea of putting down their phones and stepping away from screens for a while.

But here’s the twist: that desire to unplug has almost nothing to do with being addicted to technology.

People who score high on wanting a digital detox aren’t the ones doom-scrolling at 2 a.m. They’re the mindful, self-controlled types who’ve simply decided their attention is worth protecting.

A team from Goethe University Frankfurt and the University of Bath has developed and validated the first psychometric scale for measuring attitudes toward digital detox.

The Attitude toward Digital Detox (ADD) scale is a seven-item questionnaire. Participants rate their agreement with statements like “Reducing my digital activities improves my mental health.”

Rated on a 1-to-7 scale, the measure captures how favorably someone views the idea of temporarily dialing down their digital consumption.

Digital detox, as the researchers define it, is fundamentally different from technology avoidance.

Avoiding technology means permanently rejecting a specific device or platform because it’s too complex, too inflexible, or not worth the switching costs.

A digital detox attitude is something else entirely. It’s a conscious, temporary inclination toward balance.

The development process was exhaustive. The participants were a mix of US adults recruited online and Central European university students.

Across seven studies, the team started by asking 157 participants to generate statements describing both attitudes toward and behaviors around digital detox. That produced 628 candidate items.

Consumer behavior experts from universities including Tübingen, Bocconi, Cologne, Passau, and St. Gallen then rated each item for representativeness and comprehensibility.

The pool shrank to 72, then 27 after content validity screening.

Finally, it went down to seven items after exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses on 400 participants.

The resulting scale showed strong internal consistency and only weak correlation with social desirability.

People weren’t just saying what sounded virtuous.

Study 4 tested the scale against a web of related psychological constructs using 382 US adults. The correlations painted a clear picture  and some of it was genuinely unexpected.

Self-control correlated positively with ADD scores. So did mindfulness and holding a growth mindset about intelligence.

People who believe their cognitive abilities can develop were more favorable toward stepping away from screens.

All of that tracks with the idea that digital detox attitudes emerge from a proactive appraisal process. People consciously evaluate their digital consumption and decide they’d benefit from less of it.

What didn’t correlate was more revealing. Perceived stress showed no significant relationship with ADD.

Neither did pathological internet use or smartphone addiction. These findings suggest that the desire to unplug extends beyond people experiencing problematic technology use.

“Being able to reliably measure that attitude opens the door to understanding what makes people more receptive to stepping back from technology, how those attitudes develop and whether they ultimately translate into changes in digital behavior,” said study co-author Lisa Eckmann.

In a pre-registered study with 1,583 US adults, participants chose a video genre they enjoyed and then alternated between watching clips and doing word-search puzzles.

Afterward, they could freely choose to watch another video or do another puzzle. People scoring higher on the ADD scale spent significantly less time watching each video.

However, ADD scores didn’t predict whether participants chose another video or another puzzle.

More favorable attitudes were associated with shorter viewing times, suggesting a connection with how long people engaged rather than whether they started.

Two additional validation studies tested whether the scale could distinguish between groups with predictably different orientations toward screens.

Members of Reddit communities focused on reducing screen time or using paper journals, such as r/nosurf and r/bulletjournal, scored significantly higher on the ADD scale than members of technology-focused communities such as r/ebooks and r/SmartThings.

The gap was large: 5.33 versus 3.47 on the seven-point scale.

Among Central European university students surveyed during the pandemic, those who preferred face-to-face teaching scored markedly higher on the detox scale.

And their attitudes predicted real behavior. Higher ADD scores correlated with actually attending more lectures in person over the winter term.

The researchers grounded the scale in Lazarus and Folkman’s transactional model of stress and coping.

The framework proposes that when people repeatedly experience digital consumption as taxing, they begin to view disengagement as a way to cope.

Over time, those experiences may develop into a more stable attitude.

That’s what the ADD scale measures: the crystallized disposition, not the momentary frustration.

One practical implication is immediate. People who score high on digital device usage time score lower on the ADD scale.

That negative correlation was statistically significant. The attitude does seem to connect, however loosely, to how much time people actually spend online.

But the researchers are careful to note that the attitude-behavior gap in digital consumption is well documented. Screen-time tracking apps reliably raise awareness of heavy usage.

They rarely produce sustained behavior change.

The scale opens several doors. Marketers could use it to identify consumers receptive to intentional disengagement and design experiences accordingly.

Researchers can now investigate whether there’s a subjective tipping point where digital consumption tips from manageable into overload.

And in a landscape increasingly shaped by AI-driven personalization and algorithmically curated feeds designed to maximize engagement, the question of who wants to opt out – and why – is only going to get more pressing.

The study is published in the journal Psychology & Marketing.

Researchers used CT scans to crack a 400-year-old code and open a mysterious padlock that washed up in Wales with the Ann Francis treasure hoard.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Elizabethan padlock has been opened for the first time in more than 400 years after researchers used X-ray imaging techniques to crack its four-letter combination.

The brass lock was part of the Ann Francis treasure hoard, named after the British merchant ship that wrecked during a storm off the coast of Wales in 1583. Researchers believe the lock once secured a chest aboard the ship, before becoming separated from whatever riches it was protecting.

Some of the Ann Francis' cargo was recovered at the time of the wreck, while the rest was claimed by the sea. In recent decades, dredging and storms on Margam beach in South Wales have exposed some of the ship's lost treasure.

Between 1996 and 2017, metal detectorist Peter Hughes found the lock and much of the hoard, which included gold and silver coins. The lock was subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru — National Museum Wales, which worked with researchers at Cardiff University in Wales to decipher its combination.

To study the lock's internal mechanisms, the team used micro-CT scans, which make thousands of X-rays that can then be configured into a 3D digital image. By matching internal notches to external letters in the digital 3D image, the researchers were able to decipher the correct four-letter code — "ANCE" — and open the lock.

"We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us," David Williams, a research associate at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University, said in a statement. "It's not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!"

The Ann Francis was owned by Francis Shaxton, a merchant and notorious smuggler. Francis claimed the ship was sailing along the eastern English coast from King’s Lynn to Hartlepool, when it was actually traveling in the opposite direction, heading to Spain to deliver a cargo of wheat. Spain was dependent on grain shipments at the time and paid for such shipments in gold and silver from colonial conquests in Central and South America, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The ship was traveling back from Spain to England when, on the evening of Dec. 28, 1583, it was caught in a violent storm. After heading off course, the ship ended its journey in ruin off Margam beach.

A parish register noted the loss of 14 sailors during the same month as the wreckage, which could have been The Ann Francis's crew, according to Amgueddfa Cymru. The deaths were blamed on the nefarious work of a supposed witch.

Locals were quick to loot the Ann Francis wreck before a legal dispute ensued over who had the right to its goods. One Welsh lord claiming the wreck made an inventory list of items he impounded, which included cannons, guns, a piece of mast, Spanish silver and three chests with their locks broken. The newly cracked lock could have originally secured one of these chests, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Centuries after the ship was wrecked, Hughes found the lock near a previously undiscovered stash of Spanish silver coins and coin weights while metal detecting on the beach.

"When I found the lock I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition," Hughes said. "When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief."

Hughes said he attempted to open the lock himself over many years but could never find the right combination. After Amgueddfa Cymru acquired the lock, staff were concerned that they could hear grit moving around inside the dials, and with more than 1,000 possible combinations, they didn't want to cause any damage.

The micro-CT scans offered a nondestructive view inside the lock, and an opportunity to finally identify the correct four-letter combination.

"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalising mystery to solve," Alastair Willis, the senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said in the statement. "Of course, now we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."

Patrick Pester is the trending news writer at Live Science. His work has appeared on other science websites, such as BBC Science Focus and Scientific American. Patrick retrained as a journalist after spending his early career working in zoos and wildlife conservation. He was awarded the Master's Excellence Scholarship to study at Cardiff University where he completed a master's degree in international journalism. He also has a second master's degree in biodiversity, evolution and conservation in action from Middlesex University London. When he isn't writing news, Patrick investigates the sale of human remains.

#6371. A tiny protein ring reveals how cells keep DNA under control

Scientists filmed a tiny protein complex changing shape and gripping DNA, revealing how it captures and holds different DNA segments.

A textbook draws DNA as a tidy spiral staircase. Inside a living cell, though, it is forever being copied, strained, broken, and patched, and proteins do the handling.

A new study has filmed a protein complex called Smc5/6 at work.

The ring-shaped complex swings open and shut, closes around DNA, and sometimes holds two DNA segments at once.

Kenichi Umeda and Noriyuki Kodera of the Nano Life Science Institute at Kanazawa University in Japan led the work with Yasuto Murayama of the National Institute of Genetics.

They watched purified protein from baker’s yeast, outside any cell, so what they saw is the machine running on a bench rather than inside a living nucleus.

“By observing individual Smc5/6 structures as they interacted with DNA, we could see how changes in their shape are associated with different ways of capturing and holding DNA,” Umeda said.

“These observations bring us closer to understanding how this protein assembly carries out its roles in maintaining chromosomes.”

Smc5/6 belongs to a small family of ring-shaped complexes that organize chromosomes, the bundles that carry a cell’s DNA.

Its job is clearing away DNA structures that would jam cell division, such as stalled copying machinery and strands twisted around each other. Cells need it to divide correctly.

Earlier methods gave either a frozen snapshot of its shape or a record of its movement with no structural detail. The Kanazawa team used a microscope that works by touch.

It drags a needle tip far finer than a hair across the sample and records a new image every 0.5 to 1.5 seconds.

The complex has two long arms connected by a hinge at one end and a pair of motor domains at the other. These motor domains break down ATP, the cell’s energy currency.

Lying flat, the complex measured about 38 nanometers from hinge to motors. A human hair is more than a thousand times wider.

Without fuel, more than 80% of the complexes had their arms close together, about 5 nanometers apart at the middle. The team called this shape the I-form.

Add ATP and some of them swung open into a ring, the O-form, with the arms 19 nanometers apart.

About 60% of complexes with a mutation that allows ATP binding but prevents its breakdown were open.

So binding the fuel opens the ring, and using it up lets the arms fall back together.

The team saw single complexes flip between the two shapes as they watched.

One small subunit, Nse2, is attached partway along one arm like a splint.

Without it, a few complexes bent their arms sharply toward each other, a shape never seen when Nse2 was present.

Other complexes in the same protein family are known to fold at an elbow this way, so the splint may be what keeps Smc5/6 straight.

Loading the complex onto a loop of DNA about 1,900 letters long required both ATP and a pair of helper subunits. Once on, the ring slid freely along the strand.

The team observed two ways the complex gripped DNA.

About half of the normal complexes held the strand at the hinge end, swaying as they did so. The rest gripped it at the motor end and stayed rigid, tilted at about 73 degrees to the DNA.

The mutant that can’t burn ATP almost always gripped at the motor end. Breaking down the fuel therefore appears to help move DNA from one compartment of the ring to the other.

The two grips were also associated with different DNA bends.

DNA held at the hinge curved by a median of 110 degrees at the contact point, while DNA held at the motor end bent less than 50 degrees.

When Smc5/6 was bound to a relaxed circle of DNA, the circle shrank.

The team measured how spread out each DNA loop was.

Loops carrying the protein were about 6% more compact on average, and loops the protein had pulled into a twisted shape were about 30% more compact.

The twisted loops more often carried more than one complex.

In 33 of 38 twisted loops with multiple complexes, two sections of DNA stayed pinned together for about 100 consecutive frames.

A separate test on magnetic beads confirmed it. With ATP present, the protein tethered about 25% of free DNA circles to DNA fixed on the beads, compared with under 3% without ATP.

Cutting either DNA circle once released the other, suggesting that the protein ring encircled both.

The mutant that can’t break down ATP tethered DNA just as well, suggesting that holding two DNA segments requires ATP binding but not its breakdown.

That sets tethering apart from a better-known trick of this protein family, reeling DNA into loops, which runs on a steady supply of ATP.

The experiments used purified yeast protein and bare DNA, without the crowding, other proteins, or ongoing repair activity found inside a real nucleus.

The authors wrote that their case for DNA being enclosed within a closed protein ring rests on several converging lines of evidence rather than a direct chemical proof.

The sharply bent form appeared in only 3% of complexes lacking Nse2.

The team said the microscope’s surface may have held the molecules too flat to show how often it really occurs. Nor can the imaging rule out that some closed-looking complexes were open rings standing on edge.

The next question is whether Nse2 does more than keep the arms straight. Does it also help control how the complex pulls DNA into loops?

The team will need to film the complex while it builds a loop to find out.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.
