#6369. Tiny populations are challenging what we know about wildlife recovery

Species reduced to fewer than 50 wild individuals can still recover, a study finds, challenging assumptions about their chances of survival.

In 1974, the Mauritius kestrel was down to just four known birds in the wild.

Conservation textbooks practically wrote the obituary. Half a century later, the Mauritius kestrel numbers in the hundreds.

A team led by Donal Smith at Monash University, working with researchers from the Zoological Society of London, has now tracked every bird and mammal species that dropped below 50 individuals in the wild at any point since 1950.

The findings deliver an empirically grounded gut punch to one of conservation’s most persistent – and most dangerous – assumptions: that tiny populations are doomed.

The theory sounds airtight. When a population gets critically small, bad things compound.

Inbreeding depression. Loss of genetic diversity. Random demographic swings that can wipe out a handful of animals in one bad season.

Biologists call this the “extinction vortex” – a feedback loop that supposedly drags small populations toward zero with increasing speed. Influential thresholds emerged.

Traditional genetic guidelines suggested effective population sizes of 50 to limit short-term inbreeding and 500 to maintain long-term evolutionary potential.

These figures describe the population’s genetic contribution to future generations, rather than a simple count of animals.

The team set out to test that assumption across a comprehensive set of bird and mammal species.

Smith’s team identified 147 bird and mammal species – 98 birds and 49 mammals – known to have fallen below 50 wild individuals since 1950.

Of these, 141 had enough time elapsed to assess an outcome.

The researchers classified every conservation action each species received into three categories.

Limiting factor mitigation covers efforts to remove whatever is driving the decline – predator control, habitat restoration, supplementary feeding.

Population manipulation acts directly on the species itself through captive breeding, translocation, or egg fostering.

Indirect action includes the softer tools: legal protections, public awareness campaigns, designating national parks.

Then they ran Bayesian multi-level logistic regression models to see what actually predicted recovery.

Of those 141 species, 39 went extinct. That’s 28 percent – a grim reminder that the extinction crisis is real.

But 33 species recovered to populations of 100 or more. Recovery was strongly associated with direct conservation action.

Among the 51 species that received direct conservation action, 61 percent recovered to at least 100 individuals.

Among the 90 species that received no direct action, just 2 percent recovered. And 37 percent went extinct.

“Our work shows that population size alone shouldn’t determine whether we give up on a species,” Smith said.

The Bayesian models put hard numbers on it. Limiting factor mitigation carried an odds ratio of 8.71 for recovery to 100 or more individuals. Population manipulation had an odds ratio of 5.53.

The two together were even stronger: predicted probability of recovery hit 74 percent for birds and 71 percent for mammals when both action types were deployed.

Without either? Six percent for birds. Five percent for mammals.

The median time to recovery was 18 years. Eight species clawed back from populations below 20.

The Lord Howe woodhen might be the study’s most dramatic illustration.

Endemic to tiny Lord Howe Island in the Tasman Sea, the species was hammered by feral pigs, cats, and rodents after European arrival.

By the late 1970s, an estimated 23 birds remained. Conservationists launched a captive breeding program while eradicating pigs and cats.

Captive breeding and the removal of introduced predators helped the population recover to around 200 birds.

Following the 2019 rodent eradication campaign, numbers rose sharply, reaching an estimated minimum of 1,638 by late 2024.

Here’s what makes the findings politically charged. Conservation triage – the idea that some species are too far gone to justify spending on – has influenced real decisions.

The baiji, the Yangtze River dolphin, is the study’s starkest cautionary tale. Active conservation efforts were scaled back. The species went extinct.

But Smith’s team found surprisingly little evidence of deliberate triage actually driving extinctions. What they found instead was worse: indecision.

The Christmas Island pipistrelle was monitored for over a decade before anyone intervened. By then it was too late. Decision paralysis, not cold calculation, was the killer.

The urgency isn’t theoretical. While the study was being prepared, avian malaria was driving two Hawaiian honeycreepers – the ‘akikiki and the ‘akeke’e – toward the same cliff edge.

The ‘akikiki’s wild population had collapsed to an estimated four non-captive individuals by 2024. A captive breeding program established in 2015 is its lifeline.

The ‘akeke’e, whose population has dropped below 100, depends on whether malaria can be controlled. Recent genomics-informed modelling suggests it can survive – if the threat is addressed.

The paper is careful to note what recovery actually means. Many “recovered” species still require intensive management.

Island invasive species eradication demands permanent biosecurity. Large mammals may need anti-poaching protection indefinitely.

Captive breeding programs often maintain insurance populations for decades. Recovery, in other words, is not a finish line. It’s a commitment.

The findings challenge the idea that a critically small population is, by itself, a reason to abandon conservation efforts.

As the authors put it: predictions of extinction as an inevitable fate may be self-fulfilling.

We’re probably fortunate that so many determined conservationists refused to believe them.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

#6368. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

Sanders: The Deep End is a production of Science News. It’s based on original reporting by me, Laura Sanders. This episode was produced and mixed by Ella Rowen. Our project manager is Ashley Yeager. Seeds found in an ancient grave and chemical compounds discovered in mummy hair have revealed people got high on marijuana 2,800 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed the oldest evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old monumental tomb in Siberia. The presence of plant seeds in the grave and chemical traces of the drug in mummy hair suggest people practiced a funeral ritual that may have involved a grim practice: calming human sacrifice victims with cannabis.

In a study published Thursday (Nov. 5) in the journal Science, researchers investigated the contents of a "royal mound" burial at the Tunnug archaeological site in the Uyuk valley of southern Siberia. Archaeologists discovered four wooden structures containing several log coffins in the middle of the mound. On top of the wooden burial structures were the skeletons of horses that once formed a "spectral cavalcade," a Scythian funeral tradition that involved sacrificing horses and humans. And inside the burial structures, the archaeologists discovered piles of tiny seeds from the plant Cannabis ruderalis, a wild type of cannabis or marijuana.

Cannabis likely originated in Asia and was cultivated thousands of years ago for various purposes, including for ropes and textiles, and 6,000 years ago as an oilseed crop, according to the study. But it's unclear when people learned about the psychoactive properties of the plant. In the fifth century B.C., the ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Scythian nomads inhaled the fumes from burning hemp seeds. And evidence of cannabis use was previously discovered in a cemetery in China dated to about 500 B.C. The new study, however, pushes back this date by three centuries.

Archaeologists found evidence of cannabis use in a burial mound in southern Siberia.

Researchers discovered more than 1,000 whole cannabis seeds and around 500 partial seeds in the Tunnug burial mound, and they carbon-dated them to between 800 and 760 B.C. They also recovered several human hair samples from the grave. An analysis of the hair revealed signals matching cannabinol and THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), psychoactive chemical compounds found in cannabis. The tests could not determine how much of the drug people consumed, however.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," study first author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany, said in a statement.

But given the burial context of the discovery, the use of cannabis may have had a darker purpose.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," Caspari said. The tradition of human sacrifice, in particular, "would have potentially made the plant a useful agent to calm individuals who were to be included in the rituals," the researchers wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The new study confirms the ancient use of cannabis in funerals in Central Asia and extends the date back to 2,800 years ago, the researchers noted. Future work is planned but will focus on other aspects of ancient cannabis.

"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," Caspari said. "This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of the crop soon."

Caspari, G., Sadykov, T., Formicheva, D., Blochin, J., Armbruster, D., Happel, O., Ryabogina, N., Boxleitner, K., Spengler, R. (2026). Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago. Science. http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/science.aeg3800

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. #6366. Monterrey’s mountain folds tell a story millions of years in the making

An astronaut photograph reveals Monterrey’s sweeping mountain ridges, where ancient rock folds shape the landscape around a growing Mexican city.

Monterrey has spread across the plains of northeastern Mexico, but its mountains leave little room for straight lines.

Long ridges bend beside the city, tracing folds in the rock that formed tens of millions of years before streets and factories occupied the landscape.

Today’s Image of the Day captures this meeting of urban growth and ancient geology.

Photographed from the International Space Station on August 26, 2026, the scene shows Monterrey alongside the sweeping ridges of the Sierra Madre Oriental.

From the ground, these mountains form a familiar skyline.

From orbit, their repeating curves reveal a much larger pattern: a landscape compressed, lifted, and gradually carved into the terrain that surrounds the city today.

The ridges along Monterrey’s southern edge began as layers of sediment that became limestone during the late Mesozoic era.

Their present shape developed much later, as forces within Earth’s crust squeezed and folded the rock.

Mountain building in the region occurred roughly 80 million to 50 million years ago.

Rather than remaining flat, the layers buckled into a series of folds, creating the foundation of the parallel ridges visible today.

Erosion then changed the relief. Over millions of years, weaker layers wore away more readily than resistant rock, helping turn the folded formations into distinct ridges and valleys.

That sequence explains why the mountains appear to follow one another across the landscape. Their curves reflect related layers shaped by the same broad episode of deformation.

The photograph offers a view of both processes at once. Folding established the pattern in the rock; erosion made that pattern more apparent at the surface.

Monterrey is the capital of Nuevo León and a major center of Mexican industry.

Steelmaking and ironworks form part of an economy that also produces glass, plastics, textiles, and processed foods.

Its metropolitan area had about 5.3 million residents in the 2020 census. That figure describes the wider urban region, rather than just the municipality of Monterrey.

The city occupies a semiarid floodplain beside the mountains. As development spreads, the contrast between the built environment and the surrounding terrain becomes especially striking.

A city map can show roads and municipal boundaries. This view from space adds another set of boundaries: steep slopes, narrow valleys, and rocky ridges that influence where development can extend.

The mountains are more than a backdrop to Monterrey. Their position helps define the shape of the urban area, bringing ancient geological structures directly into the geography of everyday life.

The Río Santa Catarina connects the mountain landscape with the city below. After cutting through the Sierra Madre Oriental, it crosses the urban area and carries runoff from its watershed.

For much of the time, the river holds little water or appears dry. In this semiarid setting, however, a quiet channel still has an essential function.

Summer rainfall can send substantial volumes of water through it. The channel provides a route for that runoff to move across the metropolitan area.

It also supports living communities within the city. Vegetation along the river provides habitat for plants and animals and creates connections through an otherwise heavily developed landscape.

Part of the river channel in the metropolitan area received state protection as an urban park in 2008. Its value extends across seasons, serving wildlife even when little flowing water is visible.

Separate mountain masses also rise beside Monterrey’s urban neighborhoods. Among them is Sierra Las Mitras, a protected ridge that reaches approximately 4,900 feet above the city.

Its slopes hold a changing sequence of habitats. Cacti and thorny shrubs occupy lower, rocky ground, while cooler, wetter conditions support oak and pine forests higher up.

That change shows how elevation can create different environments within a relatively small area. The journey uphill passes through habitats that contrast sharply with the dry terrain below.

Cerro de la Silla, known for its saddle-shaped profile, adds another distinctive landmark to Monterrey’s mountain setting.

As Monterrey expands, its ancient ridges continue to shape the city’s boundaries and guide its growth.

Image Credit: NASA/JSC, ISS Expedition 75

#6365. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

P.K. Masonick et al. The repeated evolution of anti-bat bioacoustics in hawkmoths. Proceedings of the Royal Society B. 2026. doi: 10.1098/rspb.2026.2303

#6363. Scientists learn how colorblind cuttlefish constantly adjust their skin patterns to perfectly match the ocean floor

A new study reveals that cuttlefish camouflage is a complex, multi-step process. Rather than an instant match, cuttlefish continuously check and adjust their skin to blend into the seafloor.

On the seafloor, a cuttlefish can make its skin look so much like the sand and pebbles around it that the animal disappears.

Earlier experiments made the trick look simple: the eyes read the background, and the brain sends out the matching pattern with no checking afterward. Up close, the change is slower and busier than that.

The skin reaches its match in steps. The change slows down, speeds up again and slows once more, and each step brings the pattern closer to the background. The animal seems to be checking its own work as it goes.

Sam Reiter at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) in Japan co-led the study of cuttlefish camouflage. He shared the lead with Gilles Laurent at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Germany, and the study came out in Nature in June 2023.

Reiter and Laurent’s team filmed a dozen young common European cuttlefish, Sepia officinalis, in a lab tank. The animals had hatched from eggs collected in the English Channel and the North Atlantic, and their main bodies measured 1.7 to 3.5 inches (42 to 90 mm) long.

“Prior research suggested that cuttlefish only had a limited selection of pattern components that they would use to achieve the best match against the environment,” said Reiter, who heads the Computational Neuroethology Unit at OIST.

“But our latest research has shown that their camouflaging response is much more complicated and flexible – we just hadn’t been able to detect it as previous approaches were not as detailed or quantitative.”

Cuttlefish are cephalopods, the group that also includes squid and octopuses. They change their skin color with millions of tiny sacs of pigment. A set of muscles surrounds each sac, and nerve cells in the brain control those muscles directly.

When the muscles pull, the sac stretches wide and shows its color. When they relax, it shrinks back and the color is hidden. Expand some and shrink others, and a new pattern appears, the way dots on a screen make a picture.

Biologists call these sacs chromatophores. To build one pattern, the brain controls tens of thousands of nerve cells at once, and the whole routine runs on instinct. Cuttlefish branched off from the line that led to humans more than 550 million years ago.

The skin can also raise small bumps to change its texture, but this study looked only at the flat pattern of light and dark.

The filming tank was about 28 inches (70 cm) on a side. Printed photos of pebbles and rock ran across the tank floor on a roll of fabric. Every 5 to 10 minutes, a researcher turned a hand crank to change the scene.

Above the tank, 17 high-resolution cameras filmed the skin at 25 frames a second. At that magnification, a single pigment sac covered about 54 pixels. A separate wide-angle camera filmed the whole animal at the same time.

From the wide-angle footage of a single animal, the team collected more than 200,000 images. They came from 27 hours of video.

A neural network, a kind of artificial intelligence, turned each image into a list of numbers describing the pattern, with a supercomputer at OIST doing the processing.

With the patterns written as numbers, the team could ask how many independent ways a cuttlefish pattern can vary. Earlier studies had sorted the patterns into three basic types.

For these animals, the number of independent ways came out close to 60, and the method the team used usually underestimates.

Next, the team swapped one background for another and watched the skin change. A change typically took around a minute, and it didn’t happen at a steady pace.

The skin changed quickly, then almost stopped changing, then sped up again, and it settled only after several of these pauses.

In 85 such changes across three animals, the team checked which way the pattern changed each time the change restarted after a pause.

Each time, it moved toward where it would finally end up, rather than continuing in the direction it had started out in.

The closer the pattern got to its final form, the more often the change paused and the longer each pause lasted. Each step improved the match with the background.

“The cuttlefish would often overshoot their target skin pattern, pause, and then come back,” said Theodosia Woo, a graduate student at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research and one of the study’s two first authors.

“In other words, cuttlefish don’t simply detect the background and go straight to a set pattern, instead, it is likely that they continuously receive feedback about their skin pattern and use it to adjust their camouflage.”

The authors compared the process to a hand correcting its path as it reaches for something, rather than a throw that can’t be corrected once it leaves the hand.

Even repeats weren’t exact repeats. When the same animal faced the same background change again, the final patterns looked identical to a person.

Underneath, though, different sets of pigment sacs expanded and shrank together each time. In one case, about 1,100 sacs that changed size as one group during the first change split into 15 separate groups during the second.

The team also looked at a different skin change. When something threatens a cuttlefish, it turns pale, a response called blanching.

In the lab, the threat was a researcher’s hand reaching toward the animal and stopping 8 inches (20 cm) away. In other trials, it was a dark circle growing larger on a screen beside the tank.

“Unlike camouflaging, blanching was fast and direct, suggesting it uses a different and repeatable control system,” said Dominic Evans, a postdoctoral fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research.

The pale skin wasn’t blank, though. Up close, faint traces of the camouflage pattern the animal had been showing were still there. And in 16 of 17 threat trials in one animal, the skin went back to nearly the same pattern afterward.

“This suggests that information about the initial camouflage somehow remains,” said Xitong Liang, the study’s other first author, who did the work as a postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute and is now at Peking University.

“The blanching is more like a response that temporarily overrides the camouflage signals from the brain and might be controlled by a completely different neural circuit in the brain.”

If a cuttlefish adjusts its pattern by checking the result, something has to tell its brain what the skin currently looks like. The study can’t say what.

“Exactly how they receive that feedback – whether they use their eyes, or whether they have a sense of how contracted the muscles around each chromatophore are – we don’t yet know,” Woo said.

So far, nothing like a muscle-position sensor has been found around a cuttlefish’s pigment sacs. The authors also raised a third possibility: the brain might keep a copy of the commands it just sent out and use that copy to judge the result.

The authors suggested a way to test whether the eyes are involved. Cover the animal’s skin while it camouflages, so it can’t see its own pattern, and watch whether the pauses and corrections still happen.

Liang said the next step is to record activity from cuttlefish brains while the animals change pattern, to work out how they control the skin.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

New research shows that a powerful 2021 marsquake emanating from Valles Marineris — the largest canyon in the solar system — was triggered by unexpected movement in a fault line deep below the gigantic structure, revealing that tectonic activity can still occur on geologically "dead" worlds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mars' supersize Valles Marineris — the largest known canyon in the solar system — is still tectonically active even though the Red Planet is geologically "dead," new research on a previously record-breaking marsquake reveals.

On Aug. 25, 2021, NASA's InSight lander, which touched down on the Red Planet in 2018, detected a powerful marsquake, designated S0976a. The Martian equivalent of an earthquake reached magnitude 4.2, which, at the time, was the most powerful quake that InSight or any other Mars lander had ever seen. (Since then, a 4.7 magnitude marsquake in May 2022 knocked it off the top spot, but S0976a remains second on this list.)

Unlike most marsquakes, which have been minor tremors triggered by meteorite impacts near InSight, S0976a was a deep rumble that originated from the opposite side of Mars as the robotic seismologist, in the western half of Valles Marineris.

In the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Communications, researchers reanalyzed the seismic wave data of S0976a and found that the quake originated from within a fault line running below the enormous canyon. The most likely explanation, they argue, is that there was tectonic movement in this hidden crustal crack.

"Valles Marineris is one of the most spectacular geological structures anywhere in the solar system, but until now we didn't know for certain that its faults are still active," study first author Jung-Hun Song, a researcher in the Department of Earth Science and Engineering at Imperial College London, said in a statement. "What we see is that this is not just a 'dead' fossil landscape, as faults deep beneath the canyon can still slip and generate marsquakes, long after the geological processes that originally formed them have ceased."

S0976a is the second-largest marsquake ever detected by NASA's InSight lander, shown here in a NASA clean room on April 30, 2015.

Valles Marineris is an enormous set of interconnected gullies and ravines stretching up to 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) in length, or roughly 10 times longer than the Grand Canyon. It is also up to 20 times wider and five times deeper, meaning that if you found yourself stranded at the bottom, it could take you a couple of months to climb out again.

The enormous chasm — named after the Mariner 9 spacecraft, which helped discover it in 1971 — is clearly visible from space, like a giant scar carved into the Red Planet's face. From orbit, you would also see the nearby Tharsis region, which is home to Mars' giant volcanoes, including Olympus Mons, which is at least three times taller than Mount Everest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

These imposing structures are proof that Mars was once geologically active, perhaps even more so than Earth. However, scientists think the Red Planet's surface has remained relatively unchanged for nearly 3 billion years, according to the European Space Agency.

Valles Marineris is almost as long as the continental U.S. is wide. (In this photo, captured by NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter, an optical illusion known as relief inversion may make the canyon appear as if it is raised above the surface, which it is not.)

The reason for this is twofold. First, Mars is smaller than Earth, so its core and mantle have cooled much faster than our planet's and are, therefore, less dynamic. Second, Mars has no tectonic plates. Instead of giant patches of crust butting against each other, the Red Planet's outermost layer is almost completely intact and acts like a giant lid over its cooling molten innards. (Research published earlier this week throws the "dead" theory into question, hinting that magma may still lurk below dormant Martian volcanoes).

Despite this, Mars still has fault lines. But rather than being a boundary between tectonic plates, these lines are more like giant cracks in its crust, some of which are visible at the surface.

In the new study, researchers discovered proof of what they call a slip-strike marsquake, where "blocks of crust move horizontally past one another along a steep, deeply rooted fault," the team said. They believe this occurred somewhere between 12 and 25 miles (20 to 40 km) below Valles Marineris.

The researchers also simulated several other potential causes of the marsquake, including a major asteroid strike or a landslide within the canyon, but nothing else could explain the patterns they saw.

Using seismic wave data captured by InSight, researchers were able to pinpoint the epicenter of the S0976a masquake (represented as a yellow star near the top of this map).

"What makes the result compelling is that several completely different types of evidence point in the same direction," Song said.

The finding also raises hopes that similar tectonic activity could one day be detected on other worlds across the solar system.

"Our study opens up exciting possibilities for discovering ongoing seismic activity on other planetary bodies that we might otherwise consider geologically inactive," Song said.

The discovery highlights the importance of detecting and studying marsquakes, which were only officially discovered in 2019, thanks to InSight. (Scientists have since uncovered older marsquakes, using data collected by the Viking landers in the late 1970s.)

InSight sent back a final selfie to Earth on Dec. 19, 2022, showing a heavy coating of Martian dust on its solar panels. Its mission was officially ended two days later.

"S0976a has turned out to be an extraordinary event," study co-author Doyeon Kim, head of Imperial College London's Terrestrial and Planetary Seismology Lab, said in the statement. "Its waves traveled through the core and helped us investigate the deepest part of Mars, and now they are telling us what happened at the source itself. From a single marsquake, we can learn both about the center of the planet and about an active fault beneath one of its most remarkable landscapes."

Scientists have similarly used marsquake vibrations from InSight to map out Mars' interior, leading to several intriguing subsurface discoveries, including dozens of blobs left over from ancient protoplanets, the hidden cause of the planet's uneven hemispheres, a potentially active "mantle plume" and a gigantic underground water reservoir containing enough liquid to cover Mars with a mile-deep (1.6 km) ocean.

Unfortunately, in December 2022, InSight quite literally bit the dust: A thick covering of Martian powder blocked its solar panels, preventing the lander from returning signals to Earth and thus ending its mission.

This means we currently have no way of detecting new marsquakes. However, the new study proves that the lander's archived data can still lead to exciting discoveries.

Song, J., Kim, D., Kolawole, F., Davis, J. M., Parry, R., & Maguire, R. (2026). Active crustal straining and fault reactivation at Valles Marineris. Nature Communications, 17(1). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78193-6

#6361. Scientists reach record-low temperature aboard China’s space station

Physicists on China's Tiangong station cooled 20,000 atoms to the coldest temperature in space: 9.7 trillionths of a degree above zero.

For 30 years, physicists have pushed clouds of atoms toward ever lower temperatures, with Earth’s gravity limiting how far they could go.

Now, a speck of gas aboard China’s Tiangong space station has reached what its creators report is a record-low temperature.

There, physicists chilled about 20,000 rubidium atoms to an equivalent temperature of 9.7 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero, which is minus 459.67°F (minus 273.15°C).

The previous record for a cloud like this was 38 trillionths, set in a drop tower on Earth.

The temperature here is a measure of how fast the cloud spreads once released, not a reading from a thermometer. The authors wrote that the result is the lowest they know of.

Xiaoji Zhou and Xuzong Chen of Peking University led the work with Weibiao Chen of the Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics and colleagues at Fudan University.

Their apparatus has been running on the station since October 2022. When they released the atoms, they could still see the cloud seven seconds later.

The usual way to make atoms this cold is to hold them in a trap and let the hottest ones escape, the way steam leaving a cup cools the coffee.

The looser the trap, the colder the atoms that remain. On Earth, though, a trap that is too loose simply drops its atoms. Gravity sets a floor.

That is why laboratories on the ground have stalled around 350 trillionths of a degree in three dimensions.

Drop towers and sounding rockets buy a few seconds of free fall.

NASA’s Cold Atom Laboratory on the International Space Station, which holds atoms with magnetic fields, has reached 52 trillionths and watched clouds for about a second.

The Chinese team used light instead of magnets. Two crossed laser beams make a trap that can hold atoms whatever their magnetic state, which opens up experiments a magnetic trap can’t run.

No one had made a quantum gas this way in orbit before.

The experiment lives in the Cold Atom Physics Rack aboard the space station‘s Mengtian module.

About two million rubidium atoms were loaded into the first trap and the laser power was eased down over about 20 seconds.

As the trap weakened, the gas formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a state in which many atoms share a single quantum state and behave collectively.

Weightlessness turned out to have a cost. On Earth, gravity tilts the trap and helps the hottest atoms spill out.

Without that tilt, evaporation in orbit was slower and less complete, and only about 65% of the atoms joined the condensate, against 89% in an identical setup on the ground.

The team’s fix was a stand-in for gravity. A magnetic field gradient pulled on the atoms whose spins made them magnetic, speeding their escape and pushing the rest into a single, magnetically neutral state.

The fraction in the condensate climbed to 89%, about 23,000 atoms.

Even a condensate isn’t finished cooling. The atoms still push on one another, and when the trap opens that pressure becomes motion.

So the team handed the atoms to a second, wider pair of beams, let the trap relax for just over a second, and then switched it off.

Released, the cloud drifted outward at about 70 to 88 micrometers a second, a few thousandths of an inch per second.

Translated into temperature, that is 9.7 trillionths of a degree, with an uncertainty of roughly three trillionths either way. The atoms were, for practical purposes, barely moving.

The team’s computer simulation of the same steps predicted 7.4 trillionths of a degree, and the authors attributed the difference to jitter in the laser beams.

A cloud that expands this slowly could improve atom interferometers, whose sensitivity can increase with the square of the atoms’ time in free flight.

Seven seconds of free fall in orbit is a very long time by that standard.

The temperature estimate rests on the first two seconds of expansion. Although the cloud remained visible afterward, the later images were too faint to use in the calculation.

The condensate is also small. The authors wrote that a trap whose volume can be tuned should let them hold more atoms.

Their stated goals are to study exotic quantum phases that only appear at these temperatures, and to build an atom interferometer in orbit.

That is a device that could test whether all objects really fall at the same rate.

Both goals would benefit from more atoms and longer free flight. The experiment marks a step toward creating those conditions in orbit.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6359. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6358. Crystals reveal what pushed seven very different volcanoes to erupt

Crystals from seven Andean volcanoes share one chemical fingerprint, tying each volcano eruption trigger to a pulse of hot magma from below.

A volcano that erupts once and goes quiet forever seems like a different animal from one that has blown up again and again.

A study of seven Andean volcanoes suggests that, despite their different histories, their eruptions shared a trigger.

The last crystals to grow before each eruption carry the same chemical fingerprint, and it points to a pulse of hotter magma pushing up from below.

Daniela Parra-Encalada, a doctoral student in the School of the Environment at the University of Queensland, read that fingerprint out of plagioclase.

That’s the common white mineral that makes up most of the crystals in volcanic rock.

Parra-Encalada worked with senior author Teresa Ubide and colleagues from Australia, the Universidad de Chile, Spain and Argentina.

Together they collected lava and ash from seven volcanoes along 143 miles (230 kilometers) of the Central Andes.

The work rests on 28 rock samples. Whether the same signal could ever help forecast an eruption is a question the team has only begun to test.

“Plagioclase grows in magma only a few kilometers below the surface, reacting to changes in temperature, water content and magma composition,” Parra-Encalada said.

One of those reactions is a swap of calcium for sodium, so each crystal keeps a record of the melt it grew from.

Two kinds of crystal turned up in every rock the team cut open. Large ones, up to about a twelfth of an inch (2 millimeters) long, grew slowly while the magma was stored underground.

Tiny ones, shorter than about a hundredth of an inch (300 micrometers), grew during the final rise to the surface.

The tiny crystals are the only ones that formed entirely from the magma that erupted.

Across all seven volcanoes, they held nearly the same calcium-to-sodium balance, and the outer rims of the large crystals matched them.

The team named that narrow band the plagioclase eruptibility field. The volcanoes couldn’t have been much more different.

Lascar, the most active volcano in the region, has neighbors that erupted only once, some as long as 3 million years ago.

Some lie on the main volcanic arc and others far behind it, where the crust is half as thick.

In an interview with Earth.com, Parra-Encalada was asked what surprised her most about the match.

“What surprised us most was discovering that this similarity was related to the textures and shapes of plagioclase crystals,” she said.

The cores of the large crystals told a different story. About half of all the plagioclase in these rocks didn’t grow from the erupted magma at all.

Its chemistry points to a silica-rich melt that cooled and crystallized for a long time a few miles down. Along the way it soaked up material from the surrounding crust.

Volcanologists call that kind of sluggish, crystal-packed body a mush.

In the Andean rocks, pieces of it arrived as clusters of interlocking crystals and as chunks of fully solidified rock, pulled loose and carried up when the eruption came.

The trapped crystals share their chemistry with crystals in the region’s ancient super-eruption deposits, which Parra-Encalada told Earth.com was one of the two findings that excited her most.

The same stalled magma systems may also matter for how copper and gold collect underground, she said.

The team is now comparing Andean crystals with those from large ore deposits.

To work out what the fingerprint means, the researchers ran computer simulations of magma cooling and crystallizing at different depths.

The trapped crystals formed at about 1,380°F to 1,560°F (750°C to 850°C), within 7 miles (11 kilometers) of the surface.

The eruptibility-field crystals formed hotter, at roughly 1,650°F to 1,790°F (900°C to 975°C). Their magma had just been reheated by a fresh injection from deeper down.

The fresh injection also carried more dissolved water. As the mixture rose, the water began bubbling out and building pressure in the shallow magma chamber.

Strontium isotopes told the same story: crystal cores carried the signature of melt that had digested old crust, while the rims matched the fresh carrier magma.

The team’s reading is that a volcano on this arc needs a shove from below to erupt, and the shove is what the newest crystals record.

Parra-Encalada then pulled plagioclase data from a public geochemistry database covering 26 volcanic arcs.

The average crystal composition worldwide fell inside the Andean eruptibility field. So did the averages for the Cascades and for Kamchatka.

“And this was not just in the Andes!” she said.

In the Aleutians and in Indonesia, the crust changes from continental to oceanic. There too, the crystal rims fell in the field while the cores scattered.

The result also speaks to an old puzzle. Lavas with intermediate silica levels commonly erupt along these arcs, yet the silica-rich and silica-poor magmas that mix to produce them rarely reach the surface on their own.

The crystals suggest the crust works as a filter: the thick, silica-rich mush and the dense, iron-rich mush both stay trapped, and only the reheated blend in between gets out.

Two of the samples came from an ancient deposit beneath Lascar. It was left by one of the caldera-forming explosive eruptions that buried the region about 4 million years ago.

Those crystals showed almost none of the reheating signature. In a chemical map of an entire rock slice, 97% of the crystals had grown steadily without disturbance.

So the shove that sets off an ordinary Andean eruption may not be what sets off the giant ones.

The authors suggest those huge silica-rich reservoirs can destabilize and empty on their own once enough magma has piled in.

Using crystal chemistry to identify volcanoes more likely to erupt remains an untested idea.

The idea, Parra-Encalada said, is that a volcano whose large crystals also fall near the eruptibility field may hold magma already close to erupting conditions.

Some crystal interiors at Lascar do. Lascar last erupted in the year 2022, two weeks after the team finished fieldwork there.

“If we observe a similar pattern in other polygenetic volcanoes, where most plagioclase crystals have compositions within the eruptibility field, it could indicate a volcanic system that deserves closer attention,” Parra-Encalada noted.

Polygenetic means a volcano that erupts more than once.

Nothing in this study links the fingerprint to how often a volcano erupts or how soon, and the team’s next paper takes up that question.

The samples also come from one slice of one continental arc. The global comparison relies on other researchers’ data, most of it without the crystal-by-crystal sorting this study depended on.

The team is expanding its work to Tonga to test whether the pattern also holds in an oceanic setting.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

Using machine learning, astronomers developed a new way of looking at James Webb telescope data that allows far-off planets to emerge from their star's glare.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it comes to spotting planets orbiting distant stars, the biggest hurdle is often separating the signal from the noise — specifically, trying to distinguish a planet from the stellar glare around it. That's true even for the most sophisticated telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

Now, astronomers have developed a new way to spot planets that were formerly drowned out in a sea of light. Using a combination of modeling and machine learning techniques, they picked out a previously hidden giant exoplanet in data from JWST. The results were published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

"Planets are a million times fainter than their stars," study first author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, an astronomer at Northwestern University, said in a statement. "So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare."

Telescopes like JWST use instruments called coronagraphs to block out some of this excess light, similar to the way the moon and a pinhole camera operate during a total solar eclipse. But even the best coronagraphs have limitations — for example, they can't block all the glare, and the telescopes themselves move.

Even the most stable telescopes vibrate almost imperceptibly as they collect light, so the images a telescope produces contain ever-so-slight mismatches compared with what the instrument actually sees. These slight shifts can be enough to obscure even very large exoplanets.

To address this, Ferrer-Chavez and his team developed a "digital twin" of JWST that virtually recreates how light travels through the telescope's detectors, minus any movement-based imperfections. To fine-tune this digital replica, the researchers used computational models based in real-world physics alongside machine learning techniques similar to those used to train AI. But the authors stressed that this is not an AI model.

"Because we already know the physics, we don't need AI to understand what's happening," study co-author Jason Wang, also an astrophysicist at Northwestern, said in a statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP.

Using FLIP, the team analyzed data from three stars, including 51 Eridani, which is located around 97 light-years from Earth and was already suspected to have a giant exoplanet orbiting it. Although the planet, called 51 Eridani b, had been detected by ground-based telescopes, it was drowned out by light in previous JWST observations. With FLIP, however, 51 Eridani b popped out from the dataset.

The scientists hope this approach will help astronomers pick out even more hard-to-spot exoplanets, especially ones that look like the planets in our own backyard. In the nearly 35-year history of exoplanet hunting, the vast majority of planets we've found have been radically different from those in our own solar system, partially because larger and more reflective worlds are easier to spot with current telescopes.

"It's not that [solar-system-like planets] don't exist," Ferrer-Chavez said. "It's that we can't see them."

Ferrer-Chavez, R., Wang, J. J., Bouman, K. L., Freeman, W. T., Pueyo, L., Feng, B. Y., & Perrin, M. D. (2026). Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit. Nature, 659(8139), 58–62. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z

#6356. Teen messaging and well-being: Who is on the other end matters

A study of Swedish teens links messaging with offline friends to higher well-being and contact with online-only friends to lower scores.

The usual question about a teenager’s phone is how many hours. A survey of 3,034 Swedish 15-year-olds asked a different one: who is on the other end?

Teens who messaged close friends or their wider circle several times a day or more scored higher on a well-being test than teens who rarely did.

Teens who kept up with friends they had only ever met online, even just weekly, scored lower.

Viviane Straatmann of Stockholm University is the study’s senior author.

She conducted the study with first author Madeleine Björnsdotter Orfanidou, also at Stockholm, and Kenisha Russell Jonsson of the University of Gothenburg.

The survey was taken at one moment in each teen’s life, so it can show a pattern and not a cause.

In an interview with Earth.com, Straatmann said parents should take an interest not only in how much time teens spend messaging but in whom they message.

“Online communication can be a valuable way to maintain and strengthen friendships with people adolescents know offline,” she said.

The teens came from two rounds of the Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey, a long-running study of young people’s health across many countries.

One round ran in the 2017 to 2018 school year, the other in 2021 to 2022, and the team pooled them.

Each teen was asked how often they sent and received texts, emojis, photos, videos or voice messages, or made video calls, with three kinds of people.

One was a close friend. One was a larger group of friends. The third was friends they had met through the internet and never in person.

The answers were sorted into three levels: rarely, weekly to daily, and several times a day up to almost all the time. Two-thirds of the teens were in that top band with their close friends.

Well-being was measured using seven questions about the past two weeks, including feeling optimistic, useful, relaxed and close to other people. Higher scores mean better well-being.

Teens who messaged a close friend several times a day scored about 1.6 points higher than teens who rarely did.

Once the team accounted for gender, family finances, family situation and survey year, that gap shrank to about one point and was no longer statistically significant.

Frequent messaging with a larger friend group remained associated with higher well-being after the same adjustments, with a gap of nearly one point.

Straatmann called that an important finding, because it means online communication was not uniformly negative.

Digital contact, she said, can be a positive tool when it complements a teen’s everyday offline relationships.

The pattern reversed for friends a teen knew only online. Teens who messaged such friends weekly to daily scored about 0.9 points lower than teens who rarely did.

Teens who did so several times a day scored about 0.7 points lower. Both gaps survived the adjustments.

The split is not new. The authors wrote that studies in the United Kingdom and Finland found the same thing.

Teens in touch online with friends they knew offline reported higher well-being, and teens communicating mostly with online-only friends reported lower.

Those are small differences on the scale. For comparison, girls scored almost three points lower than boys.

Teens from families they described as well off scored almost three points higher than teens who said their family was not.

The association with online-only contact remained after adjustment, but the differences by gender and family finances were larger.

“This does not mean that all online-only friendships are harmful, but it underlines the importance of open conversations, age-appropriate guidance, and a safe digital environment,” Straatmann told Earth.com.

Girls were more likely than boys to message a close friend several times a day or more: 77% compared with 65%.

Teens from the most affluent families were far more likely to do so than teens from the least, 82% to 62%.

Boys were slightly more likely than girls to be in frequent contact with online-only friends, though the gap was not clearly beyond chance.

The team adjusted for those differences. But the authors wrote that their models did not test whether the link between online-only friends and well-being differs for girls or for lower-income teens.

The study could not establish which way the relationship runs.

“As this was a cross-sectional study, we cannot say whether these online relationships contribute to poorer well-being, whether adolescents with lower well-being are more likely to seek such relationships, or whether both processes are involved,” Straatmann said.

The study also measured only Swedish 15-year-olds, couldn’t apply the survey’s population weights, and didn’t ask about cyberbullying or how good the friendships were.

Teens surveyed in the 2021–2022 round scored almost two points lower than those in the earlier round, and the design can’t separate the pandemic from everything else that changed between the rounds.

Sweden’s public health agency recently issued its first screen guidance for teenagers, built around a daily limit of two to three hours for ages 13 to 18.

The authors wrote that the nature of online contact, not only its length, might belong in future updates of that advice.

Straatmann said the next step is following the same teens over time, to watch how messaging and well-being shape each other.

She also wants to know whether the pattern holds for neurodivergent teens, including those with ADHD or autism, for whom online contact may offer an unusually important route to connection.

The full study was published in the journal Child and Adolescent Mental Health.

#6354. People with early-onset Alzheimer’s often face depression and dizziness before their diagnosis, but not high blood pressure

Before early-onset Alzheimer's was diagnosed, depression, dizziness and brain injuries became more common, but high blood pressure did not.

High blood pressure and high cholesterol are two of the best-known risk factors for Alzheimer’s disease in older people.

In people diagnosed at 65 or younger, researchers in Finland found these two were no more common than in people of the same age without the disease.

What did rise was a scattered set of other problems.

In the five years before diagnosis, people who went on to develop early-onset Alzheimer’s were more often diagnosed with dizziness, depression, headaches, delirium, epilepsy, and brain injuries.

“Our findings support the view that early-onset Alzheimer’s disease is not simply a younger-age version of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease,” said Johanna Krüger, an adjunct professor at the University of Oulu and the study’s lead investigator.

“Rather than the familiar cardiovascular risk factors, we observed a range of other health problems becoming more common as diagnosis approached.”

Early-onset Alzheimer’s accounts for up to 10% of all Alzheimer’s cases. It tends to move faster than the late-onset kind, and it more often starts in unusual ways.

The early-onset disease is also slower to diagnose.

Earlier studies cited by the team put the average time to diagnosis at about 42 months, compared to about 31 months for the late-onset disease.

Diagnosis is often delayed by several years after the first symptoms appear.

The researchers wanted to know whether the years before diagnosis leave a trail in medical records.

The team came from the University of Oulu and the University of Eastern Finland. It started with every patient sent to the memory clinics at Oulu and Kuopio university hospitals from 2010 to 2021.

In Finland, suspected early-onset cases in those regions are sent to those two hospitals.

The team re-checked each record against standard criteria for Alzheimer’s. That left 407 people diagnosed at age 65 or younger, with an average age at diagnosis of about 61.

For comparison, a national agency randomly picked 4,035 people matched to the patients by age, sex, and region. None had a neurodegenerative disease.

Next, the team pulled every diagnosis for both groups from Finland’s national health records. Finnish doctors must record a diagnosis code after every visit, public or private.

The team compared the groups at three stretches of time before diagnosis: one to five years, six to 10, and 11 to 15.

Eleven to 15 years before diagnosis, none of the conditions the team examined differed between the groups. Six to 10 years out, one did.

Tinnitus and hearing loss were recorded in 4.7% of future patients compared to 2.1% of the comparison group.

The bigger change came in the last five years. Dizziness was recorded in 5.9% of future patients compared to 2.1% of the comparison group.

Depression appeared in 5.7% compared to 2.3%, and headache in 4.9% compared to 1.6%.

Brain injuries, strokes, epilepsy, thyroid disorders, alcohol-related disorders, and delirium were all more common too.

Delirium is a sudden state of confusion, and it was recorded in 1.5% of future patients compared to 0.1% of the others.

Each of these conditions was still uncommon, recorded in no more than about 6% of future patients.

High blood pressure or high cholesterol was recorded in 10.6% of future patients in the last five years, compared to 9.3% of the comparison group.

That gap was too small to rule out chance, and the two groups were close at every earlier stretch as well.

In late-onset Alzheimer’s, those heart and blood vessel risks have been linked to the disease in earlier research.

The authors wrote that only one earlier, smaller study had reported a similar result for the early-onset disease. They suggested that the causes of the two forms may differ, at least in part.

Health care visits rose only near the end. In the year before diagnosis, future patients had an average of 3.3 recorded care episodes, compared to 1.9 for the comparison group.

In the year of diagnosis it was 6.3 compared to 2.0. Two or more years out, the groups did not differ.

“Of course, no single disease or symptom predicts Alzheimer’s disease,” said Laura Leppänen, a doctoral researcher at the University of Oulu and the study’s first author.

“Our results suggest that, in the years before diagnosis, patients may accumulate a variety of seemingly unrelated symptoms and healthcare encounters. Recognizing this overall pattern could help raise suspicion of a neurodegenerative disease earlier than is currently the case.”

The study compares records, so it can’t say whether any of these conditions helps cause the disease.

Depression, delirium, or alcohol-related disorders may be early signs of brain changes already under way, and the authors wrote that the design cannot tell those possibilities apart.

The registers held no information on social and economic background, lifestyle, or genes, and diagnoses in them could not be checked independently.

Only people who lived through each stretch were counted. People in the comparison group could also have had early brain changes that had not been diagnosed.

Early onset was defined by age at diagnosis, not at first symptoms, which may have left out people whose symptoms began just before 65.

The results come from one country’s health system, and the authors wrote that they need to be checked in other datasets.

Researchers at the same universities have reported that early-onset dementia is more common than earlier international studies suggested.

Other teams are working on blood tests that might flag the disease years before symptoms.

The full study was published in the journal Alzheimer’s & Dementia.
