#6320. Celestron Origin’s Mosaic Mode brings wide-field astrophotography to the biggest smart telescope

Almost any galaxy or nebula that the Celestron Origin Intelligent Home Observatory can find will fit in its field of view in a single shot. But there is a short list of exceptions.

For instance, the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the nearest major galaxy to our own and a popular first target, stretches about 3° from end to end. And the iconic North America Nebula (NGC 7000), which lies just 2,600 light-years away in Cygnus, spans roughly 2°. Both of these objects spill out of the field of view of the Origin Mark II, which, with its 6-inch (152 mm) f/2.2 Rowe-Ackermann Schmidt Astrograph (RASA) optics, captures a field of 1.32° by 0.75°.

Celestron’s answer is Mosaic Mode, a free update that brings automated mosaic imaging to the Origin smart telescope. In the Origin app, users draw a box around their target. Origin then divides that area into overlapping tiles, slews to each position, captures the data, and stitches the results into a single wide-field image.

Celestron Innovation Specialist Eric Kopit estimates that 90 percent or more of what Origin can see fits within its field of view. “The vast majority of objects” — most galaxies, globular clusters, and planetary nebulae — “are really small,” Kopit says. “But the objects most people want to start with are bigger.”

The ease of imaging with smart telescopes has brought a wave of newcomers into the hobby, he says, and those showpieces are usually what they reach for. Mosaic Mode ensures their reach does not exceed their grasp.

Mosaic Mode changes the rhythm of an Origin session. The telescope’s standard experience is built around watching an image take shape on your phone, tablet, or smart TV in near-real time. A mosaic is closer to an overnight project. Large targets can take hours, so Kopit says users can set the telescope to turn itself off once it’s done. Users can still watch the tiles come in, but it isn’t a requirement.

Those long capture times also made mosaic image stitching a challenge to bring to life. Each tile is shot at a different point in the night, and conditions can change from one moment to the next. A passing cloud might dim one tile and leave its neighbors untouched.

Targets with a wide range of brightness, like Andromeda, presented their own challenge. “One tile is a bright core, others are faint dust lanes,” Kopit says.

Early versions of the software had trouble blending exposures that were so different, but a recent firmware update reworked the processing. According to Celestron’s release notes, the new version produces fewer visible seams, better preserves faint nebulosity, aligns tiles more accurately, and better rejects frames corrupted by external light sources.

Mosaic Mode follows another software addition to Origin’s feature set aimed at users who want to push their images further.

With dithering, the telescope nudges itself slightly between exposures so the target lands on different pixels in each frame. Hot pixels and other sensor defects stay put on the chip, so once the frames are aligned to the stars, those defects end up scattered. Stacking software can then recognize them as outliers and toss them out.

Astrophotography dithering is a technique advanced imagers have relied on for years, and Origin owners had been asking for it.

“We had it on our roadmap, and people wanted it,” Kopit says.

Both Mosaic Mode and dithering work on every Origin, not just the Mark II that Celestron introduced in October 2025. The two generations share the same optics and electronics. The only difference is the camera, which owners can replace.

Camera sensors improve quickly, largely because Sony develops them for other industries. Astronomy gets to borrow the results, meaning a telescope with a fixed camera falls behind rather quickly.

“Modularity was always the vision,” Kopit says. “It can continue to take on new features so that you can keep the rest of the system.”

The Mark II’s camera uses Sony’s IMX678 sensor, an 8.4-megapixel chip with 2.0-micrometer pixels. The original Origin used the 6.4-megapixel IMX178, with 2.4-micrometer pixels.

Those smaller pixels matter more than you might expect on a telescope this fast. At f/2.2, Kopit says, Origin’s resolution is limited more by pixel size than by its 6-inch (152 mm) aperture. With a 335 mm focal length, the Mark II samples the sky at about 1.2″per pixel, compared with about 1.5″ on the original camera.

Sensors with larger pixels used to be commonly preferred in astrophotography for their increased sensitivity, but newer designs have changed that. Kopit sees room for more gains as pixels keep shrinking. First-generation owners can buy the new Origin 678C camera and install it themselves or have Celestron handle the upgrade.

Celestron first sketched the idea for Origin in 2011, before the technology existed to support it. The original goal wasn’t deep-sky astrophotography, but rather helping people see galaxies and nebulae the way they see the Moon and planets through an eyepiece.

“The idea is to aid the eye,” Kopit says. “For us, it’s turning imaging into a visual experience.”

In practice, that means users experience very little waiting. After the app connects, Origin focuses itself, uses Celestron’s StarSense technology to recognize the sky, and aligns in about a minute. When users tap a target in the SkySafari-powered planetarium view, the telescope begins taking 10-second exposures, stacking each new frame onto the last. Because the fast optics pour so much light onto a sensitive sensor, even the first exposure can reveal detail, and this view rapidly sharpens as the telescope stacks more exposures.

Thanks to this speed, capturing ten or more objects in a night can be a realistic observing plan. The app also offers audio presentations on more than 200 popular targets along the way. When users end the session, the final stacked image saves to the device, acting as a digital souvenir of the night.

The Origin app keeps its core controls up front and tucks advanced settings into deeper menus. A first-time user never has to touch them, which makes Origin an intuitive entry point into astrophotography.

Those venturing deeper into the app will find an option for equatorial mode, which uses an optional wedge to reduce field rotation, along with support for the StarSense Autoguider. This ability for users to choose the depth of their experience speaks to the different kinds of people attracted to Origin.

Celestron always expected Origin would be alluring even to experienced imagers — not just beginners. What surprised the company, however, was how many veteran astrophotographers have made it their primary rig. Many of those buyers already own a full imaging setup, Kopit says, but Origin is far easier to get running on a given night.

Kids sit at the other end of the spectrum. These young users often want to look through a telescope but struggle to see anything in an eyepiece. On a tablet screen, they can see it.

“With kids particularly, it opens up the hobby,” Kopit says.

Mosaic Mode is available now through the app and the latest Origin firmware. Kopit says more features are on the way.

#6319. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

K. Grice et al. Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2026. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.

#6318. The Best Airbnbs in Asheville, From a Fairy-Tale Tree House to a Victorian Cottage

As someone raised in the mountains of North Carolina, I've always loved visiting Asheville. I have made the winding two-hour drive from my hometown of Boone countless times, and the city's vibrant energy never ceases to excite me. An eclectic little gem located in the heart of the Blue Ridge Mountains, Asheville’s bustling art and restaurant culture attracts visitors from all over. It's also home to famous historic sites like Biltmore Estate, which is the largest privately owned home in the United States.

What truly makes Asheville so captivating is the city's wide range of attractions, activities, and gorgeous places to stay. Unbelievable mountain views, hiking trails, and other outdoor activities are minutes from the city center, and there are dozens of gorgeous Airbnbs to hole up in no matter what area of the city you choose. The River Arts District is a hub of creativity and expression, home to hundreds of artists, galleries, and expansive outdoor murals along the French Broad River. Downtown is my favorite neighborhood, and I like to take an afternoon to mosey around, with a non-negotiable pit stop at Tupelo Honey for lunch. Wherever you stay, there's so much to do—you can spend your days soaking in a refreshing mountain spring and evenings dining at an award-winning restaurant or craft brewery, then catch live music at one of Asheville’s charming theaters. You will never run out of activities, with something to discover around each corner. Below, find 11 Airbnbs that capture every bit of Asheville’s quirky and whimsical appeal.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Unbeatable mountain views, hot tub, hammock

If you’re after a serene, nature-focused stay, this glamping dome tucked away in the Blue Ridge Mountains will provide just that. Relax in the private hot tub, take an afternoon nap in the spacious hammock, or simply watch the sunset from the couch in front of floor-to-ceiling windows. With on-site parking, a king-size bed, a full bathroom, and a kitchenette for whipping up light meals, a stay here will feel nothing like traditional camping. Situated about 20 minutes from downtown Asheville in Fairview, this property is an ideal hideaway to unplug while still offering access to Asheville’s unbeatable dining and activity options.

Neighborhood: FairviewThings to do nearby: Whistle Hop Brewing Company, Hickory Nut Gap Farm, Fairview Community Forest

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, panoramic views, wraparound deck

There’s a reason so many people want to stay in an elevated mountain cabin in North Carolina, and it’s a must-do for first-time visitors. This unique converted fire tower is on eight acres of private wooded land with direct access to the well-known Mountains-to-Sea Trail. Sixteen panoramic windows and a 360-degree wraparound deck offer expansive mountain views from every angle. The outdoor fireplace and backyard are a s'mores-making and stargazing wonderland. A short 10-minute drive from downtown, on-site parking, and a washer/dryer make this property an exemplary mix of seclusion and practicality.

Neighborhood: Haw CreekThings to do nearby: Haw Creek Park, Creekside Taphouse, Folk Art Center

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Downtown location, natural light, exposed brick

Set in a prime downtown location, this charming one-bedroom is ideal for those looking to experience Asheville’s thriving urban life. Right in the heart of downtown, you will be steps away from endless restaurants, dynamic art galleries, live music venues, and so much more. The space is warm and welcoming, with natural light pouring in from a wall of multi-pane windows. The exposed brick and natural wood tones create an ideal mix of cozy and sophisticated. There is no free on-site parking, but a parking garage across the street is available for a small fee as a convenient alternative.

Neighborhood: Downtown AshevilleThings to do nearby: Tupelo Honey, Asheville Art Museum, French Broad Chocolate Lounge

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Historic character, convenient location, on-site parking

Built in 1883, this lovely stick-style Victorian cottage was the first home in western North Carolina owned by a woman. Throughout each room, original details are blended with thoughtful updates, preserving its historic character but adding a modern twist. Both queen bedrooms are enhanced with Victorian-inspired furniture and elegant fireplaces. Located in Asheville’s Montford neighborhood, this home is just two blocks from downtown, but still has a driveway and parking for ultimate ease.

Neighborhood: MontfordThings to do nearby: Nine Mile, The Montford Park Players, historic architecture stroll

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: High ceilings, spacious backyard, firepit, multiple living areas

Embrace a little piece of Asheville’s history at this carefully restored 1870s home. Each room boasts plenty of historic charm with 13-foot ceilings, crown molding, beautifully arched double doors, and detailed windows. The furniture and decor choices are an ode to the home's past, keeping the history alive yet with a modern twist. Multiple sitting areas and exceptionally spacious bedrooms (one king and one double) make this a wonderful place to spend time with friends or family without being cramped. The shared backyard has an adorable garden, and the back porch is a glorious spot to watch the sunset over the mountains. Free on-site parking is available, and if you have a particularly large group, you can inquire about renting the unit next door to accommodate four more guests.

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Hot tub, updated interior, city and mountain views

This property is packed with amenities like a hot tub, a ping-pong table, a soaking tub, and plenty of outdoor furniture. It’s a great place for families or small friend groups, with space for up to five guests to sleep across two bedrooms and lounge comfortably throughout the house. An upstairs queen bedroom and a lofted single bed make this the perfect escape for a small family or a couple. The shared garden, firepit, and outdoor clawfoot bathtub mirror the light, airy interior. Free street parking is available, and West Asheville’s restaurants, breweries, and galleries are a short walk away. The cozy, cabin-like interior is full of wooden details and comfy furniture. You can sip a cup of coffee at sunrise on one of the two decks, relax in the upstairs bed nook, or venture onto one of the property's hiking trails (maybe even catch a glimpse of the forest’s wild animals!). This is a particularly good spot for those with kiddos, and the downstairs sofa bed makes for easy sleeping arrangements for little ones. About 10 minutes from downtown, this little haven offers the best of both worlds.

A two-minute walk from the Mountains-to-Sea Trail and a lovely on-site firepit make this a wonderful option for those who are looking to embrace nature. The primary king bedroom is filled with massive windows, and two separate bathrooms will give families enough space to be comfortable. There is on-site parking, but note that the parking space is said to be a bit steep for larger cars.

Situated right in the middle of the woods, this beautifully updated mountain cabin is a peaceful retreat. Multiple living areas, three bedrooms, and two-and-a-half bathrooms make for a very generous amount of space. The upstairs deck features plenty of outdoor seating, and the lower level is fitted with two hammocks and games for nights in. Sweeping mountain views are visible from almost every window in the house—fall here would be an absolute dream! Wooden steps lead down to a charming firepit area with extra seating. Modern touches shine throughout the house, like the exquisitely updated kitchen and bathrooms. The driveway has space for up to four cars.

Located in a serene neighborhood in West Asheville, you can easily stroll to nearby breweries or take a peaceful walk around the area. A surplus of outdoor furniture and a gas grill give ample opportunity for alfresco meals.

Researchers found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores in Mexico ‪—‬ and it’s all because the Maya loved red paint.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Maya used so much red paint that they accidentally poisoned their lakes and waterways with mercury, a new study finds.

The problem was cinnabar, a vivid-red mercury-sulfide mineral that can be used as the pigment vermilion in red paint. The run-off from the paint can enter waterways, where anaerobic bacteria then transform cinnabar into highly toxic methylmercury in the sediments of lakes. Over time, the methylmercury accumulates to higher levels in the food chain.

The ancient Maya, a people who lived in what is now southern Mexico and Central America and whose descendants are still around today, painted almost everything red. Archaeologists have found countless artifacts that the Maya reddened, including sculptures, monuments, walls, plazas, pottery and the dead for ceremonial funerals. Cinnabar was a common pigment in the paint they made, along with red ocher, which gets its color from a nontoxic iron mineral called hematite.

But the Maya passion for the color red — which to them represented the sun, blood and life — caused an environmental disaster when the nearby waters were poisoned by the cinnabar runoff, said study first author Matthew Waters, a paleolimnologist (a scientist who studies ancient waterways) at Auburn University in Alabama.

"They would have seen a strange color change in the water … and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein," he told Live Science. The Maya depended heavily on freshwater fisheries, including for freshwater shellfish.

Previous studies had already found evidence for high levels of mercury in the Maya's southern highlands and south-central lowlands, but no one had fully examined levels of the toxic mineral in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

To investigate, Waters and his colleagues studied mercury levels in Maya-era mud in the Yucatán, and found overwhelming signs of mercury poisoning, probably from cinnabar paint, they reported in their study, published Nov. 4 in the journal Science Advances.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"We did not suspect [the Maya] used it in the quantities that we were seeing," he said.

The study found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores from two Maya-era sites: Cobá Lake, a shallow lake beside the Maya city of that name, and Cenote Xcach (also spelled X-Canché), a flooded sinkhole beside a ruined city in the jungle that few have excavated.

The sediment cores chronicle the composition of earth and water over more than 2,000 years, and the times of mercury poisoning coincide with several periods during the Preclassic and Classic periods of the Maya civilization from about A.D. 40 to 820.

Waters explained that the Environmental Protection Agency in the U.S. has determined it is unsafe to drink water with mercury levels above 2 parts per billion, while the official limit for the level of mercury in fish, where it builds up over time, is 1 part per million — any number above that means the fish can be seized by authorities.

Severe poisoning occurs when the mercury levels in human blood exceed about 100 parts per billion, from drinking contaminated water or eating contaminated marine animals, such as fish. In humans, mercury poisoning can cause severe symptoms, including permanent lung damage, brain damage and death.

The reddish hue of the Maya sun god Kinich Ahau, made between the sixth and ninth centuries, now housed in Mexico’s National Museum of Anthropology, shows the Maya's love for mercury.

The most polluted parts of the Yucatan cores had a mercury level of 2.3 parts per million, the team discovered. "They experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries," Waters said.

The researchers then examined the sediment cores for signs of environmental damage caused by the mercury poisoning. They found that the cores lacked tiny fossils of freshwater shellfish, indicating that the high mercury levels were killing marine life. The team also noticed that the sediment cores had hardly any traces of algal blooms, which should have happened frequently, Waters said. That's likely because algae could not survive in the poisoned water nutrients.

Scholars debate why the Maya civilization collapsed in the eighth and ninth centuries, but a leading suspect is the disruption of food supplies caused by drought.

But although mercury levels were high during the Preclassic and Classic periods, the environmental damage caused by mercury levels had been falling in many places for hundreds of years by the time of the Maya collapse, Waters said, although it may have been a contributing factor.

Cinnabar does not occur naturally in the Yucatán, so it must have been imported there, probably from what's now Honduras, the researchers said. It seems these cinnabar imports eventually stopped at Cobá Lake, and the poisoning there fell to a background level of about 20 parts per billion by A.D. 520. However, the sediment cores showed that the mercury poisoning continued at Cenote Xcach until the collapse, they said.

Waters, M. N., Wooten, S. L., Abrook, A. M., Brenner, M., Curtis, J. H., Langdon, P. G., Medina-Gonzalez, R. M., Paradeisis-Stathis, S., & Vachula, R. S. (2026). Toxic mercury, aquatic ecosystem collapse, and the ancient Lowland Maya. Science Advances, 12(45), eaeh3280. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh3280

#6316. How We Pulled It Off: An East-Meets-West Wedding in Istanbul

Jasmin Karibzhanova and Sam Sutcliffe are a multicultural pair whose families and upbringings have spanned the globe. Jasmin was born and raised in the city of Almaty, Kazakhstan, and now lives in Toronto with Sam, a Canadian of Chinese-English descent (who grew up partly in Hong Kong). Friends introduced them in 2022 and the couple were engaged in Turks and Caicos in 2024. Quickly, they figured out that anywhere they married would require a long-haul flight for many if not most of their guests, so why not give everyone an excuse to go somewhere thrilling?

Jasmin Karibzhanova and Sam Sutcliffe have roots in Kazakhstan and Hong Kong, respectively.

Turkey affords Canadians (the couple lives in Toronto) and Kazakhs visa-free entry.

It was Jasmin’s father who suggested they wed in Istanbul for a few reasons: Turkey doesn’t require visas for Canadian or Kazakh citizens, there are direct flights to Istanbul from both Toronto and Almaty, and the city seemed like a more compelling place than typical European destination wedding locales like the countryside of France or Italy. Plus, given the bride and groom’s cultural backgrounds, an east-meets-west theme fit nicely with Istanbul’s location and history. Ahead, the couple shares how they planned their June 2026 wedding for 160 guests in Istanbul, a celebration that included a boat ride to a secret destination, a ceremony along the strait, and copious amounts of Turkish delight.

Living far away, the couple knew they’d need a lot of help plotting their destination celebration. After deciding on Istanbul, they first reached out to Turkish planners, but then struggled with the cultural divide. “Western wedding traditions are a bit different than what they were used to, and we had some communication issues with language,” Jasmin says.

They expanded their search to planners elsewhere in Europe with whom they could speak more clearly, and who were well-versed in producing larger-scale celebrations. They landed on Matthew Oliver Weddings, a London-based firm that specializes in destination weddings across Europe and the Middle East. Coincidentally, the team there had recently connected with Aylinly Events, a Turkish planner who’d directly expressed an interest in collaborating on Turkish destination celebrations. Given the serendipity, working with both firms seemed like the best way to pull off the kind of highly-produced event Jasmin and Sam wanted.

From there, the wedding was plotted via weekly Zoom meetings with the Matthew Oliver team, particularly their lead planners Bertie and Georgia, while the Turkish team tended to be most comfortable over WhatsApp. “If you're sending a WhatsApp, they'll respond in 20 minutes at 4:00 a.m. their time,” Jasmin says. “The Turkish approach to hospitality is next level. They’re never off. They work the hardest of any creative team I’ve ever met.”

The Peninsula Istanbul spans four buildings set right on the Bosphorus in the historic neighborhood of Karaköy.

The couple visited Istanbul twice during their engagement, with the first trip to tour venues about one year out from the wedding date they eventually set. They sought a space that could handle their substantial guest list, and quickly fell for the Peninsula Istanbul, which spans four buildings set right on the Bosphorus in the historic neighborhood of Karaköy.

“It was integrated into the fabric of the city,” Jasmin says. “You could just walk out into the street and enjoy Istanbul, which we really loved, and it had fantastic views of the Golden Horn.” The brand was a special touchstone for Sam and his family too, as the Peninsula has roots in Hong Kong.

Given the hotel’s size, its staff was adept at events and offered plenty of standard packages, though they were happy to work outside of the typical framework. “There was nothing they would say no to,” Jasmin says. “They had a fantastic understanding of vendors in the city and issues to consider, with amazing recommendations. Their whole approach to hospitality and wedding planning was that there is no rejection of any idea. They would just figure it out.”

A small slice of the 160 guests attended the rehearsal dinner at the Rahmi M. Koç transportation museum.

The hotel was a special touchstone for Sam and his family too; the Peninsula has roots in Hong Kong.

When reaching out to friends and family, the couple was pleasantly surprised to find how many wanted to fly to Turkey. “I sort of assumed that because it was so far, especially for the Canadians, that we’d have a smaller guest list than we did,” Jasmin says. “But people really wanted to go because it was a destination that a lot hadn’t been to before. It was a great excuse to make their way over there.”

So they felt a duty to properly entertain their loved ones. “My philosophy around the event was that I wanted it to be completely guest-facing. I wanted it to be easy for people to come and enjoy the weekend,” says the bride, who admits she went totally “overboard” in this respect. Aside from creating a wedding website with all the event info, they also offered travel tips and suggestions, fashioned suggested itineraries, and pre-booked a local tour of Istanbul for folks who arrived early.

Another reason they opted for the Peninsula was its location near many other hotels with varying price points and appeals. “Our friends stayed closer to bars and nightlife, and older guests stayed near museums and such,” Jasmin says, estimating that about a third of attendees checked into the Peninsula.

Furniture production by AND Event & Design Studio created modular custom ceremony seating.

Flower arrangements were tighter, paler, and more romantic than the complex, architectural ceremony florals.

Both Jasmin and Sam have creative backgrounds—they work together on a film production company, Jasmin studied theater and acted, and Sam’s parents are celebrated architects—and approached the aesthetics of their wedding like an artistic pursuit. “We knew that a lot of our guests would be from the creative world, and we were particular about how we wanted things to look,” Jasmin says. They suggested high-level elements like the color scheme (dusty blue and rich mulberry), and then their planning teams, along with the creative studio Event Lab, filled in the gaps with more ideas.

One key element in ensuring the wedding’s cohesion was the furniture production, for which they worked with AND Event & Design Studio to create items like modular custom chairs and a platform drenched in a velvety maroon for the ceremony space. Another was the florals, designed and arranged by Fluida Design. For the eye-popping ceremony, the flowers were lush and architectural, almost alien-like, while for dinner the arrangements were tighter, paler, and more romantic.

“I wanted it to function like a play: There’s a rising energy, then a reveal, then a resolution,” says Jasmin of the aesthetic journey. In Fluida Design, they found a creative partner that pushed them in all the right directions, outside a typical wedding comfort zone. “The initial proposition was a lot more neutral colors, just whites and greens, and then our floral team was like, ‘Well, why don't we just do color because that's just more interesting?’” Jasmin recalls. And as much as the couple cared about the look, they were happy to let the experts be the experts. “We were like, ‘Well, we would like for you also to just have fun with it,” she says. “Do whatever you want.”

A rehearsal dinner kicked off the celebrations, and the couple wanted a unique space.

The Rahmi M. Koç transportation museum space along the Bosphorus played host.

On Thursday of their wedding weekend, the couple hosted an intimate but more casual rehearsal dinner for their family and closest friends at the hotel. Friday brought the welcome party for all of their guests, who boarded boats bound for an unknown location at sunset from the Peninsula: it turned out to be the Rahmi M. Koç Museum, a funky transportation museum space along the Bosphorus.

When the couple toured venues, they found that many options were great but a little too similar in energy to the Peninsula. “The last place we went was this museum, which is a ridiculous, magical place,” Jasmin says. “It’s a private collection of vintage cars, boats, submarines, and planes, all cramped together in this hangar-like building on the Bosphorus. It was very kitschy but a great contrast to our wedding venue.”

The hotel's central location meant guests “could just walk out into the street and enjoy Istanbul.”

Sam and Jasmin’s wedding day started out a bit drizzly, a rarity for early summer in Istanbul.

The Silk Road-themed party packed in loads of Turkish details from the music to the food: carts offering grilled meatballs (or köfte), ⁠döner, and stuffed bulgur balls (or içli köfte) made for a bazaar energy, while a live dessert station formed traditional lokma, freshly fried dough balls drizzled with syrup. “Floral” arrangements were built around local vegetables, like tall piles of peppers strung on garlands, and evil-eye pendants were handed out as party favors.

Sam and Jasmin’s wedding day started out a bit drizzly, a rarity for early summer in Istanbul. One of the reasons they chose the Peninsula in the first place was for its large terrace set against the strait, with the hope of getting married at sunset along the water with boats streaming by in the background. The vision was so beloved that they refused to come up with a rain plan, even for the platform built across the space.

The couple refused to make a rain plan in order to honor their plan of a ceremony set in front of the Bosphorus.

“Our team was like, ‘Maybe we look into other things?’ And I can be very impulsive,” Jasmin admits. “‘No, we're just going to commit to this. If it rains, it rains. I don't want to hide the city from our guests, even if it's wet.’” They delayed the ceremony for a few minutes but got their dream of holding it outside without soaking their families and friends.

Waiting for that area was worth it. “It was a very special space because normally that space is just a herb garden on top of the Peninsula, but we took it over for the wedding,” Sam says. “You both got spectacular views across the entire city and felt in it, while being slightly removed from the craziness.”

The Muslim call to prayer rang out amid a ceremony officiated by family friend and noted Canadian philanthropist Nancy Lockhart, and boats slowed down in interest. “It didn't feel invasive at all,” Jasmin says. “We wanted to be integrated into the city, and that's what we got.”

Staff dressed as bellhops and a wall of ornate golden keys served as the escort cards.

Cocktail hour took place steps away in a part of the courtyard wrapped in a romantic mauve pink.

Following the ceremony, guests enjoyed cocktails steps away in a part of the courtyard wrapped in a romantic mauve pink that colored the curtains, custom loungers, and drink tables. In keeping with the ideas of travel and adventure, the cocktail hour had a hotel theme (an idea that came from the Peninsula’s staff), with staff dressed as bellhops and a wall of ornate golden keys with pink tassels serving as the escort cards.

The wall of keys also functioned to block off the dinner area as it was set up, “so when they were ushered into the next space,” Sam says, “it was a surprising and beautiful new twist for everyone.” Next to the ceremony and cocktails spaces, the dinner “room” was formed by walls of blue curtains and the soaring, upside-down umbrellas that sit permanently on that courtyard. The tables were arranged in long, wavy lines that provided open views to the water.

And while this could never have been planned—even by the considerable talents of the creative couple and their multiple event teams—the risk of rain was rewarded by an incredible sight. “We had a spectacular double rainbow from the Asian side to the European side of the Bosphorus,” says Sam.

“The rainbow is something I will never forget for the rest of my life,” says Sam.

While the couple’s welcome dinner was packed with cultural touchpoints, the wedding day itself was more traditionally Western, albeit with some Turkish details. Sam took his groomsmen to a hamam during the day for spa treatments, and the wedding dinner was based around the best of the local cuisine. Canapes included mussel “dolma’’ with black-ink bread, a lemon commape, a bite of Ezine cheese with quince, and a simit bread crumble, while the main meal began with a mezze platter before a first course of duck or mushroom baklava.

A 10 p.m. noise ordinance inspired a move off the terrace and into the nearby ballroom.

After dinner and speeches from loved ones, the party took to the dance floor.

After dinner and speeches from loved ones, the party took to the dance floor, where the Uninvited Jazz Band got the party going. The couple served a classic wedding cake in two flavors: one dark chocolate and one raspberry and white chocolate. A series of smaller sweet bites from the Peninsula’s famous high tea were also passed around the tables.

A local city ordinance that event noises die down after 10 p.m. inspired a move off the terrace and into the nearby ballroom for more dancing. The after-party space was blanketed in scarlet, with a black and white checkerboard floor. From there, DJ Live from Élan Artists spun into the wee hours, and the newlyweds poured out a Champagne tower. A poem Sam had written was displayed above the bar: “Silk Road’s starting point / union atop ancient roots / celebratory love.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6315. After LINK mission failure, Swift reenters atmosphere

Editor’s note: This story was originally published Aug. 24, 2026. Swift reentered Earth’s atmosphere Nov. 4, 2026, ending its nearly 22-year mission. See the most recent updates at the end of this story.

NASA announced Aug. 19 that the Katalyst Space LINK spacecraft built to boost the aging Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will still rendezvous with the telescope but won’t raise its orbit, after an attitude-control failure sidelined LINK during on-orbit commissioning.

The Swift Boost Mission was a quick-turnaround rescue attempt designed to save the Swift observatory from an early demise. Thanks to increased atmospheric drag from the effects of solar maximum, NASA predicts the space telescope will reenter Earth’s atmosphere later this year, cutting short the extended run of a spacecraft that has delivered a number of breakthroughs in understanding gamma-ray bursts — the highest-energy explosions in the universe.

NASA contracted Katalyst Space Technologies, a startup based in Flagstaff, Arizona, in September 2025 to attempt the rescue, giving the company less than a year to go from concept to execution. Katalyst designed and built the LINK spacecraft for the express purpose of rendezvousing with Swift in orbit, docking with the telescope, and boosting it to a higher altitude for a few more years of science.

LINK launched July 3 on a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket but quickly ran into trouble, losing control of two of its three reaction wheels over the last weekend of July. Reaction wheels are spinning flywheels that use angular momentum to let a spacecraft point itself precisely without burning propellant. Three of them, angled correctly, can hold a spacecraft steady on every axis; NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, set to launch Aug. 30, carries six for redundancy. LINK carries only the minimum three, and losing two sent it tumbling at nearly nine degrees per second, compromising communications with ground controllers. Katalyst spent the following weeks firing LINK’s electric propulsion thrusters to slow the spin, eventually taming it to about 1.47 degrees per second by early August — but for a while, it was an open question whether the mission could continue at all.

RELATED: Is NASA’s Swift Boost Mission spinning away?Katalyst uploaded a flight-software fix Aug. 11 that reestablished LINK’s attitude control. But at that point, the timeline was even tighter. Swift had decayed to an orbital height of 216 miles (347 kilometers), just 31 miles (50 km) shy of the point where an orbit-raising mission would become much more difficult. Then came the Aug. 19 announcement from NASA that the spacecraft would still attempt rendezvous and proximity operations — closing in on and flying near Swift to test the maneuvers any future servicing mission would need — but would make no attempt to boost the telescope’s orbit. Without that boost, Swift is still expected to meet a fiery end before the end of the year.

Neither NASA nor Katalyst has said how LINK’s mission will end — whether the spacecraft will dock with Swift and remain there through the telescope’s final days or drift off on its own.

The Swift Boost Mission was framed from the start as a long shot, and NASA’s messaging hasn’t shifted now that it’s fallen short. “This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in the Aug. 19 announcement.

“We knew this was a high-risk, high-reward mission — a first-of-its kind attempt, developed on an unprecedented timeline driven by the Sun’s activity,” said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA’s Astrophysics Division. “We were all hoping for more science from Swift. But we knew the takeaways from this mission would be worthwhile either way, and we have gained so much through the series of accomplishments up to this point.”

The agency plans to lean on its other missions to help cover the gap in gamma-ray burst monitoring once the 21-year-old Swift telescope is lost, as well as file away whatever lessons LINK’s rendezvous can teach us about robotic servicing for missions that follow.

Update Sept. 15, 2026: On Sept. 4, NASA announced that LINK had made its closest approach to the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, closing to within roughly 8 miles (13 kilometers) of the space telescope. That’s as close as the two spacecraft will come, NASA says, now that the agency is no longer planning to boost Swift’s orbit, thanks to lingering attitude-control problems aboard LINK.

In the days following the rendezvous, Katalyst put the robotic servicer through the paces: raising its orbit, aligning it with Swift’s path, unfurling all three robotic arms, and firing all three xenon thrusters at once on Aug. 30. With no further approach planned, Katalyst expects LINK to deorbit later this month.

With the boost off the table, Swift’s team switched its ultraviolet/optical and X-ray telescopes back on Aug. 26, months after powering them down to reduce draft and slow Swift’s decay. A third instrument, the Burst Alert Telescope, should follow in the coming weeks. NASA anticipates the gamma ray observatory will reenter and burn up before the end of the year.

Update Sept. 29, 2026: On Sept. 25, LINK deorbited and reentered Earth’s atmosphere, concluding the mission. LINK was not successful in its attempt to capture and boost Swift’s orbit, but the team collected useful data across 85 days of LINK’s operation that will help inform future missions.

Update Nov. 9, 2026: The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere Nov. 4 at 7:39 a.m. EST, according to NASA, coming down over Indonesia’s North Sumatra region. While some components may have survived the journey and made it to the surface, NASA expected most of the spacecraft to disintegrate completely.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer for Astronomy and is based in Chattanooga, Tennessee.

#6314. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

Z. Yu et al. High fiber diet mitigates exposure risk of nanoplastics in male mice. Nature Communications. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-78675-7

The Vikings are famous for being warriors, but how frequently did Viking women take part in battles?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vikings were explorers, farmers, merchants and, most famously, warriors who launched raids across large parts of Europe.

Stereotypes of Vikings usually conjure up images of muscular men. But over the past few decades, researchers have turned their attention to women of the Viking Age (roughly A.D. 793 to 1066) and the roles they held. For instance, there are stories of "shield maidens" who fought alongside men, and some of these texts mention Viking women who fought in battle. The archaeological record also holds evidence, including graves of Viking Age women who were buried with war-grade weapons and shields.

It's still a matter of debate whether women who lived during the Viking Age could be warriors, but this discussion raises another question: It's one thing to have texts describing female fighters and archaeological records of women buried with weapons, but what can the evidence tell us about how frequently Viking women fought in battle?

The answer, experts told Live Science, largely depends on our interpretation of texts, artifacts, and burials of Viking Age women, which often face higher scrutiny than burials of men who were buried with similar (or even fewer) weapons.

The Vikings used a runic system of writing, but they left precious few texts behind. Instead, much of what we know about the Vikings was written about them by people from other cultures or by their Norse descendants.

One of the most evocative texts was written in the 12th century by the Danish historian and theologian Saxo Grammaticus. In "Gesta Danorum" (Latin for "History of the Danes" and translated by Jenny Jochens), he wrote that "there were once women in Denmark who dressed themselves to look like men and spent almost every minute cultivating [combat] skills." As "if they were forgetful of their true selves they put toughness before allure, aimed at conflicts instead of kisses, tasted blood, not lips, sought the clash of arms rather than the arm's embrace, fitted to weapons hands what should have been weaving, desired not the couch but the kill, and those they could have appeased with looks they attacked with lances."

Another text about the Vikings, the medieval Irish "Cogadh Gaedhelre Gallaibh" ("War of the Irish with the Foreigners"), refers to a woman known as the "Red Lady" leading a Viking fleet in a raid on Belfast in the 10th century.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

There's a lot of uncertainty, said Neil Price, an archaeology professor at Uppsala University in Sweden who has written extensively about the Vikings. The text in the "Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh" that refers to the Red Lady is of debatable accuracy, Price told Live Science in an email.

He suspects that Viking women fought in battle but not frequently. In addition, "female warriors were probably a very small minority," Price said.

A modern-day reenactment depicting Viking warriors.

The account written by Saxo Grammaticus is also contentious. Thomas Kristian Heebøll-Holm, a history professor at the University of Southern Denmark, said Saxo Grammaticus is not a reliable source.

"Saxo Grammaticus does write about female warriors, but only in the parts of his work concerned [with] the legendary past of Denmark," Heebøll-Holm told Live Science in an email. "Furthermore, these writings are not accurate, but moral and fictitious," Heebøll-Holm said, noting that, in some instances, Saxo Grammaticus seemed to be drawing on the stories of the Amazons, a group of legendary female warriors whom the ancient Greeks believed in with stories about them dating back more than 2,500 years.

Archaeological evidence can also be challenging to interpret. Archaeologists know of about 30 Viking Age female burials containing weapons, including three with swords in Scandinavia. Even more Viking Age women's graves have items that could have been used as weapons ‪—‬ including spears, axes and knives ‪—‬ although these tools also could have been used for hunting or tending to farms. Either way, we can't be sure if these women fought in battle.

"The first concern is that the weapons were really used by the deceased and were not merely included as signs of special status or social rank acquired through inheritance," Deborah Shepherd, an independent researcher who holds a doctorate in archaeology and has studied the Vikings extensively, told Live Science in an email. She noted that graves are often not well preserved, making it difficult to gather information.

This 1889 illustration shows a grave at Birka in Sweden. It is now known that the person buried with war-grade weapons and riding gear is a woman.

There were likely "some few female warriors, but they were probably only found in the highest ranking families, and their warrior career was probably short-lived," Shepherd said. "They wouldn't have fought in the great armies of later centuries but possibly did fight in pre-Christian skirmishes." (The Vikings began gradually converting to Christianity between the ninth and 12th centuries.)

There is at least one known case of a Viking woman found with what may be combat-related injuries. A Viking woman found in Solør, Norway, had a head injury consistent with a sword strike. She was 18 or 19 at the time she died, was buried with weapons and lived around 900.

Ole Kastholm, a curator and senior researcher at the Roskilde Museum in Denmark, said there is a lot of uncertainty regarding how frequently Viking Age women fought in battle.

Weapons "do occur as a grave good in a handful of graves with female human remains," Kastholm told Live Science in an email. "Often it is just a single weapon [such] as a spear or [a] battle axe. But we know of at least one example of a female grave with a full set of weapons as well as riding equipment," which is located in Birka, Sweden.

"If this was a man's grave, researchers would have no doubt that it was a warrior grave, and this explanation must necessarily also apply when the interred is a woman," Kastholm said.

That said, there were female warriors in other cultures. "One can also note in passing that female warriors were an almost common feature of central Asian societies for at least a millennium before the Viking Age," Price wrote in his book, "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026).

For instance the Scythians are a people who flourished in eastern Europe and Asia and Scythian women have been found buried with horses and weapons. In some cases, the Scythian women suffered combat wounds such as arrowheads and it's been speculated that they may have been an inspiration for stories of the Amazons.

He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6312. Our increasingly cluttered skies

In the 2013 movie Gravity, Russia destroys its own spy satellite with a missile, creating a cloud of shrapnel and subsequent orbital collisions that rip apart spaceships and astronauts alike. Earth orbit is a place where life imitates art: Eight years later, Moscow launched an actual missile strike on a defunct Soviet satellite, blasting thousands of pieces of metal through space and threatening the International Space Station (ISS) at the nearby altitude of 250 miles (400 kilometers). As the lethal grapeshot sped through space 10 times faster than a rifle bullet, astronauts and cosmonauts huddled in escape pods. Luckily, the debris overshot them, avoiding a real-life Gravity sequel.

This close call was not a lone event. In 2009, history’s first collision between two intact satellites — an American Iridium 33 and a defunct Russian Cosmos-2251 — generated at least 2,000 pieces of debris, some of which passed on uncertain trajectories about 7 miles (11.3 km) from the ISS in March 2012 as crew sheltered in two docked Soyuz craft. And just last year, Chinese crew aboard the Tiangong space station delayed their return to Earth and left their replacements temporarily without an evacuation vehicle when a piece of space junk smaller than 0.04 inch (1 millimeter) hit their docked return capsule. Fallout from these incidents remains in orbit today, along with myriad debris from other adventures. These fragments are collectively known as space junk.

Scientists warn that space junk may be fast approaching a critical threshold that sparks cascading satellite collisions, creating an impassable belt of debris and rendering that region of Earth orbit too dangerous to use. This is called Kessler syndrome, a concept outlined in a 1978 paper by NASA researcher Donald Kessler. Surpassing that threshold is not inevitable, but avoiding it will require considerable engineering and stringent international cooperation.

The most crowded area of space is occupied by the lowest stable Earth orbits, where the equivalent mass of 150 space shuttles currently spins around our planet. Called low Earth orbit (LEO), it is loosely defined as altitudes between 120 miles and 1,200 miles (200 to 2,000 km). LEO is so frequently used because it is the Goldilocks zone where a complete orbit takes two hours or less — high enough to minimize atmospheric drag and stay aloft, yet low enough in the magnetosphere to help shield humans and electronics from radiation damage.

Large constellations of satellites are now being put into LEO. The most numerous of these is SpaceX’s Starlink, whose 10,000+ satellites comprise 66% of LEO traffic. Each rocket carries several dozen satellites weighing as much as a ton each and spanning up to 23 feet (7 meters), providing internet support for remote locations. When they fail, most will reenter the atmosphere and burn up, either within a few weeks of launch if they fail in the initial low orbit, or if they successfully push to their intended higher orbit, within a few years.

But the rate at which LEO is filling up — Starlink had 122 launches in 2025 alone — has some experts worried that we are on the cusp of eventual calamity. “We might not see a substantial change during our own generation, but we will see a steady increase in risks and collisions,” says Hugh Lewis, a University of Birmingham astronautics professor.

Ever since SpaceX launched its first batch of Starlink satellites in 2019, the company has touted its satellites’ avoidance capabilities: Ion-propelled thrusters and autonomous AI guidance systems trigger a Starlink satellite to maneuver away from an object ahead of a close pass if the risk of a collision exceeds a certain threshold. While the industry standard is to maneuver if there is a 1-in-10,000 chance of a collision, SpaceX has tightened its trigger over the years. Today, Starlink satellites take avoiding action if the likelihood of colliding is just 1 in 3.3 million. Based on the current rate of avoidance maneuvers as reported by the company in July 2026, the constellation’s satellites overall are performing more than 400,000 avoidance maneuvers per year.

With other companies and countries joining the LEO space boom — and a lack of coordination between them — SpaceX has taken further action to safeguard its fleet. The company announced in January that it was shifting the bulk of its satellites 13% lower than their original 340-mile (550 km) altitude in large part to reduce aggregate risk, as there are fewer objects that low to collide with. Additionally, lower initial orbits mean failed satellites will naturally deorbit more quickly, preventing them from becoming part of the problem.

OneWeb, a European broadband internet service, sends its satellites to a higher altitude of 750 miles (1,200 km). Because atmospheric drag decreases exponentially with altitude, higher satellites shed drag and gain longevity. But this can generate longer-lasting space junk in the event of failure: At the altitude OneWeb operates, an object could stay in orbit for centuries.

Both OneWeb and Starlink use their own propulsion to deorbit for post-mission disposal, with satellites lasting roughly five years. But if those systems fail, the satellites become space junk, with their orbital altitude determining their longevity.

While operators work to keep space debris in check, external factors can complicate their efforts, either causing orbiting objects to come down prematurely or else increasing the time they’re likely to stay in orbit, crowding the field.

Climate change can cause the latter. When solar photons hit carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, the molecules release energy as infrared heat. The troposphere, the atmospheric layer closest to the ground, is sufficiently dense to trap that heat, causing global warming. But higher up, the atmosphere is so thin that radiation escapes, cooling and thinning the mesosphere, our atmosphere’s middle layer. Excessive greenhouse gases can accelerate this process, causing successive atmospheric layers to pancake downward, reducing drag at any given altitude.

According to a study by Lewis’ team, this means satellites that were expected to come down in a couple of years could stay up much longer, quintupling the lifetime of some space debris by the end of this century.

Solar activity has the opposite effect. “In the critical range of 300 to 500 kilometers [190 to 310 miles], the density of the atmosphere is very dependent on whether we’re at solar maximum or solar minimum,” says Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist formerly at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and now based in the U.K. His decades-long dedication to developing software that catalogs and tracks all rocket launches and reentries has gained him a reputation as the unofficial guru of space traffic and space junk. Each 11-year solar maximum brings an increase in X-ray flux, which ionizes the atmosphere and causes heating, so the atmosphere expands. This, in turn, pushes denser gases higher, increasing drag at the height of LEO. Both effects cause orbiting objects to reenter sooner.

For higher LEO satellites, McDowell says, the question isn’t how many years they are designed to stay in orbit, but how many solar maxima they can survive. For example, the Hubble Space Telescope suffers a pronounced loss of altitude each solar maximum, each bigger than the last as the observatory drops lower and the atmospheric density is greater. Without intervention, it could come down in the next solar maximum.

In a paper accepted for publication in Acta Astronautica, a team led by Samantha Lawler, an astronomer at the University of Regina in Saskatchewan, created a “CRASH clock” characterizing the time it would take for a collision to occur in the absence of all avoidance maneuvers — say, during a “widespread disruptive event” such as a solar storm or massive software failure. (CRASH is an acronym for Collision Realization And Significant Harm.) Once an initial collision takes place, it could cause further, ongoing damage as its debris goes on to spark yet more strikes. Initial calculations based on 2018 satellite traffic allowed 164 days before collisions under the worst circumstances, but as Starlink and other megaconstellations have proliferated, recent calculations bring the countdown to a shocking three days.

While most of the public’s attention is on lower LEO orbits occupied by Starlink, higher LEO altitudes may soon become more crowded as well. SpaceX recently submitted an application to the Federal Communications Commission for space-based data centers with 1 million satellites orbiting much higher than its Starlink fleet. The heavier electrical load of a data center will require vast solar panels and cooling fins, considerably larger than on Starlink satellites. These would also be much more reflective than Starlink, which is already posing serious headaches for astronomers by interfering with observations. But data centers at these altitudes could also create space-junk minefields.

To sustain its million-satellite data center, SpaceX would have to launch about 200,000 satellites each year. If 1% of those fail — the same rate that SpaceX reports for Starlink satellites — “you’re replacing 2,000 satellites a year,” says Lewis. “Those failed satellites alone would meet the critical Kessler threshold, without even looking at the million satellites” making up the functional constellation itself.

Even higher orbits are not immune. Above LEO lies medium Earth orbit (MEO), from 1,240 to 22,000 miles (2,000 to 35,400 km), home to many GPS and navigation satellites. Beyond that sits high Earth orbit (HEO), including geostationary orbit (GEO) directly above Earth’s equator, where satellites sit with 24-hour periods that match Earth’s own rotation. In January, a Russian spy satellite unexpectedly fragmented in an HEO graveyard orbit. The event could have been caused by an impact, suggesting that space junk is infecting even the highest altitudes as well.

The route to addressing orbital crowding requires determining where solutions are most needed. And LEO remains the area most urgently in need of emergency triage. Astronautical engineer Darren McKnight, senior technical officer for LeoLabs, a company that helps coordinate a global network of about a dozen ground-based radars tracking space objects, worries most about LEO orbits above where Starlink — with its state-of-the-art crash-avoidance technology — operates. “I would say that right now we have a contraction of the arteries at about 975 kilometers [600 miles], and if we have a heart attack, it’s going to happen there,” he says.

In the 1970s and ’80s, countries launching spacecraft left rocket bodies and payloads in higher LEO. These large objects have no crash-avoidance capabilities. But this concentration of threats also creates opportunities for reducing risk. “If you take out the 10 worst offenders at 840 and 975 kilometers [520 and 600 miles], you can reduce debris-generating potential by 30%,” McKnight says. These altitudes were two distinct orbital highways historically favored for different missions. Of those top offenders, three are defunct satellites (one European and two Russian) and the rest are rocket stages (one Japanese, two Chinese, one Russian, and three Soviet). That space junk lingers for more than a quarter-century and has the potential to generate even more debris when it is hit, compounding the problem over time. That’s why, McKnight says, removing those worst offenders also offers “much better return on investment” when it comes to resources spent on space junk mitigation — that is, reducing or even retrieving space junk.

Such efforts are gaining traction, but still have a long way to go. Some are managed by national space agencies solely for the purposes of cleaning up their trash, while others are undertaken by private companies purely for profit.

Yet the only true mitigation of space junk to date was in 2022, when the Chinese Shijian-21 satellite retrieved and towed a defunct Beidou-2 G2 navigation satellite from crowded geostationary orbit and parked it in a graveyard orbit 1,865 miles (3,000 km) higher to reduce the risk of collisions. More recently, in 2025, the Shijian-25 satellite launched and docked with fuel-depleted Shijian-21, likely to test refueling capability to prolong its operational lifetime and prevent it from becoming space junk itself. U.S. Space Force officials labeled the maneuver a “priority watch” event due to its potential military use.

Japan-based Astroscale has flown two test missions in LEO that have rendezvoused with targets; its next mission aims to retrieve a OneWeb communications satellite slated for retirement. Other players include Switzerland-based ClearSpace, which is partnering with the European Space Agency, and TransAstra, an aspiring asteroid-mining company based in California. TransAstra has conducted preliminary tests aboard the ISS with a novel capture bag and hopes to launch in 2028 to snag a 100-ton asteroid. That same technology could be adapted for space junk retrieval, especially smaller debris.

For McDowell, the astronomer and spaceflight historian, the satellite boom brings mixed feelings. He wonders if satellite-cluttered skies mean all serious astronomical observing will one day only be done from space telescopes, rather than ground-based observatories. “I am a fan of space exploration,” he says, “but I want us to do it sustainably, in a way that doesn’t trash the environment.”

There is a long way to go. But with the space industry soaring to a value of more than $600 billion, some see the clutter in its wake as an opportunity to profit from clearing space debris out of harm’s way.

Though the sky may be falling, the same genius that placed it there has the capacity to fix it.

Randall Hyman is a science writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including Nature, Science, and Smithsonian.

NASA's Swift Observatory went out in a blaze of glory this week, but it left behind millions of images of the universe that could fuel discoveries for decades.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory fell out of space, burning up in the sky over Sumatra. It was a fitting, fiery end for a telescope that spent 22 years studying the most powerful explosions in the universe — and, even with Swift gone, its observations will continue to feed scientific curiosity for years to come.

Swift's most important contributions to astronomy are not exactly eye candy. Designed to swivel toward deep-space explosions at a moment's notice, Swift excelled at capturing bright, fleeting and faraway specks of light. The multiwavelength observatory was equipped with optical, ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray instruments, allowing it to catch cosmic bursts of energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, zeroing in on flares of light that other telescopes might miss.

One of its most significant detections was a gamma-ray burst — an incredibly bright blast, likely emitted by a giant star as it exploded in a supernova before collapsing into a black hole. Swift's famous image of GRB 221009A, or the BOAT ‪—‬ short for "brightest of all time" ‪—‬ looks like a speckled orange bull's-eye, caused by waves from the explosion rippling across space.

How the Swift Observatory saw the gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A, which may be the most energetic emission of this kind ever seen.

But Swift also took millions of observations of the nearby universe, including galaxies in our backyard. One of its most jaw-dropping images is this 24-hour exposure of the Andromeda galaxy (M31), located about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

Andromeda is the closest major galaxy to ours, and it may be destined for a shared fate. Scientists suspect that Andromeda and the Milky Way are drawing closer together and might eventually collide. The merger would add Andromeda's roughly 1 trillion stars to our sky, though there probably wouldn't be any life left on Earth to appreciate it.

In Swift's view of our encroaching neighbor, captured with the observatory's ultraviolet instrument, tens of thousands of Andromeda's stars shine like sapphires set in a sparkling ring.

According to NASA, the observatory detected some 20,000 ultraviolet light sources in this image, captured over two months from May to July 2008. These sources include thousands of dense, hot star clusters scattered across Andromeda's 150,000-light-year-wide ring, as well as the distant galaxy M32 (seen as a bright orb of light to the bottom right of Andromeda's center).

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In visible-light images of Andromeda taken with ground-based telescopes, the galaxy's bright center bleaches out many of the fiery young stars that emerge in Swift's view. While Swift likely won't be remembered best for shimmering starscapes like this one, it's a powerful reminder that looking at familiar structures in a new light can change everything.
