#6310. SpaceX goes for a Starship double catch

On Monday, Nov. 9, SpaceX is targeting 10:03 p.m. EST to launch USSF-627 on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The mission is a classified payload for the U.S. Space Force. The booster will aim for the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

On Wednesday, Nov. 11, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) is targeting 6:40 a.m. EST for a Long March 2D launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed.

On Thursday, Nov. 12, ExPace, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), is targeting 2:50 p.m. EST for a Kuaizhou 11 launch from Jiuquan, according to Next Spaceflight. Kuaizhou 11 is a solid-fueled rocket designed for fast-turnaround launches of small satellites. Its payload is also undisclosed.

Later Thursday, Nov. 12, SpaceX returns to Vandenberg at 11:23 p.m. EST for USSF-317, another classified Space Force mission on a Falcon 9. The booster is again slated to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Friday, Nov. 13, United Launch Alliance (ULA) is targeting 12:54 p.m. EST for Vulcan Leo 1 from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The launch ends a nine-month grounding that followed a nozzle failure during February’s USSF-87 mission; ULA says the boosters now carry a redesigned nozzle. It’s also Vulcan’s first flight for Amazon, carrying 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the broadband megaconstellation formerly known as Project Kuiper.

Later Friday, Nov. 13, SpaceX opens a 75-minute window at 5:45 p.m. EST for Starship Flight 15 from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. It’s the 15th test flight of the company’s reusable megarocket and only its second trip to orbit, after Flight 14’s success in September. About six and a half minutes after liftoff, the Super Heavy booster should return to the launch tower and be caught by its chopstick arms. SpaceX has made that catch before with the rocket’s V1 and V2 boosters, but this will be a first for the new V3 booster. The upper stage, called Ship, will continue to orbit and release 26 of SpaceX’s next-generation Starlink V3 satellites as it did in September.

You can watch the launch live on SpaceX’s website.

The next day, SpaceX will try to catch Ship, too. Until now, Ship’s test flights have ended with a practice landing at sea where the vehicle flips upright, fires its engines, and sets down on the water. This time, after about 14 orbits at roughly 171 miles (275 km) up — a flight of more than 22 hours — Ship must run that same landing maneuver over Starbase, settling into the tower’s arms instead.

SpaceX says Ship will head for the tower only if flight controllers confirm that every system it needs for the catch is prepared. If not, the company can bring Ship down at preplanned spots in the Pacific, with checks built into the flight for splashdowns near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile. If the catch works, Starship will become the first orbital rocket ever recovered in full. On Saturday, Nov. 14, Rocket Lab is targeting 12:30 a.m. EST for The Mountain God Rises, the 100th launch of its Electron rocket, from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula. Electron will deploy a QPS-SAR satellite for the Japanese company iQPS in Rocket Lab’s 11th dedicated launch for the operator. The iQPS constellation uses synthetic aperture radar (SAR), bouncing microwaves off the ground to map Earth’s surface even through rain, smoke, and total darkness.

On Monday, Nov. 2, Rocket Lab launched The Sea God Surveys from New Zealand at 11:41 a.m. EST, delivering another QPS-SAR radar satellite for iQPS. It was Electron’s 99th flight and Rocket Lab’s 10th mission for the Japanese operator. That evening at 7:15 p.m. EST, CAS Space’s Kinetica 2 lifted off from Jiuquan and placed 18 satellites for China’s SpaceSail broadband constellation in polar orbit. It was only the rocket’s second flight, following its debut in March.

On Thursday, Nov. 5, a Long March 2C launched from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China with three Yaogan 51 satellites. Yaogan is the label China gives its government Earth-observation spacecraft, which are widely believed to perform military reconnaissance.

Friday, Nov. 6, brought two launches about an hour apart. Galactic Energy’s Ceres 2 put four satellites in orbit from Jiuquan at 6:37 p.m. EST. Then, after several days of delays, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-432 mission from Vandenberg at 7:48 p.m. EST, landing the booster on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Saturday, Nov. 7, Russia’s Aerospace Forces launched a Soyuz-2.1b from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in northern Russia. The payload is believed to be a GLONASS satellite for Russia’s version of GPS. The week closed Sunday, Nov. 8, when a Long March 12 lifted off from the Wenchang commercial launch site on Hainan Island at 3:24 p.m. EST, carrying nine more satellites for Guowang, China’s state-run internet megaconstellation.

On Friday, Nov. 20, CASC is targeting 6:00 a.m. EST for a Long March 8A launch from Wenchang, likely carrying another batch of Guowang satellites, according to Next Spaceflight.

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 2:00 a.m. EST, a Long March 12 is slated to fly another Guowang group from Wenchang, according to Next Spaceflight.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6309. You Could Hire a Magician to Find Your Lost Stuff 400 Years Ago. The Real Danger Was If They Failed.

Service magicians known as “cunning folk” tracked down stolen goods with sieves and shears—until a spell went wrong.

Christabel Robyns was only trying to find some spoons and a pewter jug. In 1629, there were no smartphones or microchips to track lost items and no hidden cameras to play back video of how they vanished. Instead, Robyns, a widow, is thought to have turned to a more unusual way of getting her belongings back: magic. Word apparently got around, because she soon found herself accused of witchcraft and facing possible death by hanging.

Hers was hardly the only case of someone, especially a woman, being suspected of dabbling in the dark arts. In an age without modern technology, people with problems often turned to “cunning folk,” also known as service magicians, who used their own forms of magic to help. Some were healers or diviners. Others had a knack for finding lost or stolen objects. Whether Robyns was one of these cunning folk is unclear, but she must have either hired one or used magic herself, because she ended up before Ignatius Jurdain, a magistrate known for his rigid religious views. By then, courts across most of England had become skeptical of witchcraft accusations and were lenient toward the accused. Exeter retained its anti-witchcraft fanaticism.

That is where historian Mark Stoyle of the University of Southampton comes in. Stoyle was born and raised in Exeter and has long been fascinated by centuries-old accusations of the occult. His research shows that Robyns was saved when the chief justice of the Court of King’s Bench stepped in and sent her case to a higher court outside Exeter. She escaped with her life, but many others prosecuted on little more than hearsay weren’t as lucky. In Exeter, even service magicians, who were usually seen as harmless, were at risk, especially when their magic failed. That’s what happened to John Blachett in 1666, when a client hired him to find a lost hood. Blachett insisted the hood was in a neighbor’s house, but a search turned up nothing, and the client reported him. He was tried for “certain devilish and hateful arts” but, fortunately for him, wasn’t convicted.

“The city of Exeter possesses the grim distinction of being the last place in England in which people are known to have been executed for the crime of witchcraft,” Stoyle wrote in a study published in History: The Journal of the Historical Association. He also recently published the second edition of his book Witchcraft in Exeter, 1558–1666.

Executions for witchcraft in Exeter are traditionally said to have ended in 1685 with the hanging of Alice Molland. However, no record of her execution has been found, and Stoyle has argued that a court clerk may have misspelled her name, writing “Alicia” instead of “Avicia,” or Avis. Local archives record an Avis Molland who died in 1693, eight years after “Alice” was supposedly hanged. If Stoyle is right, England’s last executions for witchcraft took place three years earlier, in 1682. That year, Temperance Lloyd, Susanna Edwards and Mary Trembles, known as the “Bideford Witches,” were hanged at Heavitree, then a parish on the outskirts of Exeter. Sometimes simply being near a person considered suspicious was enough to seal someone’s fate. Long before germ theory, people who fell ill and died soon after meeting such a person were often thought to have been bewitched.

Society’s outcasts were frequent targets, too. Edwards, Lloyd, and Trembles were poor, living on parish relief and whatever scraps they could find. Each was also unmarried, widowed or abandoned, and a woman living alone was already viewed with suspicion. If someone fell ill with smallpox after meeting or even passing such a woman, she could end up in a prison cell awaiting a trial that might end in a death sentence. Female cunning folk faced particular danger in Exeter, because their work was easily mistaken for witchcraft. In 1642, a client hired Anne King, a weaver’s wife, to find out who had stolen a purse. King balanced a sieve on a pair of shears and recited suspects’ names, and the sieve turned when she said the name Marie Matthews. King herself was then reported and arrested for witchcraft, but she was released on bail and survived.

In most of England, cunning folk went about their business while the authorities looked the other way. Stoyle’s research in the archives, however, shows that they often met a hostile reception in Exeter, where the outcomes for accused witches were sometimes recorded in court documents. A conviction was marked “culpabilis,” meaning “guilty,” followed by “susp.,” short for the Latin “suspensus,” meaning “hanged.” Burial records sometimes confirm these executions. One such case was Thomasin Short, whose name appears with several different spellings. She had been arrested again and again as a “scold,” an unruly woman who constantly criticized others and picked fights. Short is said to have shouted a dark threat at a family that then suffered several deaths. She was found guilty of witchcraft, and her court record is marked “susp.”

“The particular sets of circumstances which resulted in Shorte…being hanged when a number of other supposed Exeter witches managed to escape that fate can only be guessed at,” said Stoyle. He suspects that an outburst of “popular rage,” combined with what seemed to be unimpeachable evidence, “...eventually persuaded the judges to hand down a death sentence.”

Today, finding a lost spoon takes nothing more than a look under the couch cushions, but in 17th-century Exeter, searching the wrong way could cost a woman her life.

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.
